articles.title: Ukraine war latest: St. Petersburg slammed by drones in mass Ukrainian attack
articles.body:
Key developments on Oct. 17-18
- Massive Ukrainian drone attack hits oil facility, bridge, and data center in St. Petersburg
- US resumes intel sharing on Russian missile launches with Ukraine, Zelensky says
- Ukraine hits Russian drone manufacturing plant in Rostov Oblast
- 'Planned operation' — Zelensky confirms Ukraine's Starlink access not fully restored
- Russia launches 'one of its largest attacks' on Ukraine's energy grid
Ukrainian forces struck an oil terminal, a data center, and a bridge in a large-scale overnight attack on St. Petersburg on Oct. 18, Russian officials and media reported.
Ukrainian drones hit the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal and a data center belonging to Russia's largest social media platform VK, formerly known as VKontakte.
VK confirmed that a drone had attacked its data center, saying its services remained operational. However, users reported disruptions across the social network and its affiliated platforms, according to Downdetector, a service that tracks online outages.
Russian e-commerce giant Ozon reported a drone attack on one of its logistics centers.
Ozon said some orders may be canceled as deliveries are rerouted to other logistics centers. The company is one of Russia's largest e-commerce platforms and a major rival of Wildberries, often dubbed "Russia's Amazon."
Aleksandr Drozdenko, governor of Leningrad Oblast, said 127 Ukrainian drones were shot down over the region. Drone debris damaged four cars in a parking lot, while fires were reported at several locations.
St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed the attack, reporting fires at the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses in the Kolpinsky District. According to Beglov, one person was killed and five others injured, while 12 apartment buildings and two houses were damaged.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the targets or the extent of the damage at the time of publication.
Ukrainian monitoring channels Exilenova+ and Supernova+ reported that the "massive" drone attack began at 2:50 a.m. local time.
Eyewitness footage shared by St. Petersburg residents appeared to show Ukrainian drones flying over the city as Russian air defense systems operated.
Large explosions lit up the night sky in the city of 5.6 million people, located 850 kilometers (530 miles) north of the Ukrainian border.
Numerous videos appeared to show the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal engulfed in flames. Located in the city's port, the facility is one of Russia's largest fuel storage and export facilities.
It receives and ships petroleum products by river, rail, and road, with a reported annual throughput of 12.5 million tons.
read also
US resumes intel sharing on Russian missile launches with Ukraine, Zelensky says
The United States has resumed sharing intelligence about incoming Russian ballistic missiles with Ukraine after a pause lasting several days, President Volodymyr Zelensky told NBC News' "Meet the Press" in an interview published on Oct. 18.
"Only the United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky said.
The U.S. provides Ukraine with intelligence to help its military detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats. Zelensky said the issue had since been resolved and thanked Washington for restoring intelligence sharing.
"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Now it works."
Zelensky also expressed hope that talks with the U.S. could take place next week, despite the ongoing difficulties between Kyiv and Washington.
"I'm very open to this, even with all the difficult circumstances," he said, estimating that a meeting could take place on Oct. 20-21.
The resumption of intelligence sharing follows a Russian missile attack on Kyiv on Oct. 12, when five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital, causing "massive explosions." Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
A senior Ukrainian official previously told the Kyiv Independent that Ukraine's military leadership contacted its U.S. counterparts after the strike to clarify what had happened.
"They say they didn't cut it off, but they didn't warn us (about the attack) either," the official said. "The Americans said they just didn't see (the launch)... That's a weak excuse."
read also
Ukraine hits Russian drone manufacturing plant in Rostov Oblast
Ukraine's General Staff reported on Oct. 17 that Ukrainian forces struck a Russian military drone manufacturing plant in Rostov Oblast the day before.
According to the report, the strike targeted a production and storage facility belonging to Roboavia, a company that develops and manufactures drones for the Russian military, near the settlement of Lenina in Rostov Oblast.
Among the drones it produces are the Sarych, which uses video and thermal imaging equipment for surveillance, and the Klin, a loitering munition designed to strike targets, according to Ukraine's military intelligence agency.
Roboavia is linked to Russia's Era Military Innovation Complex, a Defense Ministry project focused on developing military technology.
The General Staff said the strike was intended to interfere with drone production and deliveries to Russian forces. The extent of the damage and its result on operations remains unconfirmed.
The military also reported that Ukrainian forces struck a logistics warehouse used by a Russian missile brigade near Latyshi in Bryansk Oblast on Oct. 12.
The Ukrainian military said the strikes were aimed at aimed at disrupting UAV production and supply to Russian forces.
read also
'Planned operation' — Zelensky confirms Ukraine's Starlink access not fully restored
Speed caps on Starlink operations in Ukraine remain in place, hindering efforts to counter Russian jet-powered drones, President Zelensky said on Oct. 17.
Ukraine first experienced malfunctions with Starshield terminals — the militarized version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet system — on Oct. 14, when they began losing connectivity as they approached a certain speed.
While Ukraine reported that connectivity was restored by the next day, Zelensky now confirmed that a speed limit of 161 kilometers per hour remains in place.
"Some of our interceptor drones use Starlink to intercept the enemy's fast-moving jet-powered drones," Zelensky said.
But with the current speed cap, Ukrainian interceptor drones cannot down Russian jet-powered drones, the president said, adding that Ukraine "thankfully" also uses other anti-drone air defenses.
The disruptions also complicate other military operations, as some drones rely on Starlink to deliver food, water, and other equipment to soldiers in front-line positions, he added.
The unexpected throttling of Starlink systems sparked a debate about who made the decision, with media reports linking it to SpaceX owner Elon Musk or the White House.
The move came as Ukraine-U.S. ties plummeted with Trump concluding a diesel deal with Russia and publicly lambasting Zelensky.
The Ukrainian president confirmed that Kyiv received no warning about the restrictions and has been trying to clarify the issue with U.S. authorities and SpaceX.
Ukraine has either received no response from U.S. channels or has been told the problems stem from "technical issues," Zelensky said, dismissing that explanation.
He called the restrictions a "planned operation" targeting Ukraine, noting that the speed limits remain in effect in Ukraine but not in EU countries.
Kyiv sent several vehicles equipped with its Starlink devices to the EU for testing, where they exceeded the speed limit in place in Ukraine, he explained. The president added that European partners are already working on a possible alternative to Starlink.
read also
Russia launches 'one of its largest attacks' on Ukraine's energy grid as US 'disregards' Graham's sanctions, Zelensky says
Russian attacks against Ukraine killed seven people and injured around 90 over the past day, regional authorities said on Oct. 17, with the country reporting one of the heaviest Russian attacks against energy infrastructure so far.
Ukrainian forces downed 289 out of the 332 drones, including jet-powered attack drones, launched by Russia overnight, the Air Force reported. Russian drones and ballistic missiles of the Iskander-M or the North Korean KN-23 model struck 22 different locations, and debris fell in three areas, according to the statement.
The attacks came as Russia continued its campaign against Ukraine's energy grid ahead of winter. Attacks on energy facilities across the country overnight and on the morning of Oct. 17 left some homes without power, the Energy Ministry said.
President Zelensky described Russia's latest attack as "one of the largest strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure." Russian forces targeted more than 15 key power generation and transmission facilities across Ukraine, he said.
"At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelensky said on social media, calling on Washington to pressure Moscow through a "sanctions blackout."
"Financial rewards for (Russian President Vladimir) Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground."

articles.title: Zelenskyy Says Russia Seeking Blackout In Ukraine After Latest Onslaught On Energy Facilities
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian strikes targeted energy facilities in multiple regions, leaving thousands of households without electricity, as Ukrainian and Russian officials reported civilian deaths following drone attacks on October 18.
"Russia is not taking steps toward peace," Zelenskyy wrote on social media, adding that the Russian military had carried out 76 attacks on Ukraine's energy and oil and gas sectors in the week since US President Donald Trump unilaterally announced an energy cease-fire on social media.
Trump, who made ending Russia's war against Ukraine a priority when he began his current term, said on October 11 that he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to observe a weeklong pause in attacks on energy infrastructure amid cold weather in Ukraine.
Trump's announcement came after he and Putin had earlier agreed to a deal that would send Russian diesel to world markets. The move was sharply criticized by Kyiv, its European allies, and supporters of Ukraine in the United States, who said it could funnel more funds into Moscow's war effort.
During the week, however, Putin, who Russian media said was visiting a command post, ordered the Russian military to continue its "massive and coordinated" strikes against targets in Ukraine.
"Over the past week, Russia launched nearly 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs, and 66 missiles at Ukraine, most of them ballistic missiles," Zelenskyy wrote on social media on October 18.
Accusing Moscow of seeking to plunge Ukraine into a nationwide blackout, Zelenskyy said that just overnight power stations were targeted in the Vinnytsya, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskiy, and Odesa regions. Local authorities reported power outages following the strikes.
Moscow has previously sought to pressure Kyiv into accepting its hard-line demands by attacking the country's energy infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid freezing temperatures.
On October 18, Russian attacks killed at least two people and injured several others across the country, Ukrainian officials said.
In the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhya, a 27-year-old woman was killed and two people were injured, including a 6-year-old girl, according to the regional military administration. The attacks damaged two apartment buildings, 18 cars, and an educational institution.
In the central city of Poltava, a Russian drone attack killed one woman and injured four other people, the head of the city's military administration, Vitaliy Dyakivnych, said on Telegram. Nine residential buildings were damaged, some by falling drone debris.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia had launched 180 combat drones during the overnight attacks, of which 152 were intercepted. Impacts were recorded at 20 locations, it said.
Russia Reports Casualties, Infrastructure Damage
With a fifth wartime winter approaching, Russian strikes on Ukraine have become a daily occurrence.
Since this year, however, Kyiv has increasingly responded to Russian attacks with a campaign of long-range strikes targeting military and energy sites inside Russia and middle-range strikes targeting its key logistics in Ukraine's occupied eastern and southern regions.
Trump has repeatedly called on Ukraine to halt its strikes on Russian refineries, blaming those attacks -- and not the decreased energy flows from the Middle East resulting from the US-Israeli war with Iran -- for high diesel fuel prices.
Following Trump's latest such call last week, Zelenskyy appeared to support halting the strikes but said he expected Moscow to do the same. However, as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy sites continued, the Ukrainian president said Kyiv was "done" with unilaterally pausing its own.
On October 18, the governor of St. Petersburg, Russia's second-largest city, Aleksandr Beglov, reported that fires broke out at the city's oil terminal, an oil depot, and industrial warehouses following a Ukrainian drone attack. He said one person was killed and five others were injured.
Separately, Russian e-commerce company Ozon said a drone struck one of its logistics facilities in St. Petersburg, causing a fire. Employees were evacuated, and no one was injured at the facility, the company said.
Ukraine has accused some of Russia's largest online shopping platforms of distributing military supplies, including dual-use goods such as body armor and surveillance technology.
As Russia has recently stepped up attacks on Ukrainian data centers and telecommunications infrastructure, causing internet outages in some regions of the country, Kyiv has also vowed to mirror Moscow's tactics.
On October 18, the VK Internet company said its data center in the Leningrad region had been targeted by drones, but its services remained available to users as normal.
Separately, a drone struck a cable-stayed bridge forming part of St. Petersburg's Western High-Speed Diameter highway. The extent of the damage was not immediately clear.
The attacks also caused power disruptions in parts of the region. Two transformer substations in Yanino were reportedly disconnected, while operations at St. Petersburg's Pulkovo Airport were disrupted.
Russia's Defense Ministry said air defense units had downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight. The figure could not be independently verified.
Drone attacks also disrupted air travel across Russia. More than 350 flights were delayed or canceled at Moscow's four airports overnight on October 17, as authorities imposed restrictions amid reported Ukrainian drone attacks on the Moscow region.
The figures were based on airport departure and arrival boards reviewed by the independent Russian outlet Meduza.
Sheremetyevo was the worst affected, with 143 flights canceled and 53 delayed. Vnukovo recorded 55 cancellations and 113 delays, while Domodedovo reported 59 delayed flights. Some flights bound for Moscow were diverted to other cities, including St. Petersburg and Nizhny Novgorod.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said Russian air defenses had destroyed 75 drones heading toward the capital. Russia's Defense Ministry said more than 600 drones had been destroyed or intercepted across the country overnight.
Airports in Penza, Saratov, and Sochi also suspended operations.
Kyiv Says Starshield Connections Still Limited
The latest barrage on Ukraine came as disruptions to the Starshield satellite system, the military-grade version of the Starlink service run by Elon Musk's SpaceX, left Ukraine particularly vulnerable earlier in the week.
On October 18, Zelenskyy said the speed of Starshield connections across Ukrainian territory remained significantly limited. "Of course technically it's not a mistake. It's limited because it's a decision. Who made this decision? I don't know," he said in an interview with NBC News.
According to the Ukrainian officials the move has been causing instability in battlefield communications, medium-range strikes, and the operation of interceptor drones.
"The shortage of air defense systems, combined with the lack of confirmation that Starshield's full operational capabilities have been restored, creates additional challenges for Ukraine in protecting critical infrastructure against Russian aerial attacks," Denys Sienik, Ukraine's charge d'affaires to the United States, told RFE/RL.
Alongside the diesel deal with Russia and delays in already scarce ballistic missile interceptors, Starlink disruptions in Ukraine appeared to be Washington's latest move to pressure Kyiv into an unfavorable deal with Russia, Zelenskyy told Bloomberg on October 18.
"I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate," he said. "I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war" against Russia "could be ended sooner at Ukraine’s expense. But that’s how it looks."
Earlier in the day, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected claims that the United States had deliberately restricted Ukraine's access to Starlink, the satellite Internet service operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX.
"No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down Internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it," he told reporters on October 17 as he prepared to depart for Central Asia, calling reports of US involvement "categorically false."
Rubio said his understanding was that Starlink's performance had returned to its previous level. He also questioned the Ukrainian president's account of the incident, saying he was "not sure Zelenskyy knows what he's talking about."
Rubio distinguished Starlink from Starshield, a separate defense-oriented satellite system used by the US military. Although, Starshield terminals are provided to Ukraine under a contract from the US Defense Department, Rubio said the country does not currently have access to it.
Kyiv had earlier asked for permission to use the system over Russian territory to conduct deep strikes against military targets. Rubio said the question of how the system might be used remains under discussion.
"We openly asked SpaceX and President Trump to open Starlink on the territory of Russia to give us a chance to destroy ballistic launches of Russia," Zelenskyy told NBC News.
While Rubio's and Zelenskyy's latest comments highlighted the growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv over the administration's approach to Russia, the Ukrainian president said he had held talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Zelenskyy added that Ukraine and the United States were "preparing the next steps in diplomacy" and that his country remained "ready to work constructively, honestly, and toward a real result."

articles.title: Ballistic missile warnings are back, but the Starlink cap stays, Zelenskyy says: Ukraine’s two US lifelines, one restored
articles.body:
The US has resumed sharing intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches with Ukraine after a pause of several days, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told NBC News on 18 October. The blackout fell on days when Russia was firing ballistic missiles at Ukraine. Limits on the Starlink satellite service that Ukraine’s forces rely on remain in place, he said.
Russia has leaned on ballistic missiles in this month’s strikes on Ukraine’s grid, firing 39 in a single attack, and Ukraine is short of interceptors to stop them. Washington has used its support as leverage, reportedly telling Kyiv to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms.
Three days without warnings
The sharing had been blocked for some period of time before it was restored, Zelenskyy said on Meet the Press.
“We are very thankful for this. Now it works,” he said.
Ukraine gets other intelligence from Europeans and dozens of other partners, he explained. But only the United States has the data that tells Kyiv when Russia launches ballistic missiles.
“We didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days,” Zelenskyy said.
A timely warning gives Ukraine’s air defenses extra minutes to prepare and lets authorities alert civilians, Liga noted. Late on 12 October, Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before the air-raid alert reached people, with no advance data on launches from Russian territory. The next day, US President Donald Trump said Washington was still sharing intelligence. Two days later, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had received no US warnings of incoming ballistic missiles while it paused its strikes on Russian refineries at Washington’s request. That pause followed the energy ceasefire Trump declared on 11 October, which Russia never confirmed.
“He thinks Ukraine is a weak link and that it needs to be squeezed into giving in”: diplomat on why Trump pressures Kyiv, not Moscow
Starlink still capped, Kyiv says
Starshield, the military version of Starlink, still cuts out above 161 km/h, Zelenskyy said, too slow for Ukraine’s interceptor drones to catch Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type drones. NBC News, which aired the interview, separately reported that Starlink services had resumed at normal speed. He said Ukraine’s generals and government believe the order came from the US government and SpaceX carried it out, though he did not know who exactly made the call. Ukraine had instead asked SpaceX and Trump to open Starlink over Russia so it could hit ballistic missile launchers, he said.
“If [Trump] will personally decide to lift this decision, it will immediately work as it was before,” he said.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared on the same show, called Zelenskyy’s charge “very reckless” and said Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio had denied any administration role. Asked about the break in intelligence sharing, he said he did not know anything about it but that Zelenskyy should be “very careful about making statements like this that aren’t true.” Reuters had reported, citing three officials, that White House officials ordered the Pentagon to limit the service.
Asked whether Ukraine could win without the United States, Zelenskyy said it would be very difficult.
“But if the United States will support Putin, I mean, it’s unbelievable, it’s tragedy. It’s historic mistake and big tragedy,” he said.
He also said his team had received word that US negotiators wanted to meet, and that he had offered to meet in Brussels or London, hoping the US team would be ready this week.
The warnings are back, but they stopped once without explanation. Ukraine’s defense against Russia’s missiles still runs through decisions made in the US.

articles.title: Russia’s war on Ukraine ‘must be brought to an end’, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
Russia’s war on Ukraine ‘must be brought to an end’, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine’s president says communication between Washington and Kyiv ‘virtually nonstop’, despite a spat with Trump.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that the war with Russia “must be brought to an end” and that his country is preparing for the “next steps” of diplomacy to end the conflict.
The Ukrainian leader’s comments come amid a significant diplomatic fallout with US President Donald Trump, who on Friday night waived sanctions targeting Russia’s energy economy.
In a Sunday social media post, Zelenskyy wrote that he had a “conversation with the American president’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner”.
He added that “a lot depends” on the US position, but it’s clear there are “many things that matter to all of us”.
The Trump administration had already eased restrictions on Russian fuel imports on October 9, when it announced a deal for Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets in an effort to tackle soaring fuel prices
The US Treasury temporarily authorised the imports despite existing sanctions, prompting criticism that the move could provide Moscow with revenue to sustain its war in Ukraine.
Trump has also criticised recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure as “a disgrace”.
Nonetheless, Zelenskyy said his team is in “virtually nonstop communication” with their US counterparts and said a focus of dialogue is on the results of the talks in Florida and further steps.
US wavers on Ukraine’s access to tech
Zelenskyy also said he was “thankful” that the US had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine after a pause left the country particularly vulnerable to Russia’s regular ballistic missile attacks.
“It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was deblocked by the American side,” Zelenskyy told NBC, adding: “Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. And we didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days.”
Kyiv has also reported restrictions on the speed of satellite service Starshield, a military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite connectivity network, provided to Ukraine by Musk’s company SpaceX.
Ukraine said its relays were experiencing a limit on how fast receivers could travel while maintaining connectivity, making it almost impossible to intercept Russia’s upgraded jet-powered long-range drones.
Musk had said any restrictions imposed on Starshield connectivity were the responsibility of the US government. The White House quickly rebuked that and in an NBC interview on Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Zelenskyy “very reckless” for accusing the US of throttling connectivity.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Sunday that Ukraine is currently blocked from Starshield, and that a request from Kyiv to access the system for attacks deep inside Russia is “under discussion”.
US officials defend Russia waiver as Trump orders 60-day review
Meanwhile, in the US, Trump has faced bipartisan pushback for his executive order on Friday night, waiving parts of the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
Trump had signed the act into law in September, in honour of the late Senator Graham, a close Republican ally.
But his decision to ease sanctions and tariffs against Russia has prompted backlash even from within his own party. The penalties act was scheduled to take effect on Sunday.
Over the weekend, Trump signalled he has yet to make a final decision on easing the sanctions against Russia.
“My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” he wrote on Truth Social.
He concluded his post with further criticism directed at Zelenskyy. “He doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” Trump said of the Ukrainian leader.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that Trump wanted up to 60 days to assess the economic consequences of imposing the sanctions and tariffs that were waived on Friday.
Zelenskyy has warned, however, that the waiver could embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war.
Rubio also defended the latest deal to import Russian diesel, saying “that diesel is going to be sold one way or the other”. He argued that the fundamental question was how much the US would secure for itself.
In a series of Sunday morning media appearances, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright also backed the arrangement.
Speaking to ABC, he called the deal a “carrot to try to end the war, not an economic lifeline” for Russia.
“If Russia can bring additional diesel to the market and export it, it would benefit American consumers,” Wright told CNN. “He’s putting pressure that would both benefit American consumers and be a step forward for peace in the Russia-Ukraine war.”
Long-range attacks continue
Also on Sunday, Ukrainian media reported that Russian strikes killed two people in the western Volyn region, near the border with Poland, and injured at least five others across the country. Overnight attacks by Russia killed a woman and injured a six-year-old in the Zaporizhzhia region.
On Saturday night and in the early hours of Sunday, Ukraine hit Russia’s second-largest city, St Petersburg, with a significant drone attack. It targeted a key oil refinery and depot, a warehouse of Russian online retailer Ozon and a data centre run by Russian social media company, VKontakte.
At least one person was killed in the attack, which Russian state media said was the largest on the city since the start of the war in 2022.

articles.title: Trump defends Russia sanctions waivers, accuses Zelenskyy of 'prolonging war'
articles.body:
Trump accuses Zelenskyy of 'prolonging war'
October 19, 2026
US President Donald Trumpon Sunday defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, accusing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war.
"My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
"Zelenskyy doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past, he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," he added.
Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving broad new sanctions mandated by legislation named for the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Ukraine's defense.
He has also temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing supplies to flow into global markets in a bid to lower fuel prices ahead of US midterm elections on November 3.
Trump links Russia sanctions waiver to fuel prices ahead of midterms
Opinion polls suggest that Republicans could face significant losses in the election, as voters voice growing frustration over fuel prices that have surged since the Iran war began in late February.
Most economists believe the suspension of congressionally approved sanctions on Russia and the diesel deal with the Kremlin will do little to lower US fuel prices.
Trump also repeated his claim that Ukraine was targeting Russian refineries to hurt Republicans ahead of the midterm election.
The move drew a sharp response from Kyiv and its allies, further straining relations between Trump and Zelenskyy.
Zelenskyy warns Ukraine cannot prevail if US backs Russia
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Sunday that Ukraine would lose its defensive battle against Russia if the United States switched sides and supported Moscow.
"If the United States will take the side of Russia, of course we will not prevail," Zelenskyy told NBC's 'Meet the Press' calling a withdrawal of US support "a historic mistake and big tragedy."
He said Washington had resumed sharing intelligence after it was "blocked for some period of time," adding that Ukraine had missed critical intelligence on ballistic missile attacks for three days.
Zelenskyy also criticized US restrictions affecting Ukraine's war effort, saying, "We are strategic partners," but "we cannot applaud when someone turns against Ukraine."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended Trump's suspension of new sanctions on Russia, saying Trump wanted to assess their impact on the global and US economies.
Zelenskyy speaks to US envoys as Trump renews criticism
Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke to US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as Russia and Ukraine attacked each other's energy infrastructure, leaving thousands without power in Ukraine and setting an oil refinery ablaze near Saint Petersburg.
After the talks, Zelenskyy said "a lot depends" on the US position, adding that "this war must be brought to an end." Ukraine was ready to work "constructively" and "honestly," he said, calling for the same approach from its European and US partners.
Zelenskyy said he also discussed deliveries of US Patriot air defense systems as Kyiv struggles to counter Russian missiles.
A US-led push to end the war has yet to yield a breakthrough, with Trump expressing frustration at both Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Zelenskyy accused Moscow of violating Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warned Russia planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter. Russian strikes left "tens of thousands" without power, he said, while Ukrainian officials reported three deaths.
Ukraine launched drones at Putin's hometown of Saint Petersburg late Sunday, setting an oil refinery ablaze and killing one person, Moscow said.

articles.title: Two killed and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine trade blows on power infrastructure
articles.body:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday thanked the Trump administration for resuming intelligence sharing between the two countries, but maintained the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access so that Donald Trump could send a “message” in his ongoing feud with the Ukrainian president.
In an interview on NBC, Zelenskyy said the US had “unblocked” intelligence on impending Russian ballistic missile strikes, which have pounded the country’s energy infrastructure as winter draws in.
“It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was deblocked by the American side. We are very thankful for this. Now it works,” Zelenskyy told NBC’s Meet the Press. “Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. And we didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days.”
Zelenskyy also said that Elon Musk’s SpaceX was responsible for suddenly limiting the speed at which Starlink terminals worked in Ukraine, hampering drone operations on the frontlines as well as some air defence missions.
“It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed,” he said. “And technically, SpaceX did it.”
Two people were killed and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine continued to trade strikes on each other’s power infrastructure, after the breakdown of Trump’s short-lived and unilaterally declared “energy ceasefire”.
Trump has increasingly sought a detente with Moscow, inking a deal to import diesel fuel from Russia and waiving sanctions voted for overwhelmingly by both houses of Congress. Zelenskyy has become increasingly critical of Trump’s actions as the US has piled pressure on Ukraine to cease striking refineries in Russia and end the war quickly on Putin’s terms.
“We want to trust him and I hope that he will change his decisions,” Zelenskyy said of Trump. “Because I think that it’s all mistakes and it will not help us. And it will not help [the] United States.”
Zelenskyy on Sunday said that he had spoken with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the two Trump envoys charged with ending the war in Ukraine, as part of Ukraine’s “virtually nonstop communication” with the Trump administration.
But the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, in a separate interview on NBC on Sunday said that Zelenskyy had been “reckless” to accuse the Trump administration of standing behind the throttling of Starlink.
“President Trump and Secretary Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that,” said Bessent. “And I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge.”
He added: “President Zelenskyy should be very careful about making statements like this that aren’t true.”
On Sunday night Trump said Zelenskyy did not want his nation’s more than four-year war with Russia to end, writing on his Truth Social platform that he was in the process of negotiating a peace between Russia and Ukraine and making “great progress” but claimed: “Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”
Ukraine has resumed striking refineries in Russia and on Sunday attacked one of the country’s main oil terminals.
One person was killed and 15 wounded overnight after Ukraine used more than 1,000 drones to target Russian oil depots, logistics facilities and datacentres in one of its largest ever aerial bombardments.
St Petersburg’s governor, Alexander Beglov, said on Sunday that fires had broken out overnight at the city’s oil terminal, an oil depot and industrial warehouses. A logistics centre belonging to the Russian retailer Ozon and a datacentre for the local tech company VK were also targeted, both companies confirmed.
Alexander Drozdenko, the governor of the Leningrad region that surrounds St Petersburg, said 145 drones had been shot down and about 20,000 people were without electricity after the raid. “A large-scale [unmanned aerial vehicle] attack continues to be repelled,” he wrote on Telegram.
Fears that the conflict could be spilling over into Nato’s borders were stoked again on Sunday morning after Lithuania told residents in central and northern parts of the country to seek shelter for about an hour after an unidentified flying object entered its airspace.
During the red alert, Nato fighter jets were scrambled to the area and Kaunas airport, near Lithuania’s second largest city, was temporarily closed, the national crisis management centre said.
The Nato aircraft were unable to visually identify the object due to cloudy weather and did not attempt to shoot it down, the centre said.
Ukraine’s foreign ministry later said it regretted the possible diversion of its drones into Lithuanian airspace on Sunday, which it said may have been caused by Russian electronic warfare.
“We apologise for any disruption, risks and concern this may have caused,” a spokesperson, Heorhii Tykhyi, wrote on X. “We are committed to sharing all relevant information with our Lithuanian partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident.”
Meanwhile, local officials in the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia said Russian strikes had killed a woman and wounded at least two other people, including a six-year-old girl. Two apartment buildings, 18 cars and an educational institution had been damaged by the attack, according to Mykhailo Semikin, the head of the Zaporizhzhia regional military administration.
Tensions are deepening between Kyiv and Washington, with the US president criticising Ukraine for its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, despite continued Russian aggression.
Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” last week – which neither side said they agreed to beforehand – that quickly collapsed as Moscow continued its strikes on Ukraine’s power grid and Kyiv eventually resumed its hits on Russian oil refineries.
The Russian defence ministry said its air defence units had downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones around the country overnight. The Tass news agency quoted the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, who said Russia was responding with systematic, large-scale strikes.
“The Kyiv regime is resisting, but this cannot change the course of events,” he said, answering a question about how Russia might respond to Kyiv’s attack on St Petersburg.
On Saturday, Russia said it had carried out a major overnight attack, targeting Ukraine’s largest steelworks in the city of Kryvyi Rih and vessels using the port of Odesa. In a statement, Russia’s defence ministry said its forces had also hit an electricity substation in the north-western city of Zhytomyr and another steel plant in Zaporizhzhia.
In the Trump administration’s latest effort to reduce tensions with Russia, the US president announced on Friday that he would put a hold on a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.
Trump has yet to give details about what he has decided regarding further sanctions on Russia.
“We’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” he told reporters at a fundraising dinner at his Florida estate on Saturday. “But it’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world.”
In a post on X on Sunday, Zelenskyy said in the week since Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times.
He also said that the previous night alone, energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions had been attacked and tens of thousands of families were still without power. He accused Russia of trying to cause a blackout.
“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” he said. “On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting.”
Zelenskyy also stressed that the war was continuing due to Russia’s invasion – not because Ukraine was defending itself. “It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance. Thank you to everyone who understands this and helps,” he said.
Ukrainian drones have repeatedly entered Nato airspace in the Baltic region in recent months. Kyiv has said they were steered off course by Russian signal jamming. Such incidents have stoked concerns that Russia’s war in Ukraine could spread.
Reuters, the Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title: Who is Mehrdad Akhlaghi, Iran’s new tech-focused defence minister?
articles.body:
Who is Mehrdad Akhlaghi, Iran’s new tech-focused defence minister?
Akhlaghi’s experience centres on ballistic missiles, aerospace technology and defence-industrial production.
Tehran, Iran – Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi has been appointed Iran’s defence minister at a time when the war with the United States is expected to escalate.
The 68-year-old was approved on Sunday by parliament, which has convened online since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran on February 28, to assume leadership of the Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics. In total, 237 lawmakers voted in favour of Akhlaghi’s appointment and 15 against.
Former Defence Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed along with a large number of other senior figures, including Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, on the opening day of the war.
The position was filled temporarily by Majid Ebn-e Reza, who will now become Akhlaghi’s deputy.
Akhlaghi will be responsible for rebuilding and expanding Iran’s military-industrial infrastructure, which has been heavily targeted by the US and Israel.
The new minister’s defence plans were approved earlier by senior military authorities, President Masoud Pezeshkian and parliament’s Commission on National Security and Foreign Policy.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran will not be the instigator of aggression against any country but will defend the territorial integrity of the country strongly and to the death against any aggression,” Pezeshkian said.
The president said Akhlaghi has more than 42 years of experience in the Defence Ministry and related organisations.
His principal expertise is in ballistic missiles, solid-fuel propulsion, aerospace technology and military-industrial production, according to state media.
Previously, he served as the head of the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, the Aerospace Industries Organization and the Defence Industries Organization. Akhlaghi and these entities are all subject to sanctions by the US. He is also under United Nations sanctions.
He has been associated with developing several missile types and related weapons-development projects over the past decades, according to Tasnim, a newspaper linked with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC),
Akhlaghi reportedly played a role in expanding the major Sejjil and Zolfaghar family of Iranian ballistic missiles as well as precision-guided weapons, such as the Almas missiles and Yasin guided bombs.
He is also said to have expertise in space launchers, research rockets and infrastructure associated with the Imam Khomeini Space Center in Semnan. These have all been critical elements in Iran’s wars against Israel and the US.
This month, Iran’s Defence Ministry spokesman, Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik, told reporters that Akhlaghi’s nomination reflected Iran’s need to increase the quantity and quality of strategic weapons, particularly missiles and drones.
“Offensive arms are being actively improved,” the spokesman said.
The US has repeatedly claimed that it has destroyed most of Iran’s military-industrial capacities, but Tehran has maintained it continues to have considerable offensive and defensive capabilities outside the reach of US and Israeli bombs. These weapons have been upgraded based on Iran’s new war experience, it has insisted.
Akhlaghi told members of parliament this month that he had met with senior military commanders, including the commander-in-chief of the IRGC, Brigadier General Ahmad Vahidi, to develop a better understanding of their requirements during and after the war.
His priorities as defence minister would be faster military-industrial development, air defences, incorporation of emerging technologies using government and private sector firms, improvements in armed-forces welfare and development of international military cooperation, according to reports.
In his first comments as defence minister on Sunday, Akhlaghi taunted the administration of US President Donald Trump, which this month threatened to use the “mother of all bombs” on Iran’s nuclear and energy infrastructure.
“We have made preparations and continue our work with ease of mind,” he told reporters. “The US president must think of getting his forces out of our region in one piece. If he drops one bomb, he must see how many of his troops he will have to evacuate horizontally.”

articles.title: Trump Defends Russia Sanctions Waivers, Zelenskyy Warns Of Consequences
articles.body:
President Donald Trump defended his decision to waive sweeping sanctions planned against Russia as an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table amid strong criticism from Kyiv and some US lawmakers that it sends the wrong message to the Kremlin.
Trump signed an executive order late on October 16 that waives new sanctions mandated by legislation named for the late US senator Lindsey Graham, an ardent supporter of Ukraine, days after giving temporary relief on Russian diesel sanctions.
Trump signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched in February 2022.
But the moves in recent days to ease sanctions have sparked fierce criticism from many corners that Trump was giving the Kremlin a chance to fund its war machine, an accusation the president rejected.
"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump wrote on Truth Social on October 18.
Trump made ending Russia's war on Ukraine war a priority when he began his current term in January 2025, but Kyiv and Moscow remain far apart in their negotiating positions and talks have stalled.
The Kremlin has been offering no concessions, repeatedly rejecting calls for a full cease-fire, and sticking to demands including Russian control over the territory it has been unable to seize in battle.
The stalemate has seen the two sides step up attacks, with Moscow pummeling Kyiv and other major cities, along with targeting energy infrastructure, wreaking havoc on utilities just as Ukraine prepares for winter.
That included firing several ballistic missiles at Kyiv late on October 18, including a strike on a medical center building, according to Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko, who said at least one person died in the attack.
Ukraine's armed forces, in return, have targeted Russia's refining operations to hinder its military operations.
Those strikes have angered Trump, whose Republican party is engaged in a tight battle for control of both the Senate and House amid surging fuel prices that have angered many voters.
Trump also blamed his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for the lack of willingness to end Russia's war against his country, claiming that he "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
Zelenskyy warned of dire consequences for Ukraine if US support disappears.
"If the United States will take the side of Russia, of course we will not prevail," Zelenskyy told the NBC news show "Meet the Press" on October 18.
"We want to trust him, and I hope that he will change his decisions...Because I think that it's all mistakes and it will not help us. And it will not help United States."
He added that intelligence-sharing that Ukraine said had been interrupted earlier this week now appears to have been "de-blocked."
"We are very thankful for this," Zelenskyy said. "Now it works."
A week ago, as Trump unilaterally announced an energy cease-fire on social media, Zelenskyy appeared to support halting the strikes but said he expected Moscow to do the same.
However, as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy sites continued, the Ukrainian president said Kyiv was "done" with unilaterally pausing its own.
There was no indication Moscow had supported cease-fire announced by Trump.
Putin, who Russian media said was visiting a command post earlier in the week, ordered the Russian military to continue its "massive and coordinated" strikes against targets in Ukraine.
Moscow has previously sought to pressure Kyiv into accepting its hard-line demands by attacking the country's energy infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid freezing temperatures.
Trump's easing of sanctions has met with disdain from many lawmakers on both sides of the aisle in the United States, as well as from Ukraine's international partners.
While Trump administration officials including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the president's actions, Republican lawmaker Don Bacon said moves helping the Kremlin "will go down as a very embarrassing chapter in U.S. history."
Trump's latest comments highlighted the growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv over the administration's approach to Russia. Zelenskyy earlier announced he had held talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
He added that Ukraine and the United States were "preparing the next steps in diplomacy" and that his country remained "ready to work constructively, honestly, and toward a real result."
"Peace comes only through strength and cooperation built on trust," Zelenskyy said in a social media post about the talks.
"We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America’s position is strong and helps bring peace closer. Peace that everyone, except Russia, has been waiting for over the past four and a half years."

articles.title: A month before the diesel waiver, Trump’s envoys had already pitched Kyiv on Russian gas, NYT says
articles.body:
During their visit to Kyiv in September, US President Donald Trump’s envoys urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to consider restarting the pipelines that once carried Russian gas to Europe, The New York Times reported on 17 October. They presented it as part of a peace deal with Russia. In the weeks that followed, they pressed the idea with European officials, while Washington freed Russian diesel and spared Russia’s oil buyers from new US penalties.
Energy sales fund Russia’s war, and Ukraine’s halt of transit in January 2025 left TurkStream as Gazprom’s only pipeline route into the EU. Meanwhile, Russia has kept bombing Ukraine’s grid through the energy truce Washington declared on 11 October.
The pitch in Kyiv
Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner put the idea to Zelenskyy when they met him in Kyiv, the newspaper reported, citing people familiar with the talks. Trump officials argued that transit fees, which Ukraine gave up at about $1 billion a year, would benefit Kyiv, and that European voters would eventually want cheaper energy. Russia’s share of EU gas imports had fallen from 45% in 2021 to 13% last year.
The envoys presented renewed Russian gas sales as one of the economic incentives in a wider settlement covering Russia’s relationship with NATO, security guarantees for Ukraine, and territorial control. Some European and Ukrainian officials suspected Washington would seek a cut of the profits. The White House denied that the Nord Stream pipeline had been a subject of recent discussions. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov claimed that resuming energy cooperation is in Russia’s interest and, right now, even more in Europe’s.
Germany pushes back
At Ukraine talks the envoys hosted in Florida last week, Günter Sautter, security adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, forcefully opposed the idea. German lawmakers have called a return to Russian deliveries a disaster for European security, even treason, as the far-right AfD courts Gazprom to bring the gas back. Former Economy Minister Robert Habeck, who steered Germany off Russian gas after 2022, said Trump “seems to have more sympathies with Vladimir Putin than he has with the Ukrainians.”
Congress gave Trump 30 days to hit Russia’s oil buyers with 100% tariffs. He waives them two days before deadline, citing US interests. Moscow calls it historic
One concession after another
Rather than pressure Putin or strengthen Ukraine, the administration has spent much of its peace effort on economic incentives for Russia, the newspaper wrote. The US Treasury cleared imports of Russian diesel on 9 October. On 16 October, Trump waived the penalties on Russia’s oil buyers that Congress had passed in the Graham Act. Washington is also weighing relief for sanctioned shadow fleet tankers. And the White House ordered limits on the military satellite service Ukraine’s forces rely on, Reuters reported.
Putin’s economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev claimed the ice had broken and more joint initiatives would follow, including data centers powered by Russian nuclear energy. The talks also cover the sale of Lukoil’s foreign assets to a group that includes the US government, the newspaper reported earlier this month. Zelenskyy, who had heard the pitch in Kyiv, alluded to it in a Financial Times interview this week.
“The question will be when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas,” he said.
Reopening the pipelines could hand Moscow back significant revenue and strengthen its sway over Europe’s energy market, Liga noted. Each new concession lowers the price Russia pays for continuing the war.
Read also
- Trump calls Ukraine’s renewed refinery strikes “a disgrace” after Russia’s 39-missile strike on its energy sites
- 22 House lawmakers press Trump to implement Russia sanctions law. Diesel deal draws bipartisan backlash
- Musk pushed Trump to slow Starlink in Ukraine, weakening air defenses as Russian drones attacked cities – The Telegraph

articles.title: Iran Parliament approves new defence minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi: State media
articles.body:
Iran’s new defence minister threatens ‘enormous damage’ if US attacks
- Iran’s parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaghi as defence minister with 237 votes, replacing Aziz Nasirzadeh after his death in a US-Israeli attack.
- State media said Akhlaghi called the post a duty at a “sensitive juncture” and said defence needs clear thinking and readiness for future threats.
- Akhlaghi has 42 years in the defence ministry and has led the Defence Industries Organisation since 2013, but the UN sanctioned him in 2007 over missile or nuclear activity.
AI generated
TEHRAN – Newly appointed Iranian defence minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi threatened on Oct 18 to inflict “enormous damage” on the United States and its allies in the Middle East if Washington resumes its military campaign against the country.
“People can rest assured that they will most likely not dare to attack us,” Akhlaghi told reporters shortly after securing Parliament’s vote of confidence.
“If they (the US) do, they themselves and the region will suffer enormous damage.”
Iranian lawmakers had earlier approved Akhlaghi’s appointment as the country’s new defence minister, after his predecessor was killed on the first day of the war with the United States.
“Members of the Islamic Consultative Assembly (Parliament) today gave a vote of confidence to Mehrdad Akhlaghi, the nominee for minister of defence and armed forces logistics,” state television reported, nearly eight months after the initial US-Israeli strikes that sparked the conflict.
According to the government website, Akhlaghi “was elected to the post with 237 votes in favour”, out of a total of 277 votes cast.
The veteran defence official replaces Aziz Nasirzadeh, who was killed in a US-Israeli attack on a leadership compound on Feb 28, alongside former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and senior military commanders.
“If I receive Parliament’s vote of confidence, responsibility for the Ministry of Defence will fall to me at a sensitive juncture,” Akhlaghi said before the vote, according to the ISNA news agency.
“Under such circumstances, defending the country requires an accurate understanding of the environment, an understanding of the logic behind developments, the identification of influential trends, and preparedness to face different possible futures,” he added.
Although he does not hold a military rank, Akhlaghi has worked in the defence ministry for 42 years and has headed the Iranian Defence Industries Organisation, the state’s weapons manufacturer, since 2013.
The United Nations sanctioned Akhlaghi in 2007 over his alleged involvement in nuclear or ballistic missile activities. AFP

articles.title: US Resumes Intelligence Sharing With Ukraine, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
The US has resumed sharing military and security intelligence with Ukraine after suspending data exchanges for a “some period of time,” President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Sunday, Oct. 18.
Speaking during an interview on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” as reported by Bloomberg, the president confirmed that intelligence pipelines had been restored following operational friction with Washington.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zelensky also expressed hope that bilateral negotiations with American officials could take place within the coming week.
Warnings over energy interdiction and early-warning gaps
The temporary suspension of intelligence flows materialized amid sharp disagreements between Washington and Kyiv over battlefield targeting rules and prospective ceasefire mechanisms.
On Oct. 15, The Washington Post reported that US intelligence officials warned Ukraine that Washington would immediately halt intelligence sharing if Ukrainian forces continued long-range strikes against Russian oil refineries and petrochemical facilities.
The warning was formally conveyed to Ukraine’s embassy in Washington amid disputes surrounding an “energy ceasefire” unilaterally declared by US President Donald Trump.
The Trump administration had previously cautioned that it could suspend intelligence cooperation and block European purchases of American weapons earmarked for Ukraine if Kyiv refused to halt deep interdiction strikes on Russian energy infrastructure.
US Goes on the Offensive in Central Asia
While American sources cited by The Washington Post maintained that intelligence sharing was never completely dismantled, they acknowledged that specific data feeds had been restricted.
Prior to the restoration, Zelensky disclosed that Ukrainian defense forces received no advance warnings from Western partners regarding Russian ballistic missile launches toward Kyiv for two consecutive nights, during which kinetic impacts damaged critical capital energy installations and knocked out municipal power and water grids.
Bilateral coordination
Zelensky’s confirmation that intelligence sharing has resumed comes as Ukrainian and American officials work to arrange direct bilateral consultations.
On Friday, Oct. 16, National Security and Defense Council Secretary Rustem Umerov held consultations with US special envoy Jared Kushner to discuss a timetable and format for upcoming in-person meetings.
Zelensky affirmed that Kyiv remains prepared for direct discussions with White House representatives to explore verifiable mechanisms for a reciprocal energy armistice to protect civilian utility networks ahead of winter.
The restoration of intelligence sharing also coincides with public scrutiny over related technological restrictions affecting Ukrainian defense capabilities, including artificial speed limitations placed on commercial Starlink terminals and Ukraine’s lack of access to the Pentagon-contracted Starshield satellite network.

articles.title: Richard Branson Condemns Trump Policy on Russia, Urges European Aid
articles.body:
British billionaire and Virgin Group founder Sir Richard Branson has condemned US President Donald Trump’s foreign policy approach toward Russia, warning that Washington’s diplomatic and economic accommodations to Vladimir Putin compromise Western security and undermine allied trust.
Writing on LinkedIn on Sunday, Oct. 18, Branson criticized recent White House decisions to ease energy sanctions on Moscow and restrict technical support to Kyiv, calling on European leaders to step forward and deliver decisive military and financial support to Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I never thought I’d have to say this in my lifetime, but it’s 2026, and unfortunately, nothing is the way it used to be,” Branson wrote.
“The Trump administration has become an enabler of autocrats and dictators, placing their personal whims ahead of the interests of the American people and the free world.”
The entrepreneur questioned the administration’s posture toward the Russian head of state, asking: “What is it about [Russian President Vladimir] Putin that makes President Trump fawn over him? How can America’s allies ever trust this administration again, when it is now turning against them in a time of war and suffering?”
BREAKING NEWS: Billionaire Sir Richard Branson launches a SCATHING attack on Trump and his disgusting coziness with Russian dictator Vladimir Putin.
This is EXACTLY the kind of thing that gets under Trump’s skin...
"I never thought I’d have to say this in my lifetime, but it’s… pic.twitter.com/d2drBRfTVX
— Gianl1974 (@Gianl1974) October 17, 2026
Criticism of diesel pact
Branson highlighted a series of recent policy shifts in Washington that have raised concerns among Ukraine’s allies, pointing specifically to the commercial diesel agreement between the US and Russia alongside restrictions affecting Ukrainian defense capabilities.
Trump Envoys Push Russian Gas Transit in Ukraine Peace Talks
Under the commercial framework announced on Oct. 9, Moscow agreed to deliver refined diesel onto global markets through 2027 to mitigate fuel benchmark inflation, supported by a US Treasury general license. Branson noted that facilitating fuel exports injects direct revenue into the Russian state budget during active military operations.
The Virgin Group founder also cited reports regarding technical and intelligence constraints imposed on Ukrainian forces, including delays in US early-warning missile tracking notifications and the throttling of SpaceX’s military-grade Starshield satellite network.
“The throttling of Starlink/Starshield and the inexplicable failure to provide advance warning of Russian missile launches have already led to the needless deaths of Ukrainian civilians,” Branson stated. “How much worse can it get?”
The criticism follows statements by President Volodymyr Zelensky disclosing that an artificial 161 km/h (100 mph) velocity cap placed on Starlink terminals operating inside Ukraine had impaired domestic interceptors targeting Russian turbojet-powered strike drones.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and President Trump have denied ordering deliberate operational curbs, with Rubio stating that Starshield remains a dedicated US military capability not currently accessible to Ukraine for deep strikes inside Russia.
Call for European action, Taurus missiles, and seized assets
With transatlantic relations strained by shifting policies in Washington ahead of the Nov. 3 US midterm elections, Branson urged European governments to overcome hesitation and assume greater leadership in European security.
“If one thing is clear, it’s that European leaders must move past the initial shock of Trump’s recent actions and step up,” Branson wrote. “This is as much about European freedom as it is about Ukraine’s sovereignty. Both are worth fighting for.”
The British business leader urged European capitals to explore all available mechanisms to support Ukraine’s defense, including the full mobilization of immobilized Russian state reserves and the transfer of advanced standoff weapon systems.
“Every option should now be on the table – from transferring frozen Russian assets to Ukraine, to delivering advanced weapons systems like the German Taurus,” Branson emphasized. “We cannot allow the free world to be dismantled before our very eyes.”
The appeal arrives as EU leaders instructed the European Commission to draft proposals bridging Ukraine’s projected €70 billion ($79 billion) financial shortfall for 2027, with discussions encompassing plans to leverage proceeds from roughly €210 billion in Russian sovereign assets immobilized in European financial depositories.
