articles.title: 'We are ready for war': Iran's new defense minister threatens US and Israel
articles.body:
Iran appointed Mehrdad Akhlaqi, a longtime senior figure in the Islamic Republic's missile industry, as its new defense minister on Sunday, replacing an acting minister who had served since his predecessor was killed in an Israeli strike in February. Hours after his appointment, Akhlaqi threatened the United States and Israel with a sweeping military response, warning President Donald Trump that any renewed attack on Iran could leave American forces facing heavy casualties.
Akhlaqi, 68, succeeds Majid Ebn al-Reza, who had served as acting defense minister following the killing of Aziz Nasirzadeh in Israel's opening strikes on February 28, at the start of Operation Roaring Lion. Iranian lawmakers approved his appointment by a large majority after he presented a plan to rebuild military-industrial infrastructure damaged during the war, accelerate the development of defense technologies and expand cooperation with private-sector companies. 
The new minister has spent decades in Iran's defense industry, particularly its ballistic missile program, and has been subject to American and European sanctions for his activities. He previously headed the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, a subsidiary of Iran's Aerospace Industries Organization responsible for ballistic missile production. The UN Security Council placed him under sanctions in March 2007, followed by the U.S. Treasury in 2008, which accused him of overseeing the group's daily operations and participating in negotiations to acquire equipment.
In November 2014, Akhlaqi was appointed head of Iran's Aerospace Industries Organization, which operates under the Defense Ministry. European Union documents also link him to senior management roles in Iran's Defense Industries Organization and to the development of missiles, drones and other military technologies. He holds a degree in chemical engineering from Amirkabir University and a master's degree in strategic management from Malek Ashtar University. Despite his extensive career, he has maintained a relatively low public profile, with much of the available information about him appearing in military records and sanctions documents.
'Let's see how many bodies Trump evacuates'
Addressing lawmakers following his appointment, Akhlaqi declared that he had been a potential assassination target for decades. "I have been on the enemy's assassination list for 35 years," he said, warning that if the "American-Israeli enemy makes another mistake," Iran's response would be "surprising and extensive."
He pledged to strengthen Iran's regional network of allied armed groups, known by Tehran as the "axis of resistance," and restructure the Defense Ministry to meet what he described as daily security threats.
Akhlaqi also claimed that Iran had already taken measures to counter a potential American attack involving the GBU-43/B, commonly known as the "Mother of All Bombs," the most powerful conventional bomb in the U.S. arsenal. His remarks followed reports that Trump was considering using the weapon in a future strike against Iran.
"Trump should be thinking about how to get his people out of the region safe and sound," Akhlaqi warned. "Let him try dropping one bomb, and then we'll see how many bodies he has to evacuate."
The new defense minister also claimed that Iran was relocating its military production facilities to more heavily protected locations. "We are not building new factories in their previous locations. Instead, we are building them inside mountains and fortified, secure structures," he said. "With our fingers on the trigger, we are prepared for war against the Zionists."
He further promised that an Iranian-made heavy fighter jet would take flight next year, describing it as an entirely domestically produced aircraft.
Iran says seven-day Hormuz deal remains on the table
Alongside the military threats, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran's proposal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz under a seven-day framework remained on the table, despite Trump's rejection of the plan last month.
"Our position is completely clear. We presented it to the United States in the form of a seven-day plan," Araghchi said. "If there is any sincerity on the American side, the path forward is clear: If the conditions are met, the strait will reopen on the sixth day and negotiations will resume on the seventh."
Iran's conditions include lifting the U.S. blockade of its ports, removing oil sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian funds and ending hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon. Tehran is effectively seeking a return to the framework of a June memorandum of understanding under which Washington offered significant concessions. Trump, however, has shown no interest in returning to that arrangement and is demanding immediate nuclear concessions that Iran has refused to provide.
Amid the diplomatic deadlock, Iran has intensified attacks this month on oil tankers and commercial vessels crossing the Strait of Hormuz under an American-led protection operation, seeking to disrupt traffic through the strategic waterway. Fuel prices have remained elevated despite Trump's statements that the strait is fully open.
The U.S. blockade of Iranian ports also remains in place, further straining an already deteriorating Iranian economy. Trump has signaled that he could resume military strikes after the November 3 U.S. midterm elections, raising the prospect of renewed fighting if negotiations fail.
Araghchi insisted Sunday that Tehran would not surrender in such a scenario. "We are better prepared for self-defense than ever before," he said. "At the same time, we remain open to the diplomatic path, provided it is conducted with respect and dignity and guarantees the rights of the Iranian nation."

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine exchange overnight strikes, killing 3 and injuring 21
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
Russia and Ukraine exchanged overnight strikes Sunday, killing three people and injuring 21 others, officials on both sides said.
Ukrainian drones targeted oil facilities and an Ozon logistics center in St. Petersburg, as well as Russian social media company VK’s data center in the Leningrad region.
In St. Petersburg, one person was killed and five others were injured, Gov. Alexander Beglov said on Telegram. The city’s oil terminal, Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses caught fire during a “massive” drone attack.
Beglov said 12 apartment buildings and two private homes were damaged, and emergency crews continued to battle the fires.
An Ozon logistics facility was also hit, sparking a fire and prompting staff to evacuate. No injuries were reported at the site, the company said.
Meanwhile, Leningrad Region Gov. Alexander Drozdenko said four people were hospitalized. Drone debris fell on an apartment building in Gatchina, while 55 parked vehicles were damaged in Novosyolye, he said.
An emergency power outage affected 50 apartment buildings, leaving about 20,000 people without electricity, he added.
Russian social media company VKontakte said its data center in the Leningrad region was also targeted but that its services remained available.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones overnight over Russian territory, Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014, and the Black Sea.
Separately, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said 512 drones headed toward the Moscow region overnight, most of which were destroyed by air defenses at a distance from the capital.
Attacks on Ukraine
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, two people were killed and 12 others injured in Russian overnight strikes on residential buildings across the country, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
In a post on US social media company X, Zelenskyy accused Moscow of “deliberately” attacking Ukraine’s energy, oil, and gas sectors 76 times since US President Donald Trump announced an energy truce between Kyiv and Moscow last week.
He said Moscow targeted substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions overnight, leaving “tens of thousands” of families without power.
Zelenskyy added that Russia had attacked Ukraine with nearly 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic, over the past week, stressing that energy facilities were the main targets.
“And America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” he said. “On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting.”
The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces launched overnight strikes on Ukrainian logistics centers, ports, and vessels allegedly used to support Ukraine’s armed forces.
The ministry said a logistics center operated by Ukrainian postal company Nova Poshta in Rivne was hit. It alleged the facility stored and distributed dual-use goods, including components for long- and medium-range drones.
It added that a cargo ship carrying military and dual-use goods was hit at sea about 30 kilometers (19 miles) east of the port of Odesa.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Air Force said its air defenses shot down or suppressed 152 Russian drones during the overnight attack.
Independent verification of the claims remains difficult due to the ongoing war.

articles.title: 'You are the real target': Netanyahu warns Iran may attempt to develop missiles able to reach US
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned that Iran was developing intercontinental ballistic missiles and pursuing nuclear weapons with the aim of threatening American cities, telling FOX News on Saturday that the US, rather than Israel, was the Iranian regime's ultimate target.
Netanyahu argued that Iran's ambitions extend beyond Israel, warning that the regime intends to target both the US and Europe if it succeeds in destroying Israel. He said Iran's development of long-range missiles and pursuit of a nuclear arsenal were intended to place American cities at the mercy of the regime.
"They understand that if they can destroy Israel, then they can conquer the Middle East, control the waterways of the world... and then proceed to the next target, which is you. That's why they're building intercontinental missiles: to reach the United States," Netanyahu said.
"This is a regime that chants death to Israel, death to America. You are the real target. And I think we are well on our way to achieving this, with President Trump's brilliant leadership, both military and, then, economic blockade."
The prime minister explained that the Iranian regime views the US as "the great Satan" and Israel as the "little Satan," before directing a remark at European countries.
He said he "hoped our European friends are not offended; you are seen as the middle-sized Satan, you are mediocre in so many ways."
"Iran would be a nuclear power as we've never seen in the entire world, because they don't have this careful calculus of cause and benefit. Because they are so fanatic. So you can't win them over, you can't buy them out," he said.
Netanyahu also described the Iranian regime as a "malevolent power" operating alongside what he called the "Three Hs": Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Houthis.
"They are the arms of this toxic octopus. And it's not Iranian people; they are great people," he added.
Eliminating the Iranian threat was the first of three priorities Netanyahu outlined for his next term if reelected in the October 27 Knesset election, alongside expanding the Abraham Accords and establishing Israel as a global leader in artificial intelligence.
"First, we will achieve the complete elimination of the Iranian threat to Israel, to America, and to the entire world," Netanyahu said.
Expanding Abraham Accords as a key objective
"Second thing is to expand the historic Abraham Accords that [US President Donald] Trump and I forged here with four Arab states," Netanyahu continued.
"There are many more that are waiting in this precise moment, because they saw our strength, our power and fortitude. And they want to join us. So let's create an axis of peace and moderation against these barbarians who shoot their own people," he said.
Netanyahu also said he plans to "forge a different future, a different Middle East, and also a different world" if reelected.
Artificial Intelligence to help humankind
Netanyahu's third priority focused on artificial intelligence, and the prime minister said he agreed with Trump on both the dangers the technology poses and its potential benefits for humanity.
"I plan to seize the future with the 'Neverland AI,' the 'super intelligence,' as the president calls it. He is absolutely right; they are dangerous, but their possibilities in health, in agriculture, in transport, and in education," he explained.
"You can personalize AI for every child; they have their own potential, and you can give them the best teachers on the planet. We are doing it today in Israel, and we intend to be the world leaders in that area too. These are all amazing things," he added.
Netanyahu also pointed to Israel's economic performance, which he described as among the strongest in the developed world.
"By the way, the economy, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), is leading all the Western countries, the OCD countries, with the greatest growth. That's after three years of war. I want to push that even further, bring a better future to Israel, to our neighbors, to our great ally the United States."

articles.title: Russia hit Ukraine’s energy 76 times during a US-declared truce—and tens of thousands lost power overnight. Civilians killed and injured
articles.body:
Russia has kept striking Ukraine’s energy sector throughout the week since US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 18 October. From overnight into Sunday, Russian drones and a ballistic missile hit substations, homes, and industrial sites from Odesa to Volyn. They killed civilians and left tens of thousands of families without power.
Russia fights along the front line while hitting cities and the grid behind it with drones, missiles, and glide bombs. Ukraine says Moscow plans up to 1,000 such munitions against 60 key infrastructure sites this winter, and jet-powered drones partly free it to concentrate missiles on fewer targets, the Institute for the Study of War assessed. With Graham Act penalties on hold and US sanctions on Russian diesel suspended, Russia faces no new US cost for its strikes on Ukraine’s grid. Protecting and restoring the grid falls to Ukraine’s air defenses and repair crews.
Russia hit energy sites 76 times in a week
Zelenskyy counted 76 deliberate Russian strikes on energy and oil-and-gas facilities since Trump’s announcement. Overnight, Russia hit substations in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa oblasts, he said. In the past week, Russia fired almost 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles, most of them ballistic, mainly to cause a blackout. His message was aimed at Washington.
“America must see that Russia is not taking steps in return for the lifting of sanctions or deals. On the contrary, they take every signal that they can make money as proof that their bet on war is working and they can keep fighting,” Zelenskyy wrote.
22 House lawmakers press Trump to implement Russia sanctions law. Diesel deal draws bipartisan backlash
Overnight, Russia launched one Iskander-M ballistic missile and 180 Shahed-type drones, 26 of them jet-powered, the Air Force reported. Air defenses downed or suppressed 152 drones, but strikes hit 20 locations.
Power cuts from Odesa to Ternopil
Strikes left about 24,000 consumers in Odesa Oblast without power, oblast head Oleh Kiper said. In Vinnytsia Oblast, the attack damaged critical infrastructure and forced emergency outages, oblast head Natalia Zabolotna wrote. Drones hit three energy facilities in Ternopil Oblast, one of them for the second time, and cut power to some consumers, oblast head Taras Pastukh said.
Civilians killed and injured
A Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia killed a 27-year-old woman and injured two others, including a 16-year-old, the State Emergency Service reported. In Poltava, an evening attack killed one person, injured four, and damaged 10 detached houses, city council secretary Kateryna Yamshchykova said.
Five Russian bombs kill 17 in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia next day after Trump lets Russia ship first 300,000 tonnes of its diesel
A drone hit a high-rise in Odesa and set its roof on fire. A 13-year-old girl was hurt, city military administration head Serhii Lysak said, and Kiper put the number of injured at two.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russian drones and artillery injured three people, oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha said. In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed seven civilians on Saturday, six of them in Sloviansk, oblast head Vadym Filashkin reported.
Fires in the west, alerts across the border
A morning drone strike set warehouse and production buildings ablaze at an enterprise in Manevychi, Volyn Oblast, oblast head Roman Romaniuk said. With heavy smoke blowing toward the town, Romaniuk urged residents to stay indoors, shut windows and doors, and switch off ventilation. A repeat strike set an enterprise in the district on fire again, the State Emergency Service said, adding that air tests found no dangerous concentrations outside the site. In Lviv Oblast, drone debris damaged a logistics warehouse and two houses, oblast head Maksym Kozytskyi said.
Polish military aircraft operated in Poland’s airspace twice during the attack, as the Government Security Centre warned residents of Lublin Voivodeship and later alerted Subcarpathian Voivodeship. In Lithuania, NATO jets failed to identify an object that apparently entered from Poland, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said.
A ceasefire Moscow never confirmed
Trump announced the energy ceasefire on 11 October, news that surprised Zelenskyy. A White House official said Russia was still weighing it. Hours later, Russia hit a Kharkiv power plant, and on 14 October it fired 39 ballistic missiles at the grid. Then Trump waived Graham Act penalties on buyers of Russian oil, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the administration wants 60 days to weigh the economic effects.

articles.title: Ukrainian drone attack causes fire at oil terminal in St. Petersburg
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone attack causes fire at oil terminal in St. Petersburg
A blaze has broken out at an oil terminal in St. Petersburg as a result of a major Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s second-largest city, local governor Aleksandr Beglov has said.
One person was killed and five others wounded in St. Petersburg during the aerial raid by “the Ukrainian Nazis,” Beglov said in a social media post on Sunday. Twelve apartment blocks and two private homes sustained damage, with repairs already being underway, he added.
Emergencies services have been tackling fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal in the Great Port of St. Petersburg, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses in Kolpinsky District, the governor said.
The affected oil terminal is the largest facility of its kind in the Baltic Region, handling 125 million tons of liquefied product per year.
Ukraine continues to target Russian oil infrastructure despite demands by US President Donald Trump to curb the attacks, which he blames for surging global energy prices. He accused Vladimir Zelensky of “making problems” for the US and the whole world and suggested that Ukraine needs a “new president.”
In an attempt to alleviate the fuel shortage ahead of the midterm election on November 3, Trump eased restrictions on Moscow’s diesel exports and waived “the bone-crushing” sanctions championed by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, which proposed 500% tariffs on imports from Russia and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
Flights have been delayed at St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo International Airport due to the raid, according to Beglov.
At least 144 UAVs were shot down by air defenses overnight, Aleksandr Drozdenko, the head of Leningrad Region, which surrounds St. Petersburg, said on social media.
Four people have been hospitalized for smoke inhalation from a blaze caused when debris from an intercepted UAV fell on an apartment block in the town of Vsevolzhsk, he said.
Residential areas were also hit by debris in Gatchina, Kirovsk and several other settlements, according to Drozdenko.
Some 20,000 people remain without electricity in Leningrad Region; two transformer substations in the community of Yanino, servicing some 50 apartment blocks, went offline during the Ukrainian raid, the governor said.
Russia’s leading social media platform VK said in a statement that one of its data centers in Leningrad Region has been targeted by Ukrainian UAVs.
According to the Downdetector website, the number of reports from users about issues with VK’s services increased following the attack.
The major Russian online retailer Ozon said that one of its warehouses was attacked during the raid. There were no injuries, as staff were evacuated, according to the company.
The Russian Defense Ministry has said that a total of 1,015 Ukrainian drones were destroyed above 16 regions overnight.
Moscow has accused Kiev of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure and residential areas with long-range drones in an attempt to compensate for setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces have continued to advance.
Russia has responded to Kiev’s terrorist attacks by intensifying its long-range missile and drone campaign against Ukraine’s military-industrial facilities and logistics infrastructure. The Defense Ministry in Moscow maintains that it does not target civilians and that its strikes are directed solely at military targets and infrastructure supporting Kiev’s forces.

articles.title: The drones flew 1,000 km. St. Petersburg’s oil terminal, fuel depot, and a nearby data center were waiting at the end
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones struck St. Petersburg’s oil terminal, a fuel depot, an Ozon distribution center, and a VK data center overnight, setting off fires across the city, monitoring channels reported. Russian outlet Meduza called it apparently the largest attack on the city and Leningrad Oblast since the war began. Russian officials acknowledged fires, damaged homes and substations, and power cuts.
Russia keeps fighting along the front while bombarding Ukrainian cities and the grid behind it. Ukraine’s long-range drones, in turn, target the oil exports and logistics that fund and supply that war, and Russia’s Baltic oil ports have been hit repeatedly this year. St. Petersburg is a symbolic place: Russia’s so-called second capital and Putin’s hometown.
Oil terminal and fuel depot on fire
Ukrainian forces struck the Petersburg Oil Terminal with FP-1 drones, starting a fire, Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point said. The company described the terminal as one of the region’s largest, handling 12.5 million tonnes of petroleum products a year, including for export.
St. Petersburg Governor Aleksandr Beglov acknowledged fires at the terminal and in four city districts, adding that Pulkovo airport had restricted flights. By morning, firefighters were still battling blazes at the terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses in the Kolpinsky district, he wrote. He claimed one person was killed and five injured. Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported that the Ruchyi depot had been burning since the night.
Ozon hub, VK data center, and a bridge
An Ozon distribution center in Kolpinsky district caught fire after the attack, the company said, Russian independent outlet Astra reported. Astra’s open-source intelligence analyst described it as one of Ozon’s busiest fulfillment centers in northwestern Russia, covering up to 79,000 m².
FP-1 drones also hit a VK data center in Novosergiyevka, Leningrad Oblast, causing serious damage, Fire Point said. VK acknowledged a drone attack on the site but claimed its services were working normally. Leningrad Oblast Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko claimed air defenses downed 145 drones over the oblast alone. He acknowledged damage to the data center’s transformer equipment and warehouse complex, and minor damage to the Vostochnaya substation. Two other substations in Yanino went offline, cutting power to about 20,000 people, he said.
A drone also hit the cable-stayed bridge over the Korabelny fairway, part of a toll highway linking the city’s north and south, Exilenova+ reported, adding that the extent of the damage was still being clarified. The channel also reported a fire near a Russian Aerospace Forces radar company outside the village of Kaporskoye.
To reach St. Petersburg, Ukrainian drones had to cover 1,000 km across four Russian regions guarded by air defenses and electronic warfare, said Serhii Beskrestnov, adviser to Ukraine’s president on defense technology.
“And these are not cruise missiles with special systems, these are drones that fly at speeds of up to 200 km/h,” he wrote.
Strikes resume after a one-sided truce
The same night, Russia hit Ukraine’s grid again, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy counted 76 Russian strikes on energy since the ceasefire was announced. US President Donald Trump declared the truce on 11 October. Ukraine paused its refinery strikes for three days at Washington’s request, but Russia struck a Kharkiv power plant within hours and kept hitting the grid. Zelenskyy then said Ukraine was resuming strikes on Russian oil and would stop again only in exchange for more US interceptors for its Patriot systems. Trump called the renewed strikes “a disgrace” and said he found Zelenskyy “more difficult to deal with than Putin.”
Ukraine has hit the St. Petersburg area before. In July, drones set fire to Wildberries warehouses near the city. In August, Ukraine began striking Ozon hubs, starting in Samara Oblast. The hubs move dual-use goods such as electronics and drone components.

articles.title: Zelensky speaks to US envoys as Trump lashes out
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Zelensky speaks to US envoys as Trump lashes out
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky spoke with top US envoys Sunday to try to ease tensions, as Donald Trump accused his counterpart of not wanting to end the war with Russia.
Zelensky spoke to US officials Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as both Russia and Ukraine hit each other's energy sites, with Moscow leaving thousands without power and Kyiv carrying out the largest drone attack on Saint Petersburg since the start of the war in 2022.
Trump and Zelensky have clashed as the US president blocked new sanctions on Russia and struck a diesel deal with Moscow, fuelling fears in Kyiv and Europe that the White House was steering towards Moscow.
On Sunday Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that he was in the process of negotiating a peace between Russia and Ukraine and making "great progress," but claimed: "Zelenskyy doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him... he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
"Zelenskyy is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States," Trump said.
Earlier, after speaking to Trump's business partner Witkoff and son-in-law Kushner, Zelensky said "a lot depends" on the US position in the war but that "it is clear that there are many things that matter to all of us and that this war must be brought to an end."
Ukraine was ready to work "constructively" and "honestly", he said. "We expect exactly this approach from all our partners -- both from the Europeans and, of course, from the American side."
He said he discussed deliveries of US Patriot air defence systems, as Kyiv struggles to counter Russian missiles.
Zelensky earlier told US broadcaster NBC it would be a "historic mistake" if Washington formally supported Russia and that he hoped Trump would "change his decisions."
But he also said he was "thankful" the US resumed intelligence sharing after a pause that left his country vulnerable to Russian missile strikes.
Thousands without power
A US-led push to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II has so far not brought about a breakthrough and Trump has in the past grown frustrated with both Zelensky and Russia's Vladimir Putin because of their lack of progress.
Zelensky spoke to the American officials as he accused Russia of breaking Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warning Moscow planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter.
Russian strikes left "tens of thousands" without power in several regions, he said, with Ukrainian officials reporting three people had been killed.
Ukraine's army launched drones at Putin's hometown of Saint Petersburg late Sunday, setting an oil refinery ablaze and killing one person, Moscow said.
Rising smoke was visible from Saint Petersburg's historic city centre on the banks of the Neva River, with Russia saying Ukraine struck an oil refinery and depot.
Saint Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov said one person was killed and five hospitalised in the city.
Authorities were fighting fires at the Saint Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses, he said.
Russia's VKontakte social network said its data centre was hit and Ozon -- Russia's second largest retailer -- also reported a strike on its logistics centre.
The head of the wider Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said air defence shot down 144 Ukrainian drones, with state media saying this was the largest attack on the city since the start of the war.
'Dreadful routine of war'
The Kremlin, however, said Ukrainian attacks on its cities will not change its war aims.
Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine and, in a fifth year of war, few see a way out of the conflict.
"There's a general feeling: they're attacking, we're attacking -- it's become the dreadful routine of war," 58-year-old Galina told AFP in Saint Petersburg.
Moscow has rained drones and missiles on Ukrainian cities daily and Kyiv says its strikes are fair retribution.
Sergei, another Saint Petersburg resident who is also 58, said he felt his apartment block shake and quickly realised it was a drone attack.
"I don't know if I was scared, what must be will be," he said.
Ukrainian strikes caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia earlier this year.

articles.title: 4 New Air Defense Towers Built Near Putin’s Valdai Residence
articles.body:
Four additional air defense towers have been erected near the Valdai residence of Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Novgorod region of Russia, with the closest structure situated roughly 400 meters from the main residential compound, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Russian service reported.
Satellite imagery analyzed by investigative journalists revealed that the newly constructed elevated platforms expand an already dense protective perimeter surrounding the presidential retreat.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
With the addition of the four new towers, the total number of specialized air defense towers identified in the immediate vicinity of the Valdai compound has grown to approximately 30.
The installation of elevated ramparts and stationary towers across Russian territory is engineered primarily to host short-range surface-to-air missile and anti-aircraft artillery systems, such as the Pantsir-S1, elevating radar and kinetic engagement equipment above regional forest canopies to detect and intercept low-altitude strike drones.
The Valdai estate, located on Lake Valdai approximately midway between Moscow and St. Petersburg, serves as a heavily fortified private retreat frequented by Putin and his inner circle.
White House Defends Russia Sanctions Waiver to Aid Peace Talks
Expanding multi-layered perimeter around Valdai
The construction of the four new towers marks the latest phase in a progressive militarization of the airspace safeguarding the presidential retreat against asymmetric Ukrainian drone incursions.
In early April, investigative reports based on satellite imagery confirmed that Russian engineering units had completed seven new stationary air defense towers mounting Pantsir systems around the Valdai complex between late 2025 and March 2026.
Over subsequent months, secondary rings of fortified positions were established along surrounding access routes and peripheral forested areas.
Concurrently, Russian security agencies reinforced ground-level defenses around the complex. In early June, independent Russian media outlets, including Meduza and Agentstvo, verified the installation of anti-drone netting systems over transport routes and truck staging facilities in the Valdai district, approximately nine kilometers (5.6 miles) from the compound.
Defense analysts from the Conflict Intelligence Team (CIT) observed that the netting arrays – technologies widely employed along frontline sectors in Ukraine to shield vehicles from loitering munitions and first-person view (FPV) drone drops – were deployed around Valdai to protect security convoys and control access corridors amid Ukraine’s expanding long-range drone campaign.
Concentric air defense rings around Moscow
The continuous reinforcement of the Valdai residence forms part of a broader, systemic effort by Russian defense planners to erect dense, layered air defense networks around high-value leadership compounds, strategic command hubs, and the Russian capital.
In late June, satellite reconnaissance revealed that Russian forces established a fortified S-400 long-range surface-to-air missile position fewer than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) from the Kremlin in western Moscow.
Constructed across a 4.5-hectare concrete platform near Moscow State University’s Innovation Science and Technology Center – the flagship project of the Innopraktika Foundation directed by Putin’s daughter Kateryna Tikhonova – the site incorporates S-300 and S-400 missile launchers alongside a 40V6MR mobile radar mast designed to detect low-flying aerodynamic targets.

articles.title: Sybiha: 76 Energy Strikes Prove Moscow Flouts Ceasefire
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has warned that Russia is systematically expandeing targeted strikes against Ukraine’s power grid while feigning interest in diplomatic initiatives, stating that 76 targeted attacks on energy infrastructure over the past week prove Moscow has honored no commitments.
Writing on X on Sunday, Oct. 18, Sybiha stressed that offering economic accommodations or easing sanctions under such conditions only equips the Kremlin with fresh revenue to underwrite ongoing military operations ahead of winter.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Its message could hardly be clearer – Moscow has not abided by any obligations,” Sybiha stated, noting that tens of thousands of Ukrainian families remain without electricity as international partners attempt to explore avenues to conclude the war.
The foreign minister reiterated figures disclosed earlier in the day by President Volodymyr Zelensky, pointing out that Russian forces carried out 76 targeted attacks against Ukrainian energy facilities since US President Donald Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” one week ago.
Sybiha added that over the preceding seven days alone, Russian forces deployed nearly 2,700 strike drones, 1,700 guided aerial bombs (KABs), and 66 missiles across Ukrainian territory, with the vast majority of missile systems consisting of high-speed ballistic weapons directed at municipal utilities.
US Tech Curbs on Kyiv Expose Allied Dependency
Simulated diplomacy and economic pressure
Ukraine’s top diplomat observed that the Kremlin is pursuing an asymmetric strategy engineered to secure international sanctions relief without altering its operational conduct or military objectives on the ground.
According to Sybiha, Moscow seeks “sanctions relief without changing its behavior, preservation of profits without accountability, and the imitation of diplomatic efforts without any commitment to stop killing Ukrainians.”
Addressing international allies and policymakers in Washington, Sybiha cautioned that lowering the economic costs of Russian aggression while civilian infrastructure faces daily bombardment directly undermines prospective peace efforts.
“Easing economic pressure under these circumstances risks giving the Kremlin additional resources to finance its war,” Sybiha emphasized.
“It is time for our partners to draw the necessary conclusions. Any serious effort to end this war must increase pressure on Moscow, restrict the revenues financing its aggression, and strengthen Ukraine’s ability to defend its cities and energy infrastructure.”
The foreign minister underlined that Russia bears unilateral responsibility for prolonging the conflict, dismissing the notion that commercial accommodations can incentivize de-escalation.
“Reducing the cost of its aggression while it continues attacking Ukraine will not bring peace,” Sybiha concluded. “It can only make further aggression easier to finance.”
Sanctions waivers and energy armistice disputes
Sybiha’s public remarks arrive amid sharp transatlantic disagreements over the Trump administration’s recent foreign policy maneuvers toward Moscow.
On Friday, Oct. 16, Trump signed an executive order invoking Section 115 of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 to waive mandatory statutory penalties, including 500 percent tariffs on Russian imports and 100 percent duties targeting global purchasers of Russian hydrocarbons, just 48 hours before their scheduled implementation.
The waiver follows an Oct. 9 bilateral commercial arrangement between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, under which Moscow agreed to deliver refined diesel onto international markets through 2027 to curb fuel benchmark inflation.
The shipments were authorized under a general license issued by the US Treasury Department.
While White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers argued that enforcing statutory sanctions now would impede ongoing diplomatic efforts to broker a peace settlement, Ukrainian officials have strongly contested that assessment.
Both Zelensky and Sybiha have warned that granting Moscow access to international energy markets injects direct hard currency into the Russian state budget during active military operations, validating the Kremlin’s calculation that its war effort is yielding economic dividends rather than consequences.

articles.title: Ukraine launches 1,000 drones at Russia, strikes set oil facilities ablaze
articles.body:
Trump says he's "negotiating Peace" as Ukraine launches 1,000 drones at Russia amid continued back-and-forth strikes
President Trump said Sunday he is "in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," despite the two countries continuing to trade strikes, including one of Kyiv's largest aerial attacks of the war.
Smoke billowed on Sunday at an oil export terminal and depot in St. Petersburg, which was set ablaze after Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia.
At least one person was killed, and five others were wounded in the attack in St. Petersburg, which sparked fires at the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city's Ruchi oil depot, local Gov. Alexander Beglov said.
A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center operated by Russian tech giant VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed.
Russia's Defense Ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency Tass that Kyiv was "resisting" Moscow's invasion but could not "change the current course of events."
Meanwhile, in Ukraine, a woman was killed and a 6-year-old girl was among at least two other people wounded in two Russian attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said Sunday.
The strikes came as tensions between Ukraine and Washington deepened. President Trump has recently been critical of his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and Kyiv's attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.
Meanwhile, there is still uncertainty about the prospect of further U.S. sanctions on Moscow.
Speaking on NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday, Zelenskyy said waiving sanctions against Russia would strengthen Putin's war effort. He also said U.S.-Ukraine intelligence sharing had resumed after being "blocked for some period of time."
Mr. Trump told reporters late Saturday that they did not know what his decision on further sanctions against Russia would be, despite signing an executive order Friday night waiving planned restrictions, citing U.S. national interests.
On Sunday, Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table. Great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations! Signing that document at this time will do that, and I can sign it later, or any time that I want!"
"Perhaps more importantly, Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way," Mr. Trump said.
He also continued his criticism of Zelenskyy, again chastising him for "using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target" and alleging "he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
"He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead," Mr. Trump wrote.
Zelenskyy earlier said that while he trusted Mr. Trump, siding with Moscow would be a tragedy and a "historic mistake" for Washington.
"People want to forget what's going on. But we can't give this possibility to forget, or to change reality, or to change the truth," Zelenskyy said. "We can't compare me and Putin. He's aggressor. He occupied us. He killed adults and children, his soldiers. He's a terrorist. And that's why I hope that President Trump will be very clear with this position."
Later Sunday, Zelenskyy said on social media that he had spoken with U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about the results of an Oct. 9 meeting between U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams in Miami, as well as "next steps in diplomacy."
He also accused Moscow of breaking Mr. Trump's "energy ceasefire" 76 times and warned that Russia planned to deprive Ukrainians of heat and electricity before winter.
The Ukrainian government initially said it was observing the ceasefire.
Energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions were struck overnight, leaving tens of thousands of families without power, he said, accusing Russia of trying to cause a blackout.
"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," he wrote.

articles.title: Iran urges US to accept proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday.
Iran presented its proposal in mid-September after an interim ceasefire collapsed. Tehran later acknowledged receiving a US response, but Iran’s security chief said last week negotiations have stalled because Washington failed to address all seven conditions for reopening the strait.
"Our situation is clear and based on the seven-days proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn't, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious," Araqchi said while in Baghdad for a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
An alleged Saudi airstrike in Yemen on Sunday killed at least nine people and wounded 16 others, Houthi media reported, as fighting between the two sides in the country's revived civil war escalates further.

A flight from Tel Aviv, Israel, made an emergency landing Sunday evening in the Bulgarian capital of Sofia after a bomb threat, Bulgarian state television reported.
The BNT report, citing a statement by the transportation ministry, said the flight to Vienna carried 51 passengers and six crew members. It said a crew member reported receiving the threat, and an air force fighter jet escorted the plane until it landed.
The broadcaster said the incident was being investigated. The airline was not identified.
Bulgaria’s defense ministry said fighter jets responded after the threat was reported on the Airbus A320.

An oil tanker caught fire and exploded after striking a naval mine in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps navy said on Sunday, according to Iranian media.

The Iran-backed group's Saba news agency said an airstrike on a home in Saada governorate in Yemen's north "led to the martyrdom of nine and the injury of 16 others, most of them women and children", adding that the toll was not final.

Syria and the World Bank have agreed to set up a multi-donor trust fund focused on recovery and reconstruction, they said in a joint statement on Sunday, as Damascus aims to rebuild after a more than decade-long civil war.
The fund aims to provide concessional financing, investment guarantees, technical support, and capacity building.
Russia's Lavrov to visit Tehran on Monday, Iran says
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will visit Tehran on Monday for consultations with Iranian officials and aims to follow up on the implementation of bilateral agreements, Iran's foreign ministry said in a statement.

"On Sunday, civil defence in the city of Najran responded to the fall of an enemy projectile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia at a residential site, resulting in six citizens being injured and material damage to three homes and three vehicles," the civil defence said on X.

US officials visit Palestinian village after settler attacks
US diplomats visited a Christian Palestinian town in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Sunday following attacks by militant Israeli settlers on European diplomats and an American photojournalist in the previous two days.
Riley Barnes, assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labour, Brian Burch, US ambassador to the Holy See, and a number of other diplomats visited the Latin Convent church and were expected to meet with members of the Christian community in Taybeh.
Belgian, French and Polish diplomats, along with a French mayor and Palestinian civilians, had been attacked near Taybeh on Saturday by masked Israeli settlers.
US President Donald Trump endorsed his ally Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday for the upcoming Israeli parliamentary election.
"Bibi Netanyahu has been Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.
"This is the kind of Partner that the United States of America is demanding of Israel, a Country for which it has done so much. Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel."
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa on Sunday appointed Omar al-Halabi as chairman of the country's sovereign wealth fund, created by the transitional authorities but criticised by experts as lacking transparency.
Syria's sovereign fund sits at the heart of the country's attempts to bring in foreign capital after 13 years of war, and was created to oversee investment projects and manage state assets.
It also manages assets confiscated from businessmen close to the government of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad, who the new authorities ousted in December 2024.
In a decree published by state media, Sharaa appointed Halabi "as adviser for economic affairs to the presidency of the republic" and as "chairman of the board of directors of the sovereign fund".

Egypt's parliament postponed a vote on President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request to authorise military support for Saudi Arabia on Sunday, two lawmakers told AFP, extending deliberations to Monday.
One lawmaker said the session was extended "to give all lawmakers the opportunity to speak and express their views", while another said proceedings would continue on Monday "to allow all lawmakers to be heard".
Lebanese foreign minister urges Iran to stop attacks on Gulf
Youssef Raji, Lebanon's foreign minister, called on Iran to cease attacks against the Gulf states and Jordan, coming a day after he had a meeting with his Iranian counterpart.
Raji called for Iran to "cease their aggressions against the Gulf Cooperation Council states and Jordan”.
Raji also condemned “persistent Israeli aggressions against Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity".

Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday.

Egypt: Will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary support

Levine was seriously injured in the attack Friday in the West Bank village of Abu Falah. Tug off UAE's Khor Fakkan struck by two projectiles
The British navy-affiliated UKMTO said on Sunday that it has received a report of an incident northeast of Khor Fakkan in the United Arab Emirates, where a tug sailing southbound reported being struck by two unknown projectiles.
One minor injury was reported and the tug has sustained damage, however is continuing on its route, UKMTO added.

articles.title: Russian ‘Matryoshka’ Bot Farm Targets US Midterms With AI
articles.body:
Russian state-backed disinformation operators are deploying automated bot networks to artificially inflate view counts for fabricated videos targeting Democratic candidates and Hollywood celebrities ahead of the US midterm elections, Bloomberg News reported.
The digital influence campaign – identified by social media researchers as “Matryoshka” or “Operation Overload” – relies on artificial intelligence to generate counterfeit news broadcasts and deepfakes designed to erode public trust in electoral integrity and undermine political support for Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A review by Bloomberg of 130 fabricated videos and doctored newspaper front pages circulated between Sept. 10 and Oct. 9 revealed a systematic campaign focused almost exclusively on Democratic contenders across the country.
The findings were documented by the anonymous research group Antibot4Navalny and corroborated by US-based open-source intelligence firms Graphika and dTeam.
AI-generated celebrity fakes
The operation began circulating AI-manipulated video clips across social media platform X in early September. The media files featured synthetic likenesses of high-profile actors and musicians – including Robert De Niro, Julia Roberts, and Cher – falsely depicted as attacking Democratic politicians or encouraging viewers to join an online campaign labeled “#AllDemocratsAreCriminals.”
Additional fabricated materials mimicked established American broadcast networks to distribute unsubstantiated allegations against prominent candidates.
Trump Envoys Push Russian Gas Transit in Ukraine Peace Talks
One video carrying a counterfeit ABC News digital banner claimed that James Talarico, the Democratic nominee contesting a US Senate seat in Texas, made payments to OnlyFans models.
A spokesperson for Talarico firmly denied the assertion. Another video mimicking CBS News alleged that the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) uncovered eight undeclared real estate properties owned by Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff. No public records or official disclosures substantiate the claim.
Researchers observed that Matryoshka-linked posts frequently accumulated hundreds of thousands of impressions on X within their first hour of publication. However, digital forensic data shared by Antibot4Navalny demonstrated that view counts were systematically manipulated by automated bot networks to project artificial virality.
“The number of views for Matryoshka posts can jump as high as 200,000 within the first hour but then quickly plateau,” researchers observed, noting that organic engagement follows a steady growth curve rather than a sudden spike followed by an abrupt flatline.
Forensic analysis established that the amplifying accounts had been dormant for years, possessed few followers, and generated virtually no genuine reposts or likes relative to recorded views.
Strategic shift to down-ballot races and midterms
The operational footprint of the campaign reflects a tactical evolution from previous Russian influence efforts. While past operations focused predominantly on high-stakes presidential contests, Matryoshka has broadened its parameters to target down-ballot congressional and gubernatorial races.
According to Bloomberg’s analysis, the network disseminated targeted disinformation against Democratic candidates in 20 of the 35 US Senate races and 29 of the 36 gubernatorial contests scheduled for the Nov. 3 ballot.
US intelligence agencies have warned Congress of the escalating deployment of synthetic media by foreign adversaries.
A recent assessment by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) identified Russia as the primary foreign actor deploying artificial intelligence to degrade public confidence in American democratic institutions ahead of the midterm vote.
Antibot4Navalny, which has monitored Kremlin-aligned digital networks since 2018, initially identified the Matryoshka apparatus in September 2023 as it attempted to undermine Western military assistance for Ukraine.
The operation was named after traditional Russian nesting dolls due to its operational pattern: accounts distributing one fabricated narrative frequently pivot to distributing fresh fabrications on successive days.
French government monitoring agency Viginum confirmed in early 2024 that initial seeds of Matryoshka content were routed through Russian-language channels on Telegram before migrating to Western social networks.
“It’s evolving with the technology and is more sophisticated as a result,” said Darren Linvill, professor at Clemson University and co-director of its Media Forensics Hub. “They’re actively trying to fish for more engagement.”
Disinformation backbones and physical infrastructure hits
The exposure of the Matryoshka campaign coincides with growing scrutiny of the physical and digital infrastructure that underwrites Russian computational influence operations.
Between Oct. 8 and Oct. 11, Ukrainian precision drone strikes disabled three major data centers owned by Russian technology giant Yandex in the Vladimir, Kaluga, and Ryazan regions.
The kinetic disruptions caused widespread server outages across Russian enterprise networks and triggered a sharp reduction in automated web requests originating from Russian server clusters.
According to network intelligence provider Cloudflare Radar, automated bot traffic from Yandex’s sovereign network plunged immediately following the facility strikes.
The computational downtime was followed by reports from digital monitors across Europe describing a marked decline in automated polarization.
Polish open-source defense analyst Jarosław Wolski observed a noticeable contraction in coordinated online attacks pitting Polish citizens against Ukrainian refugees, alongside a temporary drop in bot-driven engagement boosting fringe political parties in Germany.
President Volodymyr Zelensky referenced the operational ripple effects on Oct. 12, noting that precision interdiction against Russian digital nodes resulted in “less hatred, less discord, and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots.”
Western security agencies maintain that Moscow’s influence operations increasingly blur the boundary between cognitive warfare and algorithmic manipulation.
Previous legal actions by the US Department of Justice disrupted 968 AI-powered bot profiles operated under the direction of state broadcaster RT and the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB), alongside the “Doppelganger” network of cloned media domains, underscoring allied efforts to dismantle coordinated influence operations ahead of the November vote.

articles.title: Netanyahu warns Israel could lose US support, seeks 450 billion shekels in extra defense spending
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Sunday that Israel could face a hostile U.S. administration in the future, potentially threatening its military assistance and strategic relationship with Washington, and said the country must develop new international alliances. At the same time, he announced plans to allocate approximately 450 billion shekels in additional defense spending over the next decade.
Netanyahu made the remarks during an event at which he presented his security doctrine, nine days before Israel's October 27 election. Just hours later, U.S. President Donald Trump publicly endorsed Netanyahu's reelection bid for the first time during the current campaign.
"In two years, a president, man or woman, could come to power who is very hostile to Israel," Netanyahu said. "How would you deal with that? How would you operate in relation to the United States? And beyond that, what solutions would be necessary?"
His remarks came against the possibility that a future U.S. administration could suspend military assistance to Israel or even join international sanctions and an arms embargo against the country.
Netanyahu said Israel must use the remaining years of Trump's presidency to strengthen its position while preparing for a potentially dramatic shift in American policy.
"First, we must do everything we can during these two years, and during the following two years, in the American arena, through good times and bad," he said. "The second thing is to create other alliances. That is what I am working on now with many countries in our region and outside it. India is not a small country, and there are many others."
He pointed to political developments in Latin America as another opportunity to expand Israel's network of allies.
"There is a major shift in Latin America, and there could be an enormous change in Brazil in just a few days," Netanyahu said. "We must expand our pool of alliances and develop capabilities that make us valuable to everyone."
He also addressed Israel's strained relations with European countries, accusing some governments of publicly condemning Israel while continuing to seek cooperation with it.
"Countries that condemn us, and they have some nerve, by the way, condemn us and then come to us," he said. "I tell them: It depends on you. It depends on how you behave."
Netanyahu argued that Israel still possesses diplomatic leverage but would need considerable international expertise to navigate changes in Washington and other capitals.
In a separate social media post Sunday, Netanyahu appeared to acknowledge the possibility of a change in U.S. leadership, describing Trump's remaining time in office as an opportunity to advance Israel's strategic objectives.
"We have another two years of my friend President Trump's term, and this is exactly the time to complete our major missions on every front," he wrote.
On defense spending, Netanyahu said he intended to allocate approximately 450 billion shekels over the coming decade to strengthen Israel's military capabilities. An additional defense spending package of approximately 350 billion shekels had previously been agreed upon, according to earlier reports.
Addressing the future size of the Israel Defense Forces, Netanyahu said the military would have to expand, although technological advances, particularly artificial intelligence, could reduce some of its manpower requirements.
"As for a large army or a small army, the IDF definitely needs to grow," he said. "It will grow, but not at the rate we might have expected because AI reduces many requirements. Still, it needs to grow, and for that, of course, you need to allocate both funding and personnel."
He added: "I am putting about 450 billion shekels into this so that we have the capabilities and the teeth."
Turning to Iran, Netanyahu said the regime remained a threat despite what he described as severe military and economic damage inflicted on it. He warned that Tehran would seek to rebuild its nuclear program, develop other unconventional weapons and restore its regional network of allied armed groups.
"Like cancer, this will not end as long as that regime remains in place," he said. "It will try to recover, renew its nuclear program, renew other unconventional weapons programs and rebuild the axis."
Netanyahu claimed that Israel had already accomplished approximately 90% of its objectives against Iran and described the Iranian leadership as severely weakened.
"Why aren't people taking to the streets? Because right now they are being killed. Simply killed. They are killing or wounding tens of thousands of their own people. That is the nature of this regime," he said.
He then explicitly stated that his policy was aimed at bringing down the Iranian government. "Our plan is very comprehensive and very determined, to bring about the downfall of the regime," Netanyahu said. "That is my plan. That is the directive I have given all the security agencies, and that is what will happen."
Netanyahu also discussed Israel's relationship with Russia, describing it as one based on competing national interests rather than consistent cooperation.
"We speak when necessary," he said. "But Russia has its interests, and we have the interests of the State of Israel, and they do not always overlap. Sometimes they even clash."
He cited Russia's cooperation with Iran during the war in Ukraine as an example of conflicting interests and also raised the issue of anti-Israel bot networks spreading what he described as extreme antisemitic content.
"We raise all these issues, and we do so very clearly," Netanyahu said. "And when there is an opportunity to cooperate, we do that as well."
Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the opposition Yashar! party and a former IDF chief of staff, sharply criticized Netanyahu's presentation, describing it as an empty political exercise rather than a serious national security strategy.
"Nine days before the election and three years after the gravest failure and disaster in Israel's history, with every war front still open, Netanyahu decided to present his 'security doctrine' to the public," Eisenkot said.
"Two hollow pages, full of slogans that have nothing whatsoever to do with a security doctrine, reveal more than anything the strategic vacuum Netanyahu has left the State of Israel in and his disregard for the security of Israeli citizens."
Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of attempting to manipulate public opinion and spread fear ahead of the election.
"This is Netanyahu's method: manipulating perceptions, frightening people and trying to divert attention from the parade of lies and racism surrounding his campaign tonight," he said.

articles.title: Kremlin says Ukrainian attacks won’t change war aims as Kyiv hits Saint Petersburg
articles.body:
Kremlin says Ukrainian attacks won’t change war aims as Kyiv hits Saint Petersburg
- The Kremlin said Ukrainian attacks on Russian cities will not change its war aims, after Kyiv hit Saint Petersburg with its biggest drone strike since 2022 and set an oil refinery ablaze.
- Russia said the attack killed one person, injured others, damaged homes and infrastructure, and forced airport limits, while officials claimed 144 drones were shot down.
- Zelensky said Russia broke the “energy ceasefire” 76 times and warned of a winter “blackout”, as peace talks stall and both sides keep trading strikes.
AI generated
SAINT PETERSBURG – The Kremlin on Oct 18 said Ukrainian large-scale attacks on Russian cities will not change its war aims as Kyiv hit Saint Petersburg with the biggest drone attack on Vladimir Putin’s hometown since 2022, setting an oil refinery ablaze.
Rising smoke was visible from Saint Petersburg’s historic city centre on the banks of the Neva River, with Russia saying Ukraine struck an oil refinery and depot in night time strikes that killed one person.
The attack came as Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky accused Moscow of violating an “energy ceasefire” announced by US leader Donald Trump 76 times as he warned Russia planned a “blackout” in Ukraine before winter.
Kyiv struck Saint Petersburg as its ties with Washington strained massively in recent days, with Trump waiving sanctions on Russia and striking a deal with Moscow on diesel.
Ukraine and its European allies have worried the White House is siding with Moscow, which launched Europe’s worst war since WWII in 2022.
Saint Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov said one person was killed and five hospitalised in the city.
The authorities were fighting fires at the Saint Petersburg oil terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot and industrial warehouses, he said.
Flights were restricted at the city’s Pulkovo airport, Beglov said, adding that 12 housing blocks were also damaged.
Russia’s VKontakte social network said its data centre was hit in the city and Ozon – Russia’s second largest retailer – also reported a hit on its logistics centre.
The head of the wider Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said air defence shot down 144 Ukrainian drones, with state media saying this was the largest attack on the city since the start of the 2022 war.
Ukraine has attacked Moscow and Saint Petersburg throughout the Kremlin’s dragging offensive but large-scale hits on Russia’s main cities are rare.
“The Kyiv regime is putting up a fight, but that cannot change the course of events,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian media.
Russia’s offensive against Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions.
Moscow has rained drones and missiles on Ukrainian cities daily and Kyiv says its strikes are fair retribution.
US-led peace talks have not led to a breakthrough.
In a fifth year of war, few see a way out.
Putin appeared in military uniform this week and repeated Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.
‘Dreadful routine of war’
“There’s a general feeling: they’re attacking, we’re attacking – it’s become the dreadful routine of war,” 58-year-old Galina told AFP in Saint Petersburg.
Sergei, another resident of the city who is also 58, said he felt his apartment block shake and quickly realised it was a drone attack.
“I don’t know if I was scared, what must be will be,” he told AFP.
“My main thought was that petrol would run out at the petrol stations and I’d better fill up.”
Ukrainian strikes caused nationwide fuel shortages in Russia earlier in 2026.
Leningrad governor Drozdenko said 20,000 people were without power in the town of Yanino, where a substation was hit.
He said a woman and three children were hospitalised “with symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning” in the region after drone debris fell on a house, causing a fire.
“I woke up at night, heard bangs, looked out of the window and there was a fire,” 40-year-old Saint Petersburg resident Igor told AFP.
“They’re getting on my nerves already,” he added, referring to Ukraine.
‘Bet on war is paying off’
In Ukraine, Zelensky said Russian strikes hit substations in four Ukrainian regions, leaving “tens of thousands of families without power.”
The Ukrainian authorities said Russian attacks killed at least three people on Oct 18, including a 27-year-old woman in Zaporizhzhia and two people in the western Volyn region bordering Poland.
The Saint Petersburg attack came a day after Zelensky called on allies to keep up pressure on Moscow as he denounced Trump’s move to block new sanctions on Russia.
“America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements,” Zelensky said on Oct 18, adding: “On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting.”
Trump this week blocked a package of new sanctions on Russia which was meant to target Putin, as well as Russia’s energy and defence sectors.
He also signed an agreement with Moscow in October to buy diesel, seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of elections.
“It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance,” Zelensky said on Oct 18. AFP

articles.title: IRGC profiting from sex trafficking of Iranian women, using children for proxy wars - JCFA
articles.body:
Iranian women, undocumented migrants, children, and refugees are being exploited by the Islamic Republic, specifically the IRGC, to finance and support its proxy wars across the region, according to an analysis published last week by the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs (JCFA).
Ella Rosenberg, a senior research fellow at the JCFA and a member of the Dvorah Forum, said Iran’s legal framework allows the regime to project an image of compliance with international anti-trafficking regulations while relying on flawed legislation that falls short of international standards and fails to adequately protect victims.
She noted that the Islamic Republic conflates human trafficking with migrant smuggling, and the regime has consistently refused to ratify the 2000 United Nations Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons (the Palermo Protocol).
IRGC directly benefiting from sex trafficking, Israeli study finds
Beyond failing to protect victims, Rosenberg assessed that the IRGC directly benefits from human trafficking. She noted that the IRGC uses the sex trafficking sector, often facilitated by the regime through temporary marriages, as a major source of income.
Rosenberg described Iran as a source, transit, and destination country for the sex trafficking of women and girls, citing widespread poverty, systemic corruption, and economic mismanagement as contributing factors.
She argued that Article 1041 of Iran’s Civil Code, which permits girls to marry at 13 and even younger girls to marry with parental permission and court approval, has helped normalize the sexual exploitation of minors.
Rosenberg also linked the practice of nikah mut’ah, a temporary marriage contract agreed upon for a predetermined period, to the exploitation of vulnerable women and girls for the benefit of organized trafficking networks.
Trafficking networks move victims within Iran and across its borders into neighboring countries, including Iraq, with the alleged support of the IRGC, according to Rosenberg. She said that the scale of cross-border sex trafficking could not be sustained without the IRGC’s complicity, given its role in border control and the intelligence apparatus’s oversight of internal security checkpoints and airports.
Adding more weight to her analysis, human rights groups, including the IHR Monitoring and Evaluation Framework and HRANA, have documented allegations that IRGC commanders accepted bribes to facilitate the passage of trafficking victims.
Rosenberg added that the IRGC profits directly from the exploitation of Iranian women by taxing the commercial sex trade.
IRGC exploiting Afghan, Pakistani refugees
In addition to financially benefiting from human trafficking, the JCFA report said that the IRGC’s Quds Force and the Basij systematically traffic undocumented migrants, refugees, and children to “sustain their proxy wars across the Middle East.”
The IRGC exploits vulnerable populations, particularly Afghan and Pakistani refugees, to recruit fighters through deception, financial coercion, and threats of deportation, she said. Individuals harvested from these communities are coerced into joining proxy militias like the Fatemiyoun and the Zainabiyoun Brigades, for deployment in foreign countries like Iraq.
Additionally, in violation of international law, the Basij systematically recruits and coerces Iranian children as young as 12 into military indoctrination and combat support roles. This was argued to be a severe form of human trafficking, as the recruitment exploits children’s vulnerability to coerce them into hazardous, involuntary servitude in military environments.
Though JCFA warns of the abuse of children aged 12 and up, The Jerusalem Post has previously reported on the death of an 11-year-old Basij member who was killed at a checkpoint in Iran.
Rather than directly profiting from the trafficking of vulnerable individuals into the IRGC, Rosenberg suggested, the financial gain can be categorized as cost avoidance rather than revenue.
She argued that instead of deploying trained members of the IRGC, which the regime would have to pay and has invested in, the system can deploy underpaid or unpaid vulnerable groups who are deemed disposable because of their lack of funded training.
Such deployments were estimated to save the Islamic Republic billions of dollars in military expenditure, freeing funds to be redirected into the IRGC’s domestic corporate monopolies and regional terrorist financing networks.
Again, Iran’s “tax” system also allows it to benefit from migrants transiting from Pakistan and Afghanistan who are hoping to reach Europe through Iran and Turkey.
Such migrants are also routinely subjected to debt bondage, extortion, and forced labor in Iran’s informal agricultural and construction sectors to pay off exorbitant smuggling fees by criminal networks that pay protection money to the IRGC. This alone is estimated to generate billions of dollars for Iran’s shadow economy.
Focus on Iran's nuclear program may distract from IRGC human trafficking
Rosenberg noted that Iran was able to continue to exploit these systems as sanctions from the EU and US have primarily focused on Tehran’s nuclear proliferation, ballistic missile development, support for regional terrorism, and suppression of domestic dissent. Failing to also sanction the IRGC and the front companies it uses for human trafficking continues to provide Tehran a lifeline.
Given that the funds raised by human trafficking are often liquid, Rosenberg also alerted to the fact that it was hard for international systems to monitor how much wealth Iran is accumulating through these sources.
Individuals involved in facilitating or covering for regime-backed smuggling networks can therefore continue to travel, use regional banks, and manage front companies without fear of asset freezes or international arrest warrants.
To prevent Iran from continuing to profit from human trafficking, Rosenberg advised that the US Treasury Department utilize the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act to designate IRGC border commanders, Basij recruitment officers, and complicit Iranian law enforcement officials for their roles in labor and sex trafficking.
She added that the European Commission must also use the Sixth Anti-Money Laundering Directive (AMLD6) to require European financial institutions to aggressively monitor illicit financial flows generated by Iranian trafficking networks.

articles.title: Built as a cheap Shahed lookalike, Russia’s Gerbera now flies with a 10-kg warhead and an incendiary bag
articles.body:
Russia has started fitting its enlarged Gerbera-2 drones with a 10-kg warhead and an extra bag of incendiary mixture, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi reported on 18 October. The setup is designed to start a fire where the drone hits and is probably meant for attacks on critical infrastructure and warehouses, the outlet said.
Russia’s industry makes about 3,000 jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones a month, Ukraine’s military intelligence has said, and Russian strikes have destroyed 2.1 million m² of Ukraine’s modern warehouse space since the full-scale invasion began. A cheap drone that carries fire adds one more threat for air defenses that already let nearly half of Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds through.
A fire bag behind the warhead
Ukrainian Telegram channel Polkovnyk HSh posted photos of the payload on 17 October. Gerbera-2 strike and reconnaissance drones had begun to appear with a 10-kg high-explosive fragmentation-incendiary warhead and an extra package of incendiary mixture, the channel wrote. They navigate with Kometa-M12, a 12-element antenna array designed to resist jamming, it added.
Russian drones set their own detonators at altitude: Why cutting wires won’t save from new Gerberas?
In the photos, the incendiary mixture sits in a separate soft plastic tank behind the main warhead, Militarnyi said. Gerbera-2s have been seen with warheads of 4 to 10 kg depending on range, while strike versions of the original Gerbera usually carried up to 5 kg, the outlet noted.
Half a Shahed engine
Russia has mainly fielded the Gerbera, a cheap drone shaped like a Shahed, as a decoy and reconnaissance platform flying alongside Shahed-type strike drones. It has also used bigger Gerberas to drop FPV drones.
Serhii Beskrestnov, now an adviser to Ukraine’s president, flagged a much bigger Gerbera in Ukraine’s skies on 7 August. The Gerbera-2 has a larger airframe, a reshaped wing, and a bigger tail fin, Militarnyi said. In August, the outlet reported it had a stronger piston engine: half of the one in the Shahed-type Geran-2, at about 275 cm³. Production of these engines was set up at the Izhevsk Motorcycle Plant, according to preliminary information the outlet cited.
Russia equips Geran attack drones with image-based navigation using Google map imagery, reducing reliance on satellite navigation that Ukraine can jam, defense adviser warns
Earlier versions ran on a Chinese DLE60 model-aircraft engine of about 61 cm³. The switch was likely possible because Geran-2 engine output partly freed up as jet-powered Geran-4s took a growing share of Russia’s drones, Militarnyi said. The Gerbera-2’s fuel tank also holds up to 63 liters, against 10 liters on the original.
One reached Poland’s Baltic coast
In September, a drone preliminarily identified as a Gerbera-2 was recovered from the Baltic Sea near Rusinowo, on Poland’s coast. It carried a high-explosive fragmentation warhead of about 4 kg, a Polish military prosecutor said.
