articles.title: Russian ballistic missiles slam Kyiv right as air raid alarms sound
articles.body:
Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Multiple explosions rocked Kyiv on Oct. 18 and again early on Oct. 19, Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground reported, as Russia launched successive ballistic missile attacks on the Ukrainian capital.
Unlike the previous evening's attack, air raid alerts and warnings from Ukraine's Air Force on Telegram were issued before the explosions were heard, giving residents advance warning of the threat.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that one of the capital's metro stations on the left bank of the Dnipro River was damaged in the Oct. 19 attack.
Debris also damaged railway tracks and the metro's power-supply rails near the station, Klitschko said.
In the Solomyanskyi district, debris struck the first floor of a 25-story residential building.
Debris also hit a non-residential building at another location. Emergency services were dispatched to both sites, the mayor said.
There were no immediate reports of casualties from the latest attack.
Earlier, residents had little warning before the missiles struck. The explosions were simultaneous with the blaring of air raid sirens, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
Phone alerts went off moments before the blasts, while the street sirens began "howling during the explosions," Chief Editor Olga Rudenko reported.
A medical center in the Desnianskyi district was hit during the Oct. 18 strike, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. Another building was hit in the Dniprovskyi district.
Emergency services were dispatched to the Oct. 18 attack sites, the mayor said. The death of a 21-year-old woman was reported, with no information yet available as to the total number of casualties or extent of the damage.
The Oct. 18 ballistic missile strike came just hours after President Volodymyr Zelensky said the U.S. had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine about Russian missile launches.
The president's announcement came as a relief, after Kyiv endured "massive explosions" on Oct. 12, when five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
The Oct. 12 attack came after the U.S. threatened to withhold intelligence from Ukraine unless Kyiv stopped attacking Russian refineries, sources told the Kyiv Independent.
A senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the Oct. 18 missile attack followed a similar pattern.
"The 'warning' about a ballistic threat came through only after the strike had already happened," the official said. "They're up to something again."
It can be common for Russia's high-speed ballistic missiles to hit with very little advance warning. Kyiv Independent Reporter Kateryna Denisova said she had about three minutes to shelter between receiving the mobile alert and the first explosions, which is "usual when there's a ballistic missile threat."
Ukrainian officials have previously explained that satellite surveillance of launch sites can be vulnerable to transmission delays. Bad weather may also cause interference with the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS) satellites, a surveillance network U.S. forces use to monitor Russian launch sites.
But the senior official who spoke to the Kyiv Independent said this explanation was unlikely.
"This has never happened before ... but now we're seeing 'bad weather' three times in a row," the official said.
"When nothing comes through on any channel... well, we get it."

articles.title: 'I want this war end' — Trump defends pro-Russian policies in scathing diatribe against Zelensky
articles.body:
'I want this war end' — Trump defends pro-Russian policies in scathing diatribe against Zelensky
Editor's Note: This is a developing story.
U.S. President Donald Trump took to his social media platform Truth Social on Oct. 18 to defend his recent decisions regarding Russia — including the waiving of sanctions, a deal to buy diesel, and intense pressure on Ukraine to stop targeting oil refineries.
The pro-Kremlin moves have sparked outrage and alarm in both Ukraine and the U.S., as Russia continues battering Ukrainian cities and makes no concessions towards a peace agreement in exchange for Trump's sanctions relief.
The Trump administration has gone beyond public criticism of Kyiv. The Kyiv Independent reported on Oct. 12, citing two Ukrainian officials, that Washington threatened to suspend intelligence sharing and weapons deliveries in an effort to compel Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities.
But this is all part of Trump's diplomatic plan, the U.S. president claimed in his post.
"My decision on Russia is a very simple one," he wrote on Truth Social.
"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table. Great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations!"
Trump defended his diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin by saying that Moscow is not helping Iran in the war with U.S., but is rather helping the international community by "sending, at a low price, millions of barrels of diesel to the World."
"Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way," he wrote.
The U.S. president announced a deal with Putin on Oct. 9 allowing Russia to supply millions of tons of diesel to American and international markets despite sanctions imposed over Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russia subsequently partially lifted its diesel export ban, allowing additional supplies to reach foreign markets.
With the war in Iran driving up global fuel prices, including for U.S. consumers, Trump has sought to pin the blame on another target as midterm elections approach. His choice was Ukraine — specifically, the country's increasingly successful strike campaign on Russian oil refineries.
The diesel deal has also raised questions about whether easing restrictions on Russian energy exports will provide Moscow with additional revenue to finance its war. A Kyiv Independent analysis published Oct. 14 examined the limited economic benefits of the agreement and its potential political advantages for the Kremlin.
"Zelensky is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States," Trump said in his post, despite evidence that the war in Iran is the primary driver of the price surge.
Zelensky said on Oct. 18 that Russia had attacked Ukrainian energy and oil and gas facilities 76 times since Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Oct. 11, leaving tens of thousands of families without electricity.
Ukraine initially paused strikes on Russian refineries following Trump's announcement, but resumed the campaign on Oct. 15 after Moscow continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Trump then doubled down on criticism of President Volodymyr Zelensky, accusing the Ukrainian leader of not wanting to end the war at all.
"He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead. I WANT THIS WAR END!"

articles.title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
articles.body:
Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
- Published
Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.
One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.
He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.
The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland.
Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.
He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow, Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.
There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.
The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."
And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.
The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.
There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024.
It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.
Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine
Two men tell of secret operations inside Russia.
- If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube, external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with Ukraine
Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome.
"At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the war… Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.
His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets.
"When these [drone] components are combined… it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.
He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.
If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.
Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance.
"You will get a file... from me or a colleague… with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.
Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.
He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.
"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals live… Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.
"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."
He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.
Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.
"As a rule… we also check the data [on that person]… Only after that we say whether we work or not."
But he argued that his team's actions were justified.
"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraine… to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."
Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.
Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."
But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.
Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.
Foma did his own digging on Ivan.
After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.
Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.
Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too.
"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.
To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.
Foma has the same rule for his operatives.
"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chats… leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.
Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.
"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.
Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.
Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.
So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.
Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him.
"You go to a third country… where [Ukraine's] agents meet you… and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.
Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".
But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.
Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag.
"There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holes… and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.
Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.
Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work.
"Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."
But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change.
"Putin won't live forever," he said.

articles.title: Belarus Could Enter War Against Ukraine by Deploying Ballistic Missiles at Russia’s Request, Zelenskyy Says
articles.body:
- Category

Belarus Could Enter War Against Ukraine by Deploying Ballistic Missiles at Russia’s Request, Zelenskyy Says
Russia is considering deploying additional ballistic missile systems in Belarus, potentially expanding its ability to strike western Ukraine, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned on October 17.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zelenskyy’s remarks to journalists on October 17, Moscow is seeking Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko’s cooperation to expand its military infrastructure in the country and support further attacks against Ukraine.
The Ukrainian president said Russia has already positioned communications relay equipment in Belarus to facilitate drone operations, but Moscow appears interested in expanding its capabilities beyond unmanned aerial systems.
Zelenskyy warned that deploying ballistic missiles on Belarusian territory would create an additional threat to Ukraine’s western regions, potentially allowing Russian forces to launch attacks from another direction.
He also emphasized that such a move would further involve Belarus in Russia’s full-scale invasion, exposing the country to additional security risks.
The president said Ukraine intends to strengthen its air defenses in response to the evolving threat. This includes increasing production of turret-mounted defensive systems and distributing them across regions based on the intensity of Russian attacks.
Belarus has played a supporting role in Russia’s invasion since February 2022, when Russian troops used its territory to launch an offensive toward Kyiv. Moscow has also used Belarusian airfields, military facilities, and airspace to support operations against Ukraine.
Although Belarusian armed forces have not formally entered the fighting as a separate combat force, the Lukashenko government continues to provide Russia with logistical support, access to infrastructure, and military-industrial assistance.
Earlier, on October 16, Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko ordered the creation of “people’s militia” units in every village council across the country, expanding local defense structures amid growing concerns over Belarus’s potential deeper involvement in Russia’s war against Ukraine.

articles.title: Intensifying drone attacks on ships in Black Sea bring war ever closer to Nato shores
articles.body:
The first the crew of the Bulgarian ferry Dioscuria knew of an attack on a cargo ship in their country’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea in the early hours of 6 October was a distant explosion 70 miles off the coastal town of Byala.
The Turkish-owned Alfa Watan, heading for the Romanian port of Sulina, had been struck by suspected Russian air and naval drones. Arriving on the scene, Dioscuria found an overturned lifeboat and lifejackets in the water. There was no sign, however, of Alfa Watan’s crew of 10.
Six days later drones struck another ship off the coast of Bulgaria, HS Dignity. Eleven crew members died.
By Thursday, the attacks had encroached on Romania’s airspace and territorial water. Two chemical tankers, Wine Trader and Yara J, were attacked and left burning. Seven more sailors were missing.
The attacks on six ships in 10 days – the Able and Chelsea-3 were also hit – marked a dramatic escalation in a maritime conflict that is pressing on Nato’s borders.
While global attention has focused on the risks for sailors travelling through the strait of Hormuz, in recent months it is the Black Sea that has emerged as the more dangerous passage, with more sailors lost in a week and a half than US service members killed in the entire Iran war.
The maritime insurer and risk analyst Ambrey has warned that there is no end in sight to the threats to Black Sea cargo shipping, including grain and oil, and that insurance prices for passage of the waters have rocketed.
Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey, has noted a sharp increase in the tempo of attacks beginning in July. Russian forces are estimated to be responsible for 80% of them.
The recent loss of life, he suggests, has been exacerbated by “double tap” attacks involving aerial and surface drones, the latter often carrying up to half a tonne of explosive payloads. Smaller vessels that primarily use the Danube canal system have sunk rapidly.
“While attacks against merchant vessels in the Black Sea are not new, we are seeing an escalation both in terms of the number of attacks and in the geographical scope,” Alexa said.
The profile of vessels being attacked – that is, ships trading with Ukraine – had not changed, he added. “The Russian intent is clear, which is to degrade the export of Ukrainian grain and agricultural products.”
The result has been a precipitous fall in the number of vessels visiting Ukraine. Insurance rates have soared, and seafarers and operators have become increasingly reluctant to operate in the Black Sea basin, even on ships unconnected with Ukrainian cargoes.
The vast majority of the more than 60 fatalities of seafarers in the Black Sea since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 have occurred in the past year. In September the Joint War Committee, representing the London insurance market, moved to extend the high-risk areas of the Black Sea to include the whole of the basin, excluding the territorial waters of Turkey, Romania, Bulgaria and Georgia.
The threat is not confined to the Black Sea itself. Attacks on Ukraine’s Black Sea ports have also increased sharply in the past year.
A number of factors are driving the expansion and escalation of the conflict towards the shores of Nato countries, say experts. Russia has responded to a geographical expansion of Ukrainian strikes on its shadow fleet of oil tankers by intensifying strikes on Ukrainian agricultural cargoes – a key component of Kyiv’s economy.
As ships sought safer passage further from the coastlines, so the threat has changed: from naval mines to drones, with ever longer ranges.
Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, said after the sinking of the Alfa Watan: “Commercial ships – and innocent crews – are being targeted, with lives already lost at sea.”
In a statement at the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, Col Joby Rimmer, a senior British military adviser, said: “Attacks that fail to distinguish between military objectives and civilian vessels, or that are expected to cause excessive incidental harm to civilians and civilian vessels in relation to the anticipated military advantage, may violate international humanitarian law and the UN convention on the law of the sea.
“Each attack raises the risk to crews of every nationality, drives up insurance costs and restricts the flow of food to those who depend on it. The UK is deeply concerned by the far-reaching consequences of successive crises across the global maritime domain. Stable and secure sea lanes are a global common good from which we all benefit.”
Operators have warned of the wider impact on trade in the Black Sea, including from Bulgarian ports. In a recent interview on Bulgarian television, the shipping agency owner Todor Georgiev warned the Black Sea was in danger of becoming a “dead zone”.
“Whenever the Russians are caught having struck a ship with one of their drones, they claim the vessel was carrying weapons,” he said. “Weapons are not being transported to Ukraine via the Black Sea.”
Rumen Radev, Bulgaria’s prime minister, has described the attacks in the vicinity of his country’s territorial waters as “absolutely unacceptable”.
Bulgarian officials are calling for the EU and Nato to support the efforts to enhance security, while working with Turkey and Romania on increased regional security.
Although they have refused to attribute blame to Russia, officials have said there is “no logic” for Ukraine to attack its own shipments.
“We do not have clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility to either side,” said Radev. “However, as I have already stated, the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation.”
As Russian strikes on shipping move ever closer to the borders of Nato members, they pose mounting security challenges to the mutual defence organisation, which is already confronting Moscow’s growing hybrid warfare across Europe. There is speculation that the affected Nato countries may be forced to invoke article 4 of the organisation’s treaty, a step below the article 5 invocation of mutual self defence.
Triggered twice already around the Ukraine war – in the immediate aftermath of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and by Poland in 2025 after Russian drones violated Warsaw’s airspace – it calls for formal crisis discussions on a security threat.
On Thursday Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, met Radev and Nicușor Dan, Romania’s president, to discuss security in the Black Sea. Rutte said: “Nato will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed.”
Another consequence of the escalating attacks is the renewed danger of a global food crisis. Ukraine and Russia are major exporters of grain, as is Romania.
“We’re looking at the Black Sea as a global food artery,” said Oana Toiu, the Romanian foreign minister, at a security conference in Warsaw last week. “It is currently, unfortunately, the deadliest sea when it comes to the number of casualties of sailors in the last months. That means we need to increase our investments in deterrence, defence.”
Damien Chevallier, the director of maritime safety at the UN’s International Maritime Organization, warned last month of the long-term impact on shipping caused by attacks linked to the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.
“With rising casualties across the Black Sea, Red Sea and strait of Hormuz, being a seafarer has become a genuinely dangerous profession,” he said. “Seafarers are not trained to deal with threats from actions which are linked to wider security issues or geopolitical situations.
“What makes this moment genuinely unprecedented is not just the number of incidents, but the pattern behind them. Shipping has become a deliberate instrument of geopolitical leverage.”

articles.title: Latvia’s combat-tested ground drone shows off in Finland
articles.body:
- Latvian company NATRIX demonstrated its combat-tested unmanned ground vehicle at Millog’s UGV Demo 2026 in Mikkeli, Finland, on Oct. 8.
- The vehicle showed forest mobility, obstacle crossing, cargo transport and remote control before Finnish military, border guard and police officials.
Latvian company NATRIX, already a supplier of ground drones to Latvia’s armed forces, showed its battle-tested unmanned ground vehicle to Finnish military and security officials on Oct. 8, driving it through forest terrain and hauling cargo at an unmanned ground systems demonstration in Mikkeli, Finland.
The event was organized by Millog, the Finnish defense maintenance company that services much of the Finnish Defence Forces’ equipment, and brought together several manufacturers of ground drones. NATRIX attended with its Finnish partner Armatech Finland, the company said in a LinkedIn post, and showed the vehicle to representatives from several branches of the Finnish Defence Forces, the Finnish Ministry of Defence, the Finnish Border Guard, the Police of Finland and international military delegations.
In its live demonstration, NATRIX said the vehicle showed its mobility and ability to cross obstacles in rough forest terrain, carried cargo, and was driven remotely by an operator. The company also briefed visitors on lessons from the platform’s use in combat.
The NATRIX UGV is a compact, battery-powered vehicle built for front-line resupply, casualty evacuation and reconnaissance support. The company says it can carry more than 200 kg (440 pounds) of cargo and can be fitted with a NATO-standard stretcher to bring out wounded troops, and that its communications use several backup channels to stay connected in jammed environments.
The platform began combat testing in Ukraine’s Donbas region in early 2025, after the first vehicles were funded through a donation campaign run by Latvian public media and the Ziedot.lv charity platform. Co-founder Gatis Vectirāns said at the time that a fully charged vehicle could travel about 20 km (12 miles), and that Ukrainian operators had praised its power and build quality, Latvian public broadcaster LSM reported.
In April 2026, Latvia’s Ministry of Defence signed contracts with NATRIX and two other Latvian companies, Brasa Defence Systems and LV-Teh, to supply domestically made ground drones and gradually introduce them into regular units of the National Armed Forces, The Defence Blog reported. The deals followed live demonstrations on military training ranges in 2025 and include support, repair and modernization, as well as the right for Latvia to order more systems quickly under the same framework.
Ukraine now relies heavily on ground drones to move ammunition, food and water to positions where Russian surveillance drones make vehicle and foot traffic dangerous, and to evacuate wounded soldiers under fire. Finland, which shares a 1,340 km (830-mile) border with Russia, has been studying those lessons as it expands its own forces.
NATRIX is developing autonomous features such as “follow me” and automatic return modes and plans to add mine-clearing equipment and weapon integration. Last month the company also unveiled a separate ground drone designed to patrol critical infrastructure such as energy sites, ports and airports, and it said the Mikkeli demonstration opened talks with Finnish defense and security officials on possible future cooperation.

articles.title: Egypt's top security body agrees to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against Houthi attacks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Egypt's top security body agrees to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against Houthi attacks
Egypt's top security body said Sunday it has agreed to support close ally Saudi Arabia in the major escalation of fighting between the kingdom and Houthi rebels in Yemen, which has marked the latest front in the Iran war.
Saudi Arabia has been pressing allies for military assistance. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked airports and oil infrastructure across the kingdom with drones and missiles that can change direction during flight, posing a challenge to interceptors. At least 19 people have been killed, thousands of flights have been affected and global markets have been rattled.
Also on Sunday, the Saudi defense minister was meeting with the United Arab Emirates president about ways to strengthen cooperation, according to the UAE’s news agency WAM. The countries have had tense relations in the recent past as they backed different factions in the Yemeni coalition fighting the rebels.
The Egyptian announcement on military assistance came a month after a visit by the Saudi crown prince. Chaired by President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi, the National Defense Council decided to provide “all possible forms of support” to enable Saudi Arabia to defend its security, according to a presidential statement.
It didn’t provide details. El-Sissi on Saturday called for parliament to grant him the authorization to deploy troops and military equipment abroad.
The surge in fighting has threatened civilians in both Saudi Arabia and Yemen, which has seen a return to civil war. The interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, Aden, has seen its airport and a palace used by the government attacked in the past week.
On Sunday, an airstrike killed at least nine people, including five children and two women, in Yemen’s rebel-held northern province of Saada, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said.
Spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said the strike hit a house in Sahar district and wounded 19 others, including 11 children. Some were in critical condition, he said.
Al-Asbahi blamed Saudi Arabia. There was no immediate comment from the kingdom. The Houthi-run al-Masirah satellite channel aired footage of people clearing debris with their hands and pulling two young people out of the rubble.
The rebels said attacks by Saudi-led forces had killed or wounded over 30 people in the past 24 hours. Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesperson, said 110 missiles or airstrikes were carried out against civilian sites in Sanaa and other cities. The Associated Press could not independently verify the claim.
Across the border in Saudi Arabia, a Saudi helicopter gunship crashed near the city of Najran in the southwest, killing its two-member crew, a Saudi military spokesperson said, citing a technical malfunction. The Houthis earlier claimed to have downed it.
Later, Saudi Civil Defense authorities said a projectile fired by the Houthis landed in a residential area of Najran province, wounding six people.
The Houthis have resumed attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks because the kingdom has supported Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the civil war. The rebels recently seized more territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis’ chief negotiator on Sunday blamed Saudi Arabia for the escalation. Mohamed Abdulsalam said on social media that the rebels had warned the kingdom against striking the rebel-held Sanaa airport in mid-July.
That strike prevented the landing of an Iranian flight carrying a Houthi delegation returning from the funeral of Iran’s supreme leader, who had been killed in the opening strikes of the war in February.
The Houthis, angry over the longstanding Saudi blockade on them, declared their own blockade on the kingdom.
Oman had offered a five-day truce during which the two sides would meet and settle their dispute, Abdulsalam said. He said the Houthis agreed to stop attacks if Saudi Arabia agreed to “humanitarian demands.” He didn’t elaborate.
He said Saudi Arabia didn’t show “any indication that it is ready to deal positively” with the demands. The rebels shortly after that launched their offensive down the Red Sea coast.
A Saudi diplomat last week in a rare briefing said the kingdom had called for a meeting in Oman with the Houthis in July “to resolve outstanding differences and bring an end to this escalation,” but the rebels refused to participate.
On Sunday, the Sunni Muslim world’s foremost religious institution, Al-Azhar in Egypt, called for the formation of an “urgent mediation committee” to end conflicts across the Arab region.

articles.title: Fact Check: Ukrainian Drones Did Not Silence Russian Propaganda Bots
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone strikes on three Yandex data centers this month caused widespread disruption to Russian internet services, but researchers and fact-checkers have found no evidence that they silenced Russian propaganda networks on Western social media, contrary to viral claims that circulated after the attacks.
The strikes
The attacks came in response to a Russian campaign against Ukrainian data centers. Since late September, Russian missiles and drones have damaged or destroyed data centers belonging to at least eight Ukrainian companies, and Russia’s Defense Ministry described the campaign as “a forced digital detox.” The Ukrainian Digital Transformation Ministry said around 100,000 households in the Kyiv region lost internet access after the first strikes.
On October 8, Ukrainian drones hit Yandex’s data center in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, which reportedly housed two of the company’s three supercomputers. The following night, a facility in Kaluga was struck, and several modules were knocked out. On October 11, Yandex said operations at its data center in the Vladimir region had been completely suspended after a drone attack. In total, three of Yandex’s six data centers were hit. On October 14, Ukraine also struck a Sberbank data center under construction in the Saratov region.
The damage inside Russia was significant. Users reported outages in Yandex Mail, Pay, Disk, Go and other services, and Yandex Cloud clients were also affected. Websites of other companies and media outlets operated with restrictions. Internet monitor NetBlocks measured connectivity on the Yandex Cloud network at about 30% of normal levels and on Yandex LLC’s network at 63%. Meduza reported that a full recovery is likely to take months.
The viral claim
The claim that Russian bots had been silenced originated with a chart from Cloudflare Radar, a public internet traffic dashboard, showing that automated traffic from a Yandex network (AS13238) had fallen to 0.4% of its two-week peak. Tech outlet Tom’s Hardware reported that Russian disinformation bot traffic had been nearly eliminated overnight.
Claims soon followed that online activity around Germany’s Alternative for Germany (AfD), the US MAGA movement and Britain’s Reform UK had collapsed. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on October 12, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the strikes had made it “a little easier to breathe” on social media platforms, with less hatred, division and provocation because there were fewer bots. Czech MEP Tomáš Zdechovský shared a chart showing AfD-related activity falling by 30% and then 56%, which reached millions of views and was repeated by French daily Le Parisien.
What the chart measured
AS13238 is a network that Yandex lists in its own technical documentation for its bots, and those bots are mostly the company’s search crawler, software that indexes web pages for its search engine. Google operates a similar crawler. Such programs do not post, comment or imitate users on social media. When Yandex’s servers went down, its crawler went down with them.
Cloudflare’s head of Radar, Lai Yi Ohlsen, said “bot traffic” in the dashboard refers to automated requests to websites, not activity on social media platforms. Cloudflare’s own analysis found that the YandexBot crawler fell by 99% on October 11 and has since recovered to about 85% of normal levels. Bot traffic from Yandex Cloud fell by about 40%. Malicious automation, however, moved to other Russian hosting providers such as Radist and Selectel. Russian bot traffic targeting one gambling-sector client rose from 167.7 million to 170.1 million requests over the week. Russian-origin traffic to social media platforms fell by 0.6%, while automated “post,” “reply” and “like” actions on one platform decreased by 5.7%. Cloudflare said it could not rule out a connection entirely without data from outside its network.
No decline in Western debates
Graphika, which maps online communities, tested the main claims against its data. On October 11, AfD-related accounts published 40,365 posts from 1,022 accounts, compared with 42,040 posts from 1,037 accounts a week earlier. Graphika said the 4% dip was within normal range, as the community’s Sunday activity had varied by up to 38% over the previous 11 weeks. The viral AfD chart also showed no rise on September 6, when Saxony-Anhalt held its state election, even though real AfD activity increased by 42% that day. Mentions of MAGA on X rose 25% in the hours after the Vladimir strike. A chart showing a “collapse” in mentions of Anthony Fauci started from a spike caused by Sen. Rand Paul’s release of Fauci’s diary entries the previous day. Graphika also found that moving the comparison window in viral Reddit tables by a few hours turned a 54% decline into a 109% increase.
German researchers reached the same conclusion. The Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS) said the AfD chart’s data could not be verified and was suspected to be AI-generated, although this has not been confirmed. CeMAS director Josef Holnburger told ZDF he saw no decline in Russian disinformation campaigns that could be explained by the strikes. US-based monitoring group dTeam told BBC Verify that traffic from known Russian accounts and bot clusters had not changed on any platform, and that operations such as Storm-1516 and Matryoshka remained active. Zelensky’s office later told the BBC that the president had been referring to the atmosphere on social media rather than a measured fall in bot activity.
Pro-Israel claims about Palestine
A similar claim spread among pro-Israel accounts, which shared charts purporting to show posts containing “Free Palestine” falling from about 70,000 a day to about 30,000, and mentions of “genocide” falling from a peak of about 280,000. The claim was that Russian bots had been driving anti-Israel content online. Israel Hayom reported similar figures, and the story was discussed on US cable television.
Jewish Breaking News, which posted the charts on Instagram, acknowledged that they counted keyword mentions rather than Russian bots. The charts covered October 5 to 11, a period that included the third anniversary of the October 7 attack, when such mentions rise every year before falling back. Researchers also noted that some of the graphs ended on an incomplete day. Israel365 News concluded that the anti-Israel accounts had kept posting.
Where activity did decline
Graphika did find declines in Russian-speaking spaces. Russian-language Telegram channels posted 5% to 15% less in the two days after the Vladimir strike, while Ukrainian, Iranian and Romanian channels showed little change. On Reddit, activity in r/askarussian, a forum where Russians answer questions from foreigners, fell after all three strikes. Graphika said internet disruption inside Russia was one possible explanation.
Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation (CCD) reported a sharper effect. Using Osavul software, it analyzed 22,664 messages from 5,201 accounts showing signs of inauthentic behavior in Ukraine’s information space between October 6 and 12. On October 8, messages fell from 4,032 to 660 and active accounts from 1,526 to 258, a drop of about 84%. Activity recovered within two days and exceeded pre-strike levels by October 10 and 11. After the Vladimir data center was shut down, messages fell again by 42.6% on October 12. The partial damage in Kaluga did not coincide with a decline. The CCD findings cover networks targeting Ukraine rather than Western audiences.
CeMAS also reported that it had not observed German-language activity by the Doppelgänger operation on X since October 9, though it said this could not yet be linked to the strikes. Leaked internal documents from Moscow’s Social Design Agency, a firm behind many Russian disinformation campaigns, contained links to Yandex Cloud, where screenshots of campaigns were stored. CeMAS said it was plausible that individual operations relied on Yandex services, but that a complete shutdown of their activity across platforms was unlikely.
The wider impact
Analysts say the strikes exposed a structural weakness in Russia’s digital infrastructure. Because Russia has developed a closed internet, there are no data centers abroad to fail over to. After the second strike, Yandex reached short-term agreements with competitors VK Cloud, K2Cloud and Selectel to move affected services and clients onto their infrastructure. Western technology sanctions are also expected to make it harder to replace damaged equipment, particularly GPUs.
What the episode shows
Russian influence operations are real and well documented, which is part of why the Yandex story spread so easily. CeMAS attributed its spread to misunderstanding of what “bots” are and to wishful thinking and pointed to confirmation bias: the tendency to look for information that confirms what one already believes. Graphika found that the claim was shared mostly by pro-Ukraine audiences, not by the communities it said had been silenced. Researchers recommend a few simple checks before sharing such claims: what a chart counts and on which platform, whether it compares the same days and hours in earlier weeks, and whether unrelated communities changed by the same amount. Countering Russian disinformation depends on accurate evidence and claims that confirm what audiences want to believe deserve the same scrutiny as those that do not.

articles.title: Rubio: Ukraine Does Not Have Access to Starshield
articles.body:
Ukraine currently lacks access to the specialized military-grade Starshield satellite network and has requested the technology to conduct deep-interdiction strikes inside Russia, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.
Speaking to journalists in comments released by the US Department of State, Rubio clarified the distinction between SpaceX’s standard commercial Starlink communications framework and the dedicated Starshield architecture operated under contract with the US Department of Defense.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Starlink is a commercial product, okay? And so it’s regulated and handled as a commercial product. Starshield is a defense product, a military product,” Rubio stated.
“That is something that the United States military uses. It’s not at this moment available to Ukraine, and that’s under conversation. It’s under discussion right now how they would want to use it.”
Responding to questions regarding reports of technological throttling, Rubio directly refuted claims that the Trump administration had mandated bandwidth or velocity caps on terminals operating in Ukrainian combat sectors.
“I know Ukraine wants access to Starshield. They do not have Starshield now. They’ve asked for access to it in order to conduct deep strikes inside of Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment,” Rubio emphasized.
“Those are two different products.”
Zelensky Calls Trump’s Sanctions Waiver a Mistake
White House denies intentional velocity caps
Rubio pushed back against assertions by President Volodymyr Zelensky that artificial operational constraints imposed on Starlink terminals inside Ukraine were deliberate administrative measures.
“I don’t know what Zelensky said. I’m not sure Zelensky knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate. We have nothing to do with that,” Rubio said.
“Nobody ordered that Starlink speed to be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it’s been restored. It’s back to where it was before. That’s Starlink, though. They were using Starlink for their drones.”
Addressing media reports suggesting executive coordination to limit unmanned systems, the secretary of state characterized the allegations as completely unfounded.
“Nothing to do with the White House. I saw a report on that the other day. It’s just categorically false,” Rubio told reporters.
“No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it. But my understanding is it’s back up and running. That’s what I read – that’s what we heard two days ago.”
Zelensky’s 161 km/h disclosure
Rubio’s comments follow detailed disclosures delivered on Saturday, Oct. 17, by President Zelensky, who revealed that Starlink terminals operating inside Ukrainian territory had been subjected to a strict velocity limitation of 161 km/h (100 mph).
According to Zelensky, whenever equipped domestic platforms exceeded the 161 km/h threshold, satellite connections automatically severed, causing operators to lose control of unmanned interceptors in mid-flight.
The velocity cap effectively disabled domestic drone interceptors tasked with neutralizing high-speed, turbojet-powered Russian Shahed loitering munitions, which penetrate sovereign airspace at speeds exceeding 400 km/h (250 mph).
Zelensky highlighted that Ukrainian technical teams conducted cross-border comparative evaluations, sending Starlink-equipped vehicles into EU territory, where the devices operated uninterrupted at velocities of 180 km/h (112 mph). The Ukrainian leader argued that the trials confirmed the restrictions were geographically targeted at Ukrainian airspace rather than stemming from global software glitches.
The Starshield controversy
The technological dispute underscores widening geopolitical friction between Washington and Kyiv over long-range interdiction limits and commercial communications dependencies.
Rubio’s denials echo statements by US President Donald Trump, who told that neither he nor SpaceX founder Elon Musk ordered operational caps on Ukraine’s military communications, asserting that “everything is the same as it’s always been.”
However, both official denials contradict reporting by The Telegraph, which cited four sources familiar with the matter stating that Musk directly proposed satellite service limitations to Trump, who approved the measure, clearing the way for the Pentagon to restrict Starshield functionality.
Sources cited in the report claimed Musk sought to shift public accountability onto the White House amid concerns over potential consumer boycotts across European markets following civilian casualties in Kyiv.

articles.title: U.S. Army tests Ukrainian uncrewed surface vessels as drone carriers
articles.body:
- Ukrainian-built Magura drone boats took part in the U.S. Army’s Bayonet Quest 26 exercise in Michigan, launching aerial drones from a platform on the hull.
- The same boat family sank a target ship during Balikatan 2026 in the Philippines on April 24, 2026.
Ukraine’s Magura-type MV7 uncrewed surface vessels, the drone boats that have sunk Russian warships in the Black Sea, took part in a U.S. Army exercise in Michigan, where they were used as floating launch pads for aerial drones.
The boats appeared during Bayonet Quest 26, which the 7th Infantry Division, part of Multi-Domain Command-Pacific, ran across Michigan from Sept. 26 to Oct. 6, 2026. The division said soldiers used the exercise to test autonomous systems and uncrewed aircraft as it experiments with how new technology can extend sensing, reach and decision-making.
According to images and materials released by the division, the exercise included crewed-uncrewed maritime testing that paired a Mk VI patrol boat with autonomous systems, giving the U.S. Army a look at how the two could work together in complex terrain. The MV7 boats, built by Ukrainian manufacturer UFORCE, carried a dedicated platform on the front of the hull from which aerial drones took off.
The 7th Infantry Division did not say how many MV7 boats took part, which model was used, or what type of aerial drones they carried.
The Michigan exercise is the second publicly known use of the Magura family by U.S. forces this year. During Balikatan 2026, the largest annual U.S.-Philippines military exercise, Magura boats destroyed a decommissioned target ship in a live-fire maritime strike off Itbayat in the Batanes islands on April 24, 2026. UFORCE confirmed on June 8 that its vessels had taken part, after The Defence Blog reported that U.S. special forces had sunk a ship with Ukrainian-designed drone boats.
Magura boats became one of Ukraine’s best-known weapons after its military intelligence used them to strike Russian Black Sea Fleet ships near Crimea, forcing much of the fleet to move away from the peninsula. Ukraine has since developed versions armed with missiles and machine guns, and in 2025 Ukrainian military intelligence said Magura boats armed with air-to-air missiles had shot down Russian fighter jets over the Black Sea.
Using a drone boat to carry and launch aerial drones extends how far a small craft can see and strike without putting a crewed ship close to the target. Ukraine has used drone boats in a similar way to carry smaller strike drones toward Russian-held coastlines, and the U.S. Army has been looking at uncrewed boats for its units in the Pacific, where many operations would play out among islands and along coastlines.
The 7th Infantry Division, based at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington state, was reorganized under Multi-Domain Command-Pacific as part of the U.S. Army’s efforts to prepare for operations in the Indo-Pacific region.

articles.title: Lavrov’s pivotal Monday visit to Tehran with a mediation flavor
articles.body:
Lavrov’s pivotal Monday visit to Tehran with a mediation flavor
Arman-e-Emrooz analyzed Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov’s upcoming visit to Tehran on Monday. Reports suggest that the trip is part of Russia’s ongoing mediation efforts between Iran and the United States. In recent months, Moscow has sought to position itself as a facilitator in reducing tensions between Tehran and Washington.
The timing of the visit coincides with US review of sanctions and measures related to the so-called shadow fleet, highlighting the complexity of the current situation. On one hand, the United States faces domestic pressure to lower energy prices ahead of elections. On the other, Iran is seeking meaningful economic relief. These circumstances have created an environment in which both sides may be inclined toward tactical flexibility. The meeting between Lavrov and Araghchi could represent an important step in that direction, provided both parties enter discussions with a shared understanding of existing realities and align their expectations with practical possibilities. The outcome of the visit could influence developments in the coming weeks.
Khorasan: Trump, the mother of all lies
Khorasan addressed Trump’s recent claim about using the “Mother of All Bombs” in a future strike against Iran. Trump is making such threats at a time when the economic consequences of tensions in the region have significantly increased costs related to energy and essential goods for American families and other countries, putting additional pressure on his administration. The paper described Trump as a gambler seeking a face-saving exit from the Iran war quagmire. After previous efforts, including military deployments to the region and severe economic pressure campaigns that were expected to quickly force Iran into submission, failed to achieve their goals, Trump has now turned to the rhetoric of the “Mother of All Bombs.” The article contends that the purpose of such statements is to create psychological pressure inside Iran and gain leverage in ongoing exchanges of messages between the two sides.
Shargh: An open-ended American policy or an open-ended Iranian one?
Shargh devoted its editorial to decision-making regarding the current conflict. The newspaper argued that decisions made today are linked not only to the future of 90 million Iranians but, in some respects, to global developments as well. The editorial proposed moving beyond the simple pro-war versus pro-peace divide and distinguishing among three separate positions: first, ending the war at any cost; second, negotiating an end to the conflict while preserving core national red lines; and third, continuing resistance until specific political and security conditions are achieved. This conceptual distinction is important for policymaking. A person who favors negotiations does not necessarily support surrender or territorial fragmentation, just as someone who considers resistance necessary is not necessarily indifferent to its human and economic costs. The paper argues that recognizing this distinction prevents an “open-ended American policy” from automatically being interpreted as an “open-ended Iranian policy,” which it describes as the key issue.
Ettelaat: Possibility of a longer conflict process
Ettelaat examined possible future scenarios for the conflict. US demands have shifted from redefining Iran’s regional role to focusing on the nuclear issue and the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Iran’s demands have reportedly evolved from direct compensation by Washington to a conditional investment fund financed by other parties. Nevertheless, the newspaper argued that two major ambiguities remain unresolved and may even have deepened as a result of the conflict. Continued American pressure is said to intensify divisions among Iranian elites and increase their reluctance to take the first step. Washington, however, may interpret this hesitation as evidence that pressure is working and therefore warrants further action. According to the analysis, diplomacy has reached a deadlock. As US midterm elections draw closer, there remains a possibility that the conflict will add another chapter to the historical memories each side holds of the other, extending a process that has already lasted for more than four decades.
Hamshahri: The impact of war and economic tensions on US elections
Hamshahri focused on concerns influencing American voters. The newspaper argued that economic conditions and the conflict involving Iran have become major public concerns. Rising prices for gasoline, diesel fuel, and essential goods, along with inflation and growing concerns about living costs, have increased pressure on the Trump administration. The paper noted that these concerns are reflected in public opinion polls and political analyses. At the same time, the Iran conflict remains among voters’ principal worries. Hamshahri also linked these concerns to allegations regarding corruption and the financial interests of individuals close to Trump in connection with the conflict. As a result, the newspaper concluded that the economic pressures associated with the conflict cannot be ignored in assessing the US political climate. According to its analysis, these pressures have fueled public dissatisfaction and could present a significant challenge for Republicans in upcoming elections.

articles.title: Rubio says Ukraine without access to Starshield, future ‘under discussion’
articles.body:
Rubio says Ukraine without access to Starshield, future ‘under discussion’
US secretary of state says Ukraine has requested access to military-grade version of Starlink for strikes deep inside Russia.
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite service, is currently unavailable to Ukraine, but a request from Kyiv to access the system for attacks deep inside Russia is “under discussion”.
Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Rubio stressed Starshield’s distinction with Starlink, the internet service provided by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
“Starlink is a commercial product, okay? And so it’s regulated and handled as a commercial product. Starshield is a defence product, a military product,” said Rubio, in comments released by the Department of State.
“They’ve asked for access to it in order to conduct deep strikes inside of Russia. They do not have access to it at this moment,” he added. “That’s under conversation.”
Launched in 2022 and provided to the US government, Starshield is designed for military use as it allows for deeper encryption to process sensitive information. SpaceX says it is primarily used by US defence agencies and other “government partners”.
Last week, Ukrainian officials said restrictions on Starlink terminals had slowed some drones on the battlefield, as Ukraine tries to hold back Russian forces in their nearly five-year war.
In his comments at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, Rubio also rejected Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s suggestion that the reported disruption to Starlink services in Ukraine on Wednesday was deliberate.
“Well, I don’t know what Zelenskyy said. I’m not sure Zelenskyy knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate. We have nothing to do with that,” Rubio said.
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that the satellites are not tracking antennas on flying objects travelling faster than 161 kilometres per hour (100 miles per hour). This is affecting Ukrainian drones in their defence against Russian jet-powered drones and in their own medium-range attacks, he added.
Rubio said the US had not ordered Starlink speeds to be reduced and that the service had reportedly been restored to its previous level.
“No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it,” he said, calling the reports “categorically false”.
The remarks came as US President Donald Trump drew criticism from Democrats and Republicans after waiving sanctions on Russia and countries that buy its oil and gas, days before the restrictions were due to take effect under a law he signed last month.
Zelenskyy also criticised the sanctions waiver on Saturday, saying easing pressure on Russia would encourage further attacks.
“Financial rewards for [President Vladimir] Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking,” Zelenskyy posted on social media, urging the US to maintain pressure on Moscow.

articles.title: Romania downs two Russian jet drones near Sulina, days before NATO allies meet on Black Sea security
articles.body:
Two Romanian F-16s shot down two jet-powered Russian Geran attack drones over Romania’s territorial waters near Sulina on the evening of 17 October, Romania’s Defense Ministry said. The ministry released cockpit images of the mission the next day, as NATO allies prepare to discuss Black Sea security at a special session Romania requested.
This comes as Moscow continues its air attacks on Ukraine, while the US is trying to make deals with Russia over its diesel and lift sanctions. Russia keeps striking Ukraine’s energy system and cities, while its drones and suspected saboteurs keep turning up inside NATO, from tankers hit off Romania to a foiled arson attempt at a Starlink site in Lithuania.
Down within minutes
The F-16s took off from the 86th Air Base at Borcea at 17:43 after radar detected a group of air targets about 120 km east of Zmiinyi (Snake) Island, flying southwest, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi reported, citing the ministry. The first drone entered Romanian airspace at 17:59 and was shot down at 18:01 southeast of Sulina. The second entered at 18:01 and was downed at 18:05 east of Sulina.
Both were jet-powered attack drones of the Geran family, the ministry said. The Geran is Russia’s version of the Iranian-designed Shahed. When first detected, the drones were about 65 km from the coast of Russian-occupied Crimea and 140 km from the Ukrainian-held shore, and their southwest course may point to Russian origin, Militarnyi calculated.
Congress gave Trump 30 days to hit Russia’s oil buyers with 100% tariffs. He waives them two days before deadline, citing US interests. Moscow calls it historic
The ministry posted the cockpit images on 18 October, showing a missile launch and a fireball over the sea. “Targets spotted, identified, engaged and neutralized!” it wrote.
Allies to meet on the Black Sea
A special session of the North Atlantic Council, NATO’s top decision-making body, will discuss defense and deterrence in the Black Sea on 20 October at Romania’s request. Romanian President Nicușor Dan has confirmed that the two tankers that caught fire near Sulina last week were hit by drones, and a NATO military source told Reuters they were Russian.
Romanian radar has logged 54 drone intrusions into the country’s air and sea space since Russia’s full-scale invasion, 35 of them this year, and the military has shot down six such targets in 2026, Defense Ministry data show.
Searches in Poland and Lithuania
Within hours, Poland’s Operational Command said it was checking a possible airspace violation by an unknown object overnight into 18 October. Troops, police, and military police searched for a possible crash site south of Lublin after residents reported the loud sound of a flying object around 02:00, Militarnyi reported.
On the morning of 18 October, an unknown drone entered Lithuania’s airspace and triggered air raid alerts, the country’s crisis management center said. NATO jets accompanied it but could not shoot it down because of bad weather, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said. Debris preliminarily identified as drone parts was later found in the village of Juodžioniai in Pasvalys district, and the army said the drone may have entered from the direction of Poland.
Romania moved from escorting Russia’s stray drones to firing on them in July, when its F-16s downed three in 72 hours.
Read also
- Romania finally holds Russia responsible for the drone attacks on ships off its coast, and wants a joint NATO command for the Black Sea
- US weighs relief for sanctioned shadow fleet tankers, days after freeing Russian diesel
- Romania hits cost trap Ukraine spent years escaping: $400,000 missiles against $20,000 drones

articles.title: Zelensky: Ukrainian forces have liberated more territory since start of fall than Russia has captured
articles.body:
Zelensky: Ukrainian forces have liberated more territory since start of fall than Russia has captured
President Volodymyr Zelensky announced this in an evening video address, according to Ukrinform.
“The report by Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapaty was important. I thank our soldiers. We are seeing results on the front lines. The situation in Dobropillia: we are repelling Russian attempts to storm our positions there and thwarting infiltrations. It’s not easy, but our boys are doing it,” he said.
The head of state emphasized that Ukrainian troops are defending their positions on other fronts in the Donetsk, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia regions.
“We are recording the results of operations by the Airborne Forces and the Third Army Corps—our active defense. This year’s trend continues: since the beginning of fall, our soldiers have liberated more territory than the Russians have managed to capture. And it has been the same in other parts of the year,” the President stated.
According to him, the defenders continue to apply pressure on the front lines.
“Dobropillia, Kostiantynivka, Oleksievo-Druzhkivka, Orikhiv, Novopavlivka, Novoandriivka, and Velykomykhailivka—all are under Ukraine’s control. And we are defending areas near Kramatorsk. We are defeating the Russians 20 kilometers from Zaporizhzhia, not five, as someone over there in Russia is trying to convince Putin,” the President emphasized.
At the same time, he assured that the Ukrainian front is strong.
The head of state expressed his gratitude to every soldier and every unit that is fully carrying out their missions.
He singled out the 82nd Separate Airborne Assault Brigade, which is operating in the Oleksandrivka sector, for its confident assault operations and sound combat planning.
“I thank the soldiers of the 128th Separate Heavy Mechanized Brigade, which is also fighting with confidence and destroying the occupier’s forces in the direction of our city of Zaporizhzhia. I thank the 59th Separate Assault Brigade of Unmanned Systems and the 414th Separate Brigade of Unmanned Systems. Thank you, soldiers, for your outstanding results in defeating the occupier in the Donetsk region. We thank our assault units on the Pokrovsk front. We should also commend today the soldiers of the 1st Separate Unmanned Systems Center of the Special Operations Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine for the timely and precise delivery of our long-range strikes into Russian territory. And I also thank the soldiers of the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU), the Special Operations Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, and our intelligence agencies—the Main Intelligence Directorate (DIU) and the Foreign Intelligence Service (FISU)—for their precision. Thank you all! Well done!” Zelensky added.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that the U.S. has resumed the exchange of intelligence data with Ukraine after a period during which it had been suspended.
