articles.title: Romania Downs Two Russian-Type Geran Drones Over the Black Sea
articles.body:
Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two jet-powered Geran-series strike drones over the country's territorial waters in the Black Sea on October 17, with the Romanian Ministry of National Defense identifying the aircraft as belonging to a type used by Russia in the war in Ukraine.
The ministry said the drones were jet-powered models from the Geran family, the designation Russia uses for Iranian Shahed kamikaze drones. According to BGNES, two separate aircraft destroyed the drones within four minutes of each other.
The Romanian Air Force F-16s took off at 17:43 while conducting an air policing mission. The first drone was destroyed at 18:01 southeast of Sulina, after spending two minutes in Romanian national airspace, while the second was downed at 18:05 east of the same town, five minutes after entering the country's airspace. The targets were intercepted about 20 kilometers (13 miles) southeast of Sulina, near the Danube Delta.
Romanian authorities have not disclosed where the drones originated.
Following the incident, Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu wrote on X that “The Black Sea will be safe again.” She said NATO would address the situation at a North Atlantic Council meeting on Tuesday.
Țoiu also stressed the importance of the waterway to international trade and security, saying, “The Black Sea is a vital maritime corridor for global exports of grain, energy resources, and industrial goods; therefore, its stability is crucial for international food and energy security.”
The latest incident follows a series of drone attacks on civilian vessels in the Black Sea within the exclusive economic zones of Bulgaria and Romania.
On October 14, drones struck the Yara J while it was inside Romanian territorial waters. The vessel was anchored 8-10 nautical miles (15-19 kilometers) southeast of Sulina, marking the first reported drone strike against a ship in the territorial waters of a NATO member state.
The following day, drones hit the Wine Trader off Romania's coast, about 13 nautical miles (24 kilometers) southeast of Sulina, close to the country's territorial waters. Of the 12 people aboard, five were reported safe and seven remained missing.
On October 13, two vessels were attacked by drones in Bulgaria's contiguous zone, while two other commercial ships had been struck a week earlier within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
Seven commercial vessels were hit by drones off the Bulgarian and Romanian coasts between October 5 and October 15 alone. The official death toll from these attacks has not been confirmed, although the number of people killed could reach 30.
On Friday, the European Council condemned the attacks on ships near Bulgaria and Romania as “unacceptable,” without identifying Russia as responsible. Bulgaria and Romania have meanwhile announced plans to propose establishing a new NATO headquarters in the Black Sea.

articles.title: New Iranian defense minister has background in missile development, broader defense industry
articles.body:
Iran’s parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi as the country’s new defense minister on Sunday. His rise to the position in recent weeks is important. It helps stabilize Iran’s top defense leadership amid rising tensions in the Gulf. Iran expects more fighting to break out with the US or Israel. It is therefore trying to shore up its defenses at home and prepare for operations in the region.
Akhlaghi is believed to have a background in Iran’s missile program and its broader defense industry. Given the Islamic Republic’s attempts to rebuild its industrial defense base, this matters.
Reuters noted that Ketabchi is replacing Majid Ebn al-Reza, who took over in an interim capacity after then-defense minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed by US-Israeli strikes in February.
The Iranian parliament widely supported Akhlaghi's appointment. He has said he will rebuild the country’s defense sector.
Iran International, a media outlet critical of the Iranian regime, said that Akhlaghi was born in 1958. He studied chemical engineering at the Amirkabir University of Technology.
Akhlaghi then earned a master’s degree in strategic management from the Malek Ashtar University of Technology, an institution affiliated with Iran’s Defense Ministry.
Iranian state media provided a short bio, noting that “his previous positions include heading the Shahid Bakeri Industrial Group and serving as managing director of the Aerospace Industries Organization.”
Akhlaghi worked in Iranian defense industries for over four decades
Per the Iran International report, Akhlaghi “entered Iran’s defense industries in the early 1980s and spent more than four decades in technical, industrial, and managerial positions, according to Iranian state-linked media.”
It added that “much of his career has involved solid-fuel missile propulsion systems and the management of industrial facilities associated with ballistic missile development.”
The new defense minister also worked at the “Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, a subsidiary of the Aerospace Industries Organization involved in Iran’s ballistic missile program.”
He became the head of the Aerospace Industries Organization in 2014 and then headed the Defense Industries Organization.
Akhlaghi played a role in Iran’s Fateh-110 missile project, Iran International reported, as his “close relationship with Hassan Tehrani Moghaddam, a founder of the [IRGC’s] missile program, was central to his involvement in developing Iran’s missile industry.”
New Iranian defense minister sanctioned by UN for involvement in missile program
The new defense minister was sanctioned for his role in the missile program. In 2007, the UN listed Akhlaghi on a sanctions list “as an individual involved in nuclear or ballistic missile activities.”
This was because he was listed as “head of the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group, which is designated under resolution 1737 (2006) for its role in the ballistic missile program (designated under IRe.066),” the UN said.
The US Treasury Department also sanctioned Akhlaghi in 2008. He is well known for his role in Iran’s missile program. He has also been involved in procuring items for the program.
The person now in charge of Iran’s defense ministry is uniquely positioned to try to rebuild its missile program.
In March, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed that “after 20 days, I can tell you – Iran today has no ability to enrich uranium, and no ability to produce ballistic missiles.”
Recent reports, however, indicate that Iran is rebuilding its missile program and has also repaired many missile launchers.

articles.title: US resumes intelligence-sharing with Ukraine after pause, Zelensky says
articles.body:
US resumes intelligence-sharing with Ukraine after pause, Zelensky says
The United States has resumed providing Ukraine with critical intelligence to help it defend against Russian missile strikes, after a brief pause, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said in comments published on Oct 18.
Ukraine has relied on US intelligence to spot the fast-moving ballistic missiles that Russia has fired in waves at its cities. 
US President Donald Trump had said earlier this week that Washington was still sharing intelligence, although Ukrainian officials said some Russian strikes had occurred without warning.
Speaking to NBC’s Meet the Press, Zelensky said intelligence-sharing had been interrupted but later “de-blocked”.
“We are very thankful for this,” he said. “Now it works.”
But Zelensky said other US actions, such as signing a deal to import Russian diesel and waiving sanctions on Russia that had been slated to take effect this week, will hurt Ukraine.
“If the United States will officially take the side of Russia, of course if these two countries will be together, of course we will not prevail and we will not be able to stand,” he said.
Over the past week, a widening rift between Trump and Zelensky has sparked concerns that their tumultuous relationship could lead to even worse outcomes for Kyiv. 
Zelensky told NBC that he hopes Trump will remain an ally of Ukraine.
“We want to trust him, and I hope that he will change his decisions,” Zelensky said. “Because I think that it’s all mistakes and it will not help us. And it will not help United States.”
In a Truth Social post in the afternoon of Oct 18, Trump wrote that his decision-making was aimed at avoiding anything “that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table”.
Ukraine gets US help that Russia does not receive, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told NBC, citing intelligence-sharing and the provision of US munitions to other countries for resale to Ukraine.
But Bessent, speaking with Meet the Press after it aired the Zelensky interview, did not directly answer when asked multiple times whether the United States views Ukraine as an ally.
“Zelensky presents a false binary this morning that Ukraine must win,” Bessent said. “The war must end, and that will be with some kind of a negotiated settlement.” REUTERS

articles.title: US resumes intel sharing on Russian missile launches with Ukraine, Zelensky says
articles.body:
US resumes intel sharing on Russian missile launches with Ukraine, Zelensky says
The United States has resumed sharing intelligence about incoming Russian ballistic missiles with Ukraine after a pause lasting several days, President Volodymyr Zelensky told NBC News' "Meet the Press" in an interview published on Oct. 18.
"Only the United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky said.
The U.S. provides Ukraine with intelligence to help its military detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats. Zelensky said the issue had since been resolved and thanked Washington for restoring intelligence sharing.
"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Now it works."
At the same time, he said Ukraine was still experiencing an ongoing speed restriction on its use of Starshield — the militarized version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet system
Asked whether U.S. President Donald Trump or SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had personally ordered the restrictions, Zelensky said he did not know but believed "both" were involved. He added that if Trump decided to lift the restrictions, the service would return to its previous state.
read also
The resumption of intelligence sharing follows a Russian missile attack on Kyiv on Oct. 12, when five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital, causing "massive explosions." Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
A senior Ukrainian official previously told the Kyiv Independent that Ukraine's military leadership contacted its U.S. counterparts after the strike to clarify what had happened.
"They say they didn't cut it off, but they didn't warn us (about the attack) either," the official said. "The Americans said they just didn't see (the launch)... That's a weak excuse."
The incident came amid broader tensions over U.S. support for Ukraine. The Kyiv Independent earlier learned that the Trump administration had threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials in a push to protect Russian oil refineries.
Zelensky also told NBC that if thet U.S. chooses to support Russia over Kyiv, consequences would be dire — for both the Ukraine and the United States.
Such a move would be a "historic mistake" for Washington, Zelensky said. A U.S-Russia alliance would also destroy Ukraine's chances of defending itself against the full-scale invasion.
"“If these two countries will be together ... we will not prevail, and we will not be able to stand," Zelensky warned.
But the president also expressed hope that talks with the U.S. could take place next week, despite the ongoing difficulties between Kyiv and Washington.
"I'm very open to this, even with all the difficult circumstances," he said, estimating that a meeting could take place on Oct. 20-21.
Zelensky also denounced Kremlin narratives — sometimes repeated by Trump — that he opposes democratic elections in Ukraine.
If the U.S. and Russia believe Ukraine must hold elections during wartime, Moscow must grant Kyiv an unconditional ceasefire for 60 days, he said. The president said he made it clear that a minimum of 60 days was necessary for Ukraine to change its laws, prepare election infrastructure, and guarantee soldiers the opportunity to vote.
"If you think that I don't want elections, it's not true, and it's not fair," he said.
Zelensky said he would run for office again if elections were held during wartime, citing a responsibility to continue defending his country.

articles.title: US Congress Stalled on Response to Trump Russia Waiver – AP
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump’s decision to indefinitely postpone statutory sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia has triggered condemnation from lawmakers across both parties, though formal congressional intervention remains stalled due to the pre-election legislative recess, the Associated Press reported.
Congress previously passed the sanctions package with overwhelming veto-proof majorities, reflecting broad bipartisan backing for Ukraine and international deterrence.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
However, Trump’s executive order on Friday, Oct. 16, waiving enforcement just 48 hours before statutory enactment ignited pushback among key Republican and Democratic legislators.
Despite the outrage, lawmakers are not positioned to mount an immediate legislative response, as both the Senate and the House of Representatives remain in recess until after the crucial Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Republican fury and challenges to energy rationale
Senior Republicans voiced open frustration over the administration’s decision to shield Moscow from statutory trade duties and secondary financial penalties.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis characterized the executive waiver as “more than irresponsible,” pointing out that the Senate enacted the statute by an overwhelming 86-11 margin. Tillis accused the White House of offering unwarranted concessions to Russian President Vladimir Putin while undermining congressional prerogatives.
Tillis further pushed back against the administration’s economic defense, stating that if the White House seeks to reduce domestic energy prices, policymakers must focus on resolving the armed conflict involving Iran rather than enacting commercial steps that subsidize Russia.
Zelensky Calls Trump’s Sanctions Waiver a Mistake
Democratic leadership pledges congressional pushback
Democratic leaders similarly condemned the indefinite suspension, warning that easing economic pressure underwrites the Kremlin’s wartime economy and sustains long-range bombardments against Ukrainian civilian population centers.
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer accused Trump of directly propping up the Russian economy at the expense of American allies and democratic norms.
Senator Elizabeth Warren stated that the president is openly defying Congress, asserting that waiving statutory enforcement enables Putin to prolong an aggressive war of conquest.
Warren urged lawmakers to prepare legislative mechanisms to reverse the executive order once Congress reconvenes in Washington following the November vote.
The Associated Press reported that Trump suspended the penalties indefinitely, citing US national security considerations under statutory waiver authorities.
Because members of Congress are dispersed across their home districts campaigning ahead of the Nov. 3 balloting, any formal legislative counter-measures – such as the bipartisan “Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act” introduced by Representative Gregory Meeks or the “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act” drafted by Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick and Don Bacon – will face procedural delays until post-election sessions commence.
Background on the Graham Act and the diesel deal
Trump’s executive action waives core enforcement mechanisms codified within the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which the president signed into law on Sept. 18.
The suspended provisions, which were scheduled to take statutory effect on Sunday, Oct. 18, mandated an additional 500 percent tariff on all Russian-origin imports alongside 100 percent duties targeting the five largest global purchasers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, including China and India.
The statute also required trade penalties against third-party nations facilitating petroleum sanctions evasion and established aggressive actions to dismantle Moscow’s maritime “shadow fleet.”
In issuing the waiver, Trump invoked Section 115 of the statute, which grants executive discretion upon certifying to Congress that such action serves US national interests.
The suspension aligns with a commercial arrangement unveiled on Oct. 9 between Trump and Putin, under which Moscow consented to export refined diesel onto international markets through 2027 to lower retail fuel costs.
The waiver was met with condemnation from Kyiv, where President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that lifting economic penalties constitutes a grave policy error that provides financial lifelines to the Russian military and signals to Moscow that persistent infrastructure bombardments will carry no economic consequence.

articles.title: Egypt parliament delays vote on military support to Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Egypt parliament delays vote on military support to Saudi Arabia
Egypt's parliament on Sunday postponed a vote on President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request to authorise military support for Saudi Arabia, two lawmakers told AFP, with deliberations set to continue on Monday.
The session was convened after Sisi asked lawmakers to approve support for Saudi Arabia's defence if requested by the kingdom, which has come under near-daily attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis since early October.
"The session was extended to give all lawmakers the opportunity to speak and express their views," lawmaker Ibrahim Kholeif told AFP, adding that parliamentarians were mostly in support of the move.
Another member, Maha Abdel Nasser, said proceedings would resume Monday "to allow all lawmakers to be heard".
Egyptian media reported that deliberations would continue into Tuesday.
Both lawmakers said no details were being discussed about what form Egypt's military support for Saudi Arabia could take.
Sisi on Saturday requested parliamentary authorisation to help defend Saudi Arabia "if requested", saying it was "inconceivable" for Cairo to stand by as Saudi Arabia's security and stability are threatened.
The decade-plus war between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally-recognised government reignited in July.
The Houthis seized Yemen's Red Sea coastline in September and have since launched attacks on Saudi Arabia, including state oil giant Aramco and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed a week ago.
On Saturday, Sisi called for an end to the fighting and said Egypt was not seeking to "confront or attack anyone. We are speaking only about defence".
Houthi threats to Egypt
Egypt's constitution requires the approval of both parliament and the National Defence Council -- which includes the leaders of Egypt's security apparatus -- before troops can be deployed on combat missions abroad.
Shortly before the parliamentary session, the council, chaired by Sisi, approved providing Saudi Arabia with "all necessary and available forms of support" to help defend its security, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites, the presidency said.
Potential military involvement would constitute a break from Egypt's historically conservative foreign policy, which has prioritised protecting its own national security.
For years Cairo has positioned itself as a regional mediator with channels open across conflict lines, including with Hamas, Israel and Iran.
In response to Sisi's call on Saturday, Houthi parliament speaker Yehia Ali al-Rai addressed a letter of warning to his Egyptian counterpart.
"Egypt's slide down this path would pose a grave danger to its own national security and internal stability before anyone else's," he wrote, according to the Houthis' Saba news agency.
Throughout this year, as its Gulf allies have come under attack in the war between Iran and the US, Cairo has repeatedly preached caution.
The Arab world's largest military did not issue a response even when its own Damietta port was struck by an unidentified drone in July.
It has not joined the Mecca defence pact signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan in August, according to experts to maintain its strategic autonomy.
But Riyadh is one of Cairo's strongest allies, and a key financial backer to Sisi's administration for over a decade.
Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen in 2015, contributing naval and air forces and deploying warships to the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Along with Saudi Arabia, Egypt is hardest hit by disruptions through Bab al-Mandab, the southern gateway to its Suez Canal, revenues from which have not recovered since Houthi attacks began in 2023.
Military expert Samir Farag told AFP that Egyptian assistance could take several forms, ranging from intelligence, military advisers, ammunition and spare parts to weapons and, ultimately, troop deployments.

articles.title: Blunder in, abandon allies and court a dictator: it’s the Trump doctrine, now playing out in Myanmar | Steve Bloomfield
articles.body:
Marco Rubio was once adamant that the US had to do everything in its power to end what he described as the “ethnic cleansing” of the Rohingya in Myanmar. In a 2017 letter he signed along with 20 other US senators, Rubio called for “strong multilateral sanctions against specific senior Burmese military officials associated with the gross human rights abuses”. Those responsible for the atrocities should be prosecuted, he argued.
In the years since, the Myanmar military’s crimes have only increased. What was then deemed ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya is now widely viewed, including by the US, as genocide. What little democracy existed in Myanmar was eradicated in 2021 when Aung San Suu Kyi was arrested and imprisoned and her party’s election victory overturned, and the military took full control.
This sparked a civil war that has now turned into a brutal series of overlapping conflicts between the military, resistance forces and a medley of ethnic militias. Around 100,000 people have been killed in the conflict, which has forced 5 million people to flee their homes. The UN estimates that 16 million are now in need of urgent assistance. It is one of the world’s biggest humanitarian disasters – and entirely human-made.
Earlier this year, Myanmar held sham elections, and Min Aung Hlaing – the general most responsible for Myanmar’s genocide and one of the targets of Rubio’s letter – became president.
But Rubio, now the US secretary of state, no longer believes that Min Aung Hlaing should be prosecuted. Instead he’d rather like him to become an ally. This month the Trump administration decided to upend nearly a decade of united western policy and open direct talks with the Myanmar regime. The possibility of lifting sanctions is now being discussed. The move has shocked other western nations – none of which, it appears, was warned.
Inevitably, a Maga figure lingers in the background. This time it’s Roger Stone, the Donald Trump ally who was found guilty in 2019 of lying to Congress, witness tampering and obstructing the investigation into whether the Trump campaign conspired with Russia in the 2016 presidential election.
Stone, who was spared jail after Trump commuted his sentence, recently started working as a lobbyist for the Myanmar regime, helping to “rebuild relations between the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and the United States”.
It seems to be working. Earlier this month Michael Vance, the assistant secretary of state for intelligence and research, travelled to Myanmar’s capital Naypyidaw. The trip was supposedly to secure the release of a US citizen, but Vance also held talks with the generals. The purpose of the talks was not to persuade the military regime to reintroduce democracy or stop its brutal war. Instead it appeared to be about securing American access to Myanmar’s rare earth minerals.
In recent years, the race to control a steady supply of rare-earth minerals – elements used in a host of military technology and hi-tech manufacturing applications – has become increasingly fraught. China controls most of the world’s rare-earth mines and almost all of the processing capacity. The Trump administration’s desire to turn the tables has led it to strike one-sided deals with Ukraine and the Democratic Republic of Congo that have placed US business interests over practically everything else.
There are more than 600 rare earth mines in Myanmar, most of which currently supply China. Since the 2021 coup, rare-earth shipments from Myanmar to China have totalled $3.6bn, making up the majority of China’s rare-earth imports. This is the prize the US appears to have its eyes on.
Vance’s trip has handed Myanmar’s generals a propaganda victory at a moment when they are doing everything they can to legitimise the regime. The US, unfortunately, is not the only country welcoming Myanmar’s generals back into the fold. Min Aung Hlaing this month flew to Malaysia, once a strong opponent of the junta, where the prime minister Anwar Imbrahim floated the idea of Myanmar being welcomed back into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean). Trips to Indonesia and Brunei are also on the cards, while the Philippines has indicated that it too would like to see relations normalised.
The junta’s diplomatic victories follow growing military success. Over the last two and a half years, with the help of more sophisticated drones supplied by Russia and China, and the conscription of another 100,000 young men, the junta has regained control over several towns and pushed the resistance back into the countryside.
For Myanmar’s civilians, the long nightmare continues. Last month more than 50 people were killed when the military bombed a busy market in a rebel-held area. Every week brings fresh atrocities, while the hope of a peaceful, democratic Myanmar slips further into the distance.
The one silver lining that those fighting for Myanmar’s freedom can cling to is that the rest of the west hasn’t given up on it yet. British diplomats are adamant that there will be no change in the UK’s position, while Canada, Australia and the EU are all likely to hold the line too. But even here there are concerns.
Campaigners point to the UK’s recent reduction in aid to Myanmar from £66m a year to £55m. Just half of the $889.6m the UN has requested for Myanmar this year has been provided by international donors. They would also like to see Britain and others engage more directly with Myanmar’s pro-democracy camp, including the resistance.
Trump is not the first president to prioritise resources over democracy, as a cursory glance at US relations with Saudi Arabia since it discovered oil in 1938 shows. But Trump’s rapacious attitude to oil and minerals, his willingness to enrich his friends and family, and his brazen support for dictators makes this a very different America. Myanmar is simply another example of the corrosive nature that Trump’s foreign policy is having in every corner of the globe.
The question is whether Trump will get what he wants. US policy on Myanmar has been driven by Congress, and there remains bipartisan support for keeping it in place. The House of Representatives recently passed a bill that would extend the sanctions regime for another six years. Particularly at a time when his support is waning, Trump is unlikely to have much joy in persuading senators and members of Congress who have long supported Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement to turn a blind eye to genocide and war crimes.
Even if he did, the bigger question is whether Myanmar’s generals can give Trump what he wants. The vast majority of Myanmar’s rare earth mines are near the border with China and many are controlled by militia groups, not the junta. “There is no way China is going to let the US get anywhere near the rare earths,” Joshua Kurlantzick at the Council on Foreign Relations told me.
And yet even if none of this leads to any real change, the Trump administration’s decision to open talks with a genocidal regime responsible for one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises is a disaster for those in Myanmar fighting for their freedom. Many Myanmar resistance figures, including Aung San Suu Kyi, have placed their hope in US help. Like other democrats fighting demagogues, such as Volodymyr Zelenskyy, they have been deserted.
Here is yet another example of the Trump administration blundering into a part of the world where it knows little, offering a prize to an authoritarian and leaving with not much to show for it.
- Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

articles.title: Trump yet to give final decision on Russia tariffs, sanctions, as Rubio says more time needed
articles.body:
The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter, as Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation.
Rubio said on Saturday that the president will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlier.
"A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida.
In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump wrote that his decision-making was aimed at avoiding anything "that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table."
The waiver comes just weeks before November's midterm elections, with Trump under pressure over high energy prices as war with Iran disrupts global oil supplies.
Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham Act, which he signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next week. Friday's order didn't specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump chose a 60-day review.
"I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan.
Complicating matters is the Graham Act's call not only for sanctions on Russia but also for tariffs on goods from countries that import Russian energy supplies. Rubio pointed to India, an important US partner that has diversified its energy supplies but remains heavily dependent on Russian oil.
Trump's decision draws criticism from Zelensky, Republican senator
Friday's executive order drew criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who warned it would embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war.
Senator Darline Graham, a South Carolina Republican whose late brother Lindsey Graham championed the legislation that bears his name, said she disagreed with Trump's decision and planned to discuss it with him when he campaigns for her next week.
"Personally, I would choose to keep the pressure on Russia," she told reporters on Saturday. "Because I don't trust Putin and I don't trust Russia."
Rubio also defended a separate US agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies.
Under the agreement, Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States, followed by shipments in November and beyond.
"That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get."
Rubio said the diesel deal and sanctions waiver reflected the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies.
"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," he said.

articles.title: US resumes intelligence-sharing with Ukraine after pause, Zelensky says
articles.body:
The United States has resumed providing Ukraine with critical intelligence to help defend against Russian missile strikes after a brief pause, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in comments published on Sunday.

Speaking to NBC's Meet the Press, Zelensky said intelligence-sharing had been interrupted but later "de-blocked."

Zelensky in talks with Trump envoys over new peace meeting this week
Zelensky said he is holding talks with US President Donald Trump’s envoys with a view to arranging a new peace meeting as early as this week, Bloomberg News reported on Sunday, citing an interview with the Ukrainian president.
Zelensky also said on Sunday he had spoken with US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner as part of "virtually nonstop communication" between the two countries' teams aimed at the "next steps in diplomacy."

articles.title: US Treasury Secretary downplays Russia sanctions waiver, warns Zelensky to 'be careful'
articles.body:
US Treasury Secretary downplays Russia sanctions waiver, warns Zelensky to 'be careful'
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent denied accusations that Washington’s recent actions were tipping the scales in Russia's favor and warned President Volodymyr Zelensky to "be careful," in an Oct. 18 interview with NBC News.
The comments came two days after U.S. President Donald Trump waived most of the sanctions and tariffs introduced in a bipartisan Russia sanctions bill he signed last month. They also follow Zelensky's claim that the recent decision to slow down Ukrainian Starlink access came from inside the American government.
"President Zelensky should be very careful about making statements like this that aren't true," Bessent said when asked by NBC host Kristen Welker about Zelensky's comments.
When SpaceX abruptly implemented a speed cap on Ukraine's Starshield services earlier this week, a blame game ensued. It was not immediately clear if the restrictions came from SpaceX, the U.S. government, or outside sabotage. The Ukrainian Armed Forces relies on Starshield services to conduct military operations.
In what seemed a remarkable coincidence, the restrictions followed a threat from the U.S. government to withhold intelligence support should Ukraine continue to bomb Russian oil refineries. The Telegraph reported on Oct. 16 that Elon Musk, SpaceX CEO, proposed the speed cap to Trump — and Trump "agreed," citing multiple sources familiar with the matter.
Zelensky appeared earlier on Welker’s "Meet the Press," where he said Ukrainian intelligence reports show the decision to curb Starlink access came from the U.S. government.
"It was a message from the American government to limit this feed," Zelensky said, "and technically SpaceX did it."
Both Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio have "categorically" denied the accusation, Bessent said, adding that it was "reckless" of Zelensky to make such a charge.
Bessent also commented on the Trump administration’s decision to waive sanctions included in the recently passed Graham Act.
When asked what concessions Russian President Vladimir Putin had made to earn sanctions relief, Bessent claimed that "the only thing that has been lifted is the diesel embargo" and said "no one has been tougher" on sanctioning Russia than Trump.
The U.S. president, in an effort to lower diesel prices before the U.S. midterm elections, has sought to strike a diesel deal with Russia, despite the rising cost of diesel having been widely attributed to the U.S. war with Iran.
Pressed by Welker about the executive order waiving the sanctions in the recently passed Graham Act, Bessent repeated that "no sanctions have been lifted."
The new sanctions, which never went into effect, were waived rather than lifted.

articles.title: What are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?
articles.body:
Warnings about what artificial intelligence might do in the future – together with alarming reports of what it has gotten up to already – are being issued so quickly that even security experts have difficulty triaging what to worry about.
Yet a report this week from Anthropic’s offensive research team grabbed attention by describing a new, practical threat, one devoid of human characteristics or apocalyptic musings. The red team, as such internal testers are called, said it created a malicious AI program that spread autonomously through internet-connected “smart” televisions and could do the same inside other ordinary devices. While machines running AI usually need a fair amount of computing power, the researchers said that their program split parts of itself among 15 televisions and was still able to function by using a bit of power from each.
In addition to evoking the horcruxes that kept pieces of Lord Voldemort’s soul alive within objects in the Harry Potter series, the report alarmed some professionals because the generally weak security of smart televisions and many other “internet of things” devices would be very hard to correct, even with a concerted effort.
“It’s something to worry about just like every other wave of cyber-attacks. We need to mitigate the possible effects,” said Joshua Saxe, who led development of Meta’s AI security effort. “I’m concerned right now that folks in the cybersecurity community are not taking these kinds of real risks as seriously as they should be.”
The damage of such “AI worms” could be astonishingly large. Self-replicating computer viruses, which need not trick a human to propagate, are known as worms, and earlier worms have wreaked some of the worst havoc in the history of the internet.
That legacy includes the Morris worm of 1988, which arrived before the mainstream consumer internet, when a graduate student released a program that took advantage of various software flaws and weak passwords, copying itself so rapidly that many infected machines slowed to a stop. The US and Israel brought worms into international espionage with the stealthy Stuxnet in the lat 2000s, which sabotaged Iranian nuclear centrifuges. Other worms like the Russian NotPetya and North Korean-attributed WannaCry have caused tens of billions of dollars’ worth of damage worldwide.
Many of the world’s most destructive worms have depended on known vulnerabilities that device owners have not patched, sometimes months after patches became available. The Anthropic team predicted that a worm like theirs could function in the same way and be harder to stop, because smart devices receive patches less often than phones or laptops. Worse, they theorized that an AI worm could keep adapting to other types of hardware by researching newly disclosed vulnerabilities.
What differentiates AI worms from typical reproducing viruses is that AI models can learn as they go, said Ariel Herbert-Voss, an early security expert at OpenAI who now runs AI security startup RunSybil. Existing cybersecurity infrastructure is not ready for the proliferation of such threats, Herbert-Voss said. “We need to better enable our security teams. We need to be giving them more resources to fix problems.”
Worms could also be used for benevolent purposes, suggested Chris Inglis, a former deputy director of the National Security Agency who served as National Cyber Director in the Biden White House.
“The question of whether AI worms are plausible has been settled by several breakout events over the past six months,” Inglis said by digital message. “The better question is how we will employ them, counter them, and/or combine them with other emerging technologies.”
Anthropic researchers said a successful AI worm would need to have more capability on less powerful devices than is possible right now – but they added that current trends will make that feasible by year’s end. Their research follows a paper published by experts at the University of Toronto a few months ago, which infected a full-size computer and could spread to similar machines more rapidly than the television worm.
“The capabilities have been developing very rapidly,” said co-author and Toronto PhD student Jonas Guan.
Guan and other experts said that, as a practical matter, an AI worm should not top anyone’s list of AI fears. The Anthropic version moves very slowly, Guan said, and worms have predictable and detectable actions that can be blocked at multiple layers. Basic security hygiene, including requiring strong passwords and two-factor authentication, would stop most worms and other hacking, experts said.
“Nothing about this is truly feasible or impactful,” said Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade, vice-president of research at security firm SentinelOne. “It’s nifty stunt hacking that’s getting way more amplification in service of the ridiculous doomer narratives that suggest models have a mind and will of their own.”
Anthropic did not respond to an interview request.
Outside Washington, many in the AI and security worlds believe greater government oversight of AI is now essential. But members of Congress have introduced mutually conflicting bills, while the White House has so far created only a small review board.
Security researchers and laypeople alike find themselves weighing the motivations behind fearful prognostications from AI companies, which range from espousing quasi-religious beliefs, to seeking legislation to exclude rivals or save money, to hyping the anticipated multi-trillion-dollar public valuations of the San Francisco AI giants.
“The claim that a lot of this is marketing is correct, but the reality dwarfs any PR,” said Gadi Evron, who is running a conference on AI security in San Francisco this month called Unprompted. “Whatever claims the labs are making, they are not warning us enough. We need to understand that nobody can stop the AI storm.”

articles.title: Ukraine runs out of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles as Trump snubs Zelensky - report
articles.body:
Ukraine has run out of missiles for the US-made Patriot air defense system, a source familiar with the situation told CNN on Thursday.
This development comes amid a series of public jabs between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky.
Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, Zelensky said on Saturday, predicting even more US sanctions relief.
"The decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me," Zelensky wrote on X. "It definitely helps only the Russians."
An executive order issued by Trump on Friday night waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs, including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas, that were scheduled to take effect next week under the Graham Act, which he signed into law last month.
Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the United States.
The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming toward Moscow while publicly criticizing Zelensky, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.
Zelensky hopes for meeting with US and Russia during G20 summit
Ukraine, the United States and Russia could meet during a G20 summit in the US, but Washington and Moscow have not confirmed the meeting and other venues are also possible, Zelensky said on Saturday.
The Group of 20 major economies, which includes the US and Russia but not Ukraine, is due to hold a summit in Miami in December.
"The meeting could then take place in the United States during the G20 summit. But there has been no confirmation yet from either Russia or the United States. It could also be held in a European country," Zelensky told reporters in a WhatsApp media chat.
Ukraine says unable to use interceptors due to Starlink limits, in touch with US
This comes as Starlink disruptions are being felt on the front lines of the war in Ukraine.
Ukraine cannot use its interceptor systems against Russian drone attacks because of speed restrictions imposed on Starlink, Zelensky said on Saturday, adding that Kyiv was discussing the issue with US officials.
Zelensky told reporters in a WhatsApp media chat that Ukrainian officials had been told the restrictions were linked to technical issues.
He said Ukraine had tested Starlink on European Union territory and encountered no such problems there, with the system operating at higher speeds.

articles.title: British startup develos modular ground drone for front line
articles.body:
- UK-based Stratonex Defence Technologies unveiled VARAN, a modular unmanned ground vehicle concept for ISR, logistics, force protection, electronic warfare and counter-drone missions.
- The company says VARAN can navigate without GPS, uses passive 3D sensing and is designed for low visual, thermal and acoustic signatures.
British defense technology company Stratonex Defence Technologies has unveiled VARAN, a modular unmanned ground vehicle concept designed to accompany and support forward units on the battlefield, with swappable mission equipment and the ability to navigate without satellite positioning.
The company introduced the vehicle on social media and on its website, describing VARAN as a payload-agnostic platform that can be configured for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, logistics, force protection, electronic warfare and counter-drone missions.
Stratonex says VARAN uses autonomous navigation and passive 3D sensing to move across rough terrain, including in areas where GPS and other satellite navigation signals are jammed or unavailable. Passive sensing means the vehicle builds a picture of its surroundings without emitting signals such as radar or lidar pulses that an enemy could detect, and the company says the platform is designed to keep a low visual, thermal and acoustic signature.
The vehicle is built on an open systems architecture, which Stratonex says allows mission-specific payloads and future technologies to be integrated as requirements change. The company pitches VARAN as a way for troops to move farther and carry more in expeditionary operations, from reconnaissance support to counter-drone and rapid deployment tasks.
Stratonex framed the platform around configuration and integration, asking what capabilities potential users would want added to an unmanned ground vehicle.
Stratonex is a UK-based company co-founded by Ben Everitt, a former Conservative member of Parliament for Milton Keynes North, and describes itself as a developer of autonomous systems and mission software focused on sovereign capability for Britain and its allies. In July 2026, Nasdaq-listed VisionWave Holdings appointed Stratonex as its commercialization and integration partner for the UK and Europe under a non-exclusive distributor agreement covering VisionWave’s autonomous systems, sensing and counter-drone technologies.
Uncrewed ground vehicles have become a growing focus for European armies after their wide use in the war in Ukraine, where both sides rely on them to haul supplies, evacuate wounded troops and carry weapons along front lines exposed to constant drone surveillance. Britain’s Ministry of Defence has also been funding and trialing uncrewed ground platforms for logistics and combat support roles.
Stratonex presents VARAN as a concept platform, and the company is inviting feedback from potential users on which capabilities to integrate as development continues.

articles.title: Bessent warns Zelenskyy to 'be very careful' about claims U.S. is throttling Starlink
articles.body:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday to "be careful" in public statements about U.S. support for Ukraine.
U.S.-provided Starlink internet was recently restricted in Ukraine, hindering the war-torn country's ability to respond to Russian assaults. Ukraine uses Starshield, the military and government-controlled version of the commercial Starlink, to conduct military operations.
In an earlier interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," Zelenskyy said he believed the U.S. government was responsible for the slowdown, and that Ukraine was "blocked" from U.S. intelligence for a period of time. Zelenskyy said Starshield-linked vehicles and drones are still being restricted in speed.
Bessent cautioned Zelenskyy about making those claims.
"President [Donald] Trump and Secretary [Marco] Rubio have categorically said that no one under the Trump administration did that, and I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge," Bessent said on "Meet the Press."
"President Zelenskyy should be very careful about making statements like this that aren't true," he added.
Starlink, high-speed satellite internet provided by Elon Musk's SpaceX, is critical to Ukraine's defense. Musk himself said in a post on X last week that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump are "ultimately" responsible for any slowdowns to the military version of Starlink known as Starshield.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Musk wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment from CNBC.
Reuters reported last week that the White House ordered the technology restrictions, but Trump has denied responsibility for the slowdown.
"Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," the president said last week. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been."
The U.S. relationship with Ukraine has been highly scrutinized throughout Trump's second term, as he has frequently antagonized the war-torn country while pushing for a peace deal.
Trump has recently expressed frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries as he faces pressure from voters over sky-high gasoline and diesel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The president has even personally blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in energy prices: "He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Trump said.
Soaring energy prices are largely due to the U.S. war with Iran, which severely disrupted the Strait of Hormuz and choked oil shipments from the Persian Gulf. The national average for a gallon of gas in the U.S. was nearly $4.30 on Sunday, according to AAA. Diesel was roughly $6.32 per gallon, about 20 cents off September's record high.
Trump has tried to offset the energy pinch by importing Russian diesel. In a post on Truth Social earlier in the month, he said: "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!"
Many U.S. lawmakers, including Republicans, have condemned the president's plan to buy Russian diesel. Congress recently sent Trump an overwhelmingly bipartisan sanctions package aimed at crippling Russia's energy industry. Trump signed the bill into law, but waived portions of it over the weekend, citing the national interest in an explanation to Congress.
"Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said in a post on X. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day."

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Trump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting to end war as feud rumbles on
articles.body:
- Donald Trump has defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, while once again accusing Volodymyr Zelenskyy of not wanting to end the war. “My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” the US president wrote on Truth Social. “Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him … he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” he added. Trump’s remarks come after he signed an executive order on Friday putting on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy.
- Earlier on Sunday, Zelenskyy had thanked the Trump administration for resuming intelligence sharing between the two countries, but maintained the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access to send a “message” to Kyiv, write Andrew Roth and Sam Jones.
- Lithuania said Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites. Prime minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius made the claim on broadcaster LRT after authorities discovered flammable liquids at the company in question. Sinkevicius said the firm, whose location he did not mention, houses “nine satellite antennas to guarantee the Starlink connection, which of course supports and assists Ukraine”. He added: “It is obvious this is part of the hybrid war being waged by Russia, involving acts of sabotage.”
- In September, a satellite station belonging to the network located in central Poland was set ablaze with Warsaw claiming sabotage. In Bulgaria, an investigation is under way amid claims that antennas linked to the Starlink satellite network were set on fire.
- Shipping Russian diesel to the US market will take 15 to 20 days once contracts are signed, a senior Russian official said on Sunday, though a date for signing has yet to be announced. Trump announced the controversial agreement with Moscow last week, seen as a way to try to lower fuel prices for American consumers ahead of crucial midterm elections. “Negotiations are currently under way regarding the commercial terms – that is, on finalisation of the contracts,” Russian deputy prime minister for energy Alexander Novak said in an interview with state media. “Once the contracts are signed, the fuel will reach the markets – in this case, the US markets – within 15 to 20 days.”
- Ukrainian strikes set an oil export terminal and a depot ablaze in St Petersburg on Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of its largest aerial attacks of the war. One person was killed and five others were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at the Petersburg oil terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, officials said. A logistics centre belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a datacentre operated by Russian tech company VK were also targeted, the companies confirmed. Russia’s defence ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
- A Russian air strike killed one person and injured two in Kyiv overnight, mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram early on Monday. A medical facility and a non-residential building were damaged in the attack, he said.
- A suspected drone exploded over Lithuania after triggering an alert that forced residents in northern and central areas to seek shelter for an hour on Sunday, officials said. Ukraine’s foreign ministry said later it regretted the incident in Lithuania’s airspace, adding that it may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones off course. The object flew into Lithuania’s airspace from Poland, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas told reporters.

articles.title: Slovenian firm arms drone killer systems with Gatling gun
articles.body:
- Valhalla Turrets announced a new Skythunder air defense system combining a 20 mm M197 Gatling gun, 70 mm laser-guided rockets and 360-degree radar.
- Company renders show the counter-drone system on an Oshkosh FMTV 6x6 truck chassis, the type used to carry HIMARS.
Slovenian turret maker Valhalla Turrets is preparing a new version of its Skythunder air defense system armed with General Dynamics Land Systems’ 20 mm M197 Gatling gun and 70 mm laser-guided rockets, designed to shoot down drones and protect critical infrastructure.
The company announced the system as “coming soon” in a social media post and released renders showing the turret mounted on a 6×6 Oshkosh truck chassis from the U.S. military’s Family of Medium Tactical Vehicles, the same type of truck that carries the U.S. Army’s HIMARS rocket launcher.
The three-barrel M197 is the cannon carried in the nose turret of U.S. Marine Corps AH-1Z Viper attack helicopters, and Valhalla says it will give the new Skythunder high-volume fire against drones and other low-flying targets. The 70 mm laser-guided rockets add a longer-reach option for targets beyond the gun’s effective range, giving the system what the company describes as layered kinetic effects across different distances.
According to Valhalla, the system will have full 360-degree radar coverage, use its sensors to find and track targets, and plug into wider layered air defense networks. The company describes it as mobile and modular, and says it is meant to provide cost-effective protection against large numbers of drones.
The new Skythunder adds a lighter gun option to a family Valhalla introduced this year. At Eurosatory in Paris in June 2026, the company showed the Skythunder 300 on a Mercedes-Benz Zetros 8×8 truck, armed with a Northrop Grumman MK44S Bushmaster 30 mm cannon, a separate rotating station with a 7.62 mm M134D Gatling gun and Arnold Defense laser-guided rockets. Valhalla also builds the MANGART 25 AD short-range air defense turret, which it unveiled on a Patria 8×8 vehicle for Slovenia in May 2026.
Its turrets are also turning up abroad. Azerbaijani defense company Zireh unveiled the HMS30 mobile air defense system at ADEX 2026 in Baku, built around a Valhalla Turrets turret with an electro-optical sighting system and two Russian-designed 30 mm 2A42 cannons. Zireh says the HMS30 can engage drones at about 1.5 to 2 km (0.9 to 1.2 miles).
Valhalla, based in Ljubljana, specializes in remote-controlled turrets and weapon stations and works as a development partner for several larger European defense companies. In August 2026, General Dynamics European Land Systems integrated a Valhalla turret into its ASCOD tracked combat vehicle.
Gun-based systems have become a major part of drone defense in Europe since the war in Ukraine showed how many cheap drones an army may need to shoot down, often with interceptor missiles that cost far more than their targets.

articles.title: Romanian F-16 Fighter Jets Shoot Down Two Russian Jet-Powered Drones Over NATO Airspace
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Romanian F-16 Fighter Jets Shoot Down Two Russian Jet-Powered Drones Over NATO Airspace
Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two Russian jet-powered attack drones over the Black Sea on October 17 after the aircraft entered Romania’s airspace, marking another incident involving Russian drones crossing into NATO territory.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Romania’s Ministry of National Defense on October 17, the intercepted aircraft were identified as jet-powered Geran attack drones. Both were destroyed over Romanian territorial waters near the coastal town of Sulina.
Romanian radar systems initially detected a group of aerial targets approximately 120 kilometers east of Ukraine’s Snake Island, moving southwest toward Romania.
In response, two F-16 fighter jets operating under Romania’s air policing mission took off from the 86th Air Base at Borcea at 5:43 p.m. local time. The first drone entered Romanian airspace at 5:59 p.m. and was intercepted at 6:01 p.m. southeast of Sulina, approximately two minutes after crossing the country’s airspace boundary.
A second drone entered Romanian airspace at approximately 6:00 p.m. and was destroyed at 6:05 p.m. east of Sulina, following five minutes inside Romanian airspace. Both interceptions occurred within four minutes of each other.
The Romanian Defense Ministry also reported repeated drone activity near its border during the preceding week. Radar surveillance systems recorded eight separate incidents involving aerial targets operating in Ukrainian airspace near Romania. In four cases, drones briefly crossed into Romanian airspace.
The ministry said it continues to adjust its defensive measures in response to evolving aerial threats and to protect the country’s sovereignty. The latest interceptions followed several drone attacks against commercial vessels operating in the Black Sea, including incidents within Romanian territorial waters.
On October 14, a drone struck the Comoros-flagged tanker YARA J in Romanian waters. The following day, another drone attack caused a fire aboard the San Marino-flagged vessel Wine Trader. Additional attacks on October 6 and 13 targeted four commercial vessels operating within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone.

articles.title: Ukrainian forces strike St Petersburg and Leningrad region
articles.body:
It comes as Zelenskyy said Russian forces had targeted Ukraine's energy sector in strikes on four regions on Saturday night. He said attacks on residential buildings had also left two people dead and 12 others reportedly injured.
An oil terminal and a data centre belonging to the VK social networking service were reportedly among the targets of a drone attack on St Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad region overnight into Sunday.
The attack is being described by Russian media as one of the largest on the area since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. One person was killed and 15 people were injured in the strikes, local officials said.
A total of 144 drones were shot down over the Leningrad region, regional governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said.
According to Drozdenko, drone debris fell on houses in Gatchina and other districts, causing fires and damaging 55 vehicles.
"Emergency power cuts were recorded; specialists are carrying out emergency work and the electricity supply is being promptly restored. At the moment, two transformer substations in Yanino remain switched off, and 50 apartment blocks, home to around 20,000 people, are in the outage zone," he said.
The VK press office reported an attack on its data centre in the Leningrad region but said the company's services remained available to users as normal.
In St Petersburg, governor Aleksandr Beglov said fires broke out at civilian infrastructure facilities in the Nevsky, Krasnoselsky, Krasnogvardeisky, and Moskovsky districts and on the grounds of the St Petersburg oil terminal.
Preliminary information indicated that no one was injured. The oil terminal is located in the Great Port of St Petersburg.
The terminal is capable of receiving and shipping 1.1 million tonnes of fuel a month, using four berths for sea-going vessels and tankers. Its 32 storage tanks occupy an area of 442,000 square metres.
One of the fires broke out at an Ozon warehouse. According to the company, staff were evacuated. Smoke is rising above the warehouse complex, and several roads have been closed in the area.
Due to the attack, flights were suspended at Pulkovo airport for more than seven hours. Rosaviatsia, Russia's aviation authority, lifted the restrictions at 10 am Moscow time.
Russian strikes on Ukraine
It comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday that Russian forces had carried out further strikes against Ukraine's energy sector on Saturday night, targeting substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, and Odesa regions.
"Tens of thousands of families remain without power. Energy workers and repair crews are working virtually around the clock to restore electricity supply," he wrote in a post on X.
Zelenskyy said attacks on residential buildings had also left two people dead and 12 others reportedly injured.
According to the Ukrainian leader, Russia hit Ukraine with close to 2,700 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 66 missiles over the last week.

articles.title: Italian NATO jets scrambled after drone enters Lithuanian airspace, damages car
articles.body:
Necva Tastan Sevinc and Kanyshai Butun
18 October 2026•Update: 18 October 2026
Two Italian Eurofighter jets operating under NATO command were scrambled Sunday after a drone was detected in Lithuanian airspace, with debris later damaging a moving civilian vehicle in the country’s north.
“We can confirm that this morning, two Italian Eurofighter jets were scrambled in response to the presence of a drone in Lithuanian airspace. The aircraft were operating under NATO command,” a NATO official said, according to Italian news agency ANSA.
The official said an investigation was underway and the alliance remained in close contact with Lithuanian authorities.
“NATO is ready and able to respond to any potential threat, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, to safeguard our territory and protect our population,” the official said.
Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said preliminary information indicated that the object entered the country from Poland, public broadcaster LRT reported.
“I have already contacted the Polish defence minister and asked Poland to join the investigation so that we can look into this incident together,” he told reporters.
Authorities confirmed that debris damaged a car traveling from Birzai toward Pasvalys, but no one was injured.
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said the driver heard an explosion before debris struck the vehicle, denting its door. Police cordoned off the area and were gathering evidence.
Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Center, told LRT Radio that the object was most likely a Ukrainian drone that could have entered the country during Kyiv’s strikes on Russia’s St Petersburg region.
Kaunas said poor weather prevented the scrambled pilots from visually identifying the object.
He also questioned why an air alert was issued only in northern Lithuania, describing the situation as “strange and unacceptable.”
The military was instructed to provide a detailed report, while authorities would examine whether public warnings were delayed.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said Russia’s war against Ukraine “is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU.”
“What appears to be a drone exploded over the northern part of the country, posing a danger to the civilian population,” he wrote on US social media company X.
 
Ukraine cites possible Russian electronic warfare in drone incident
Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said Kyiv regrets the drone incident, which he said may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting a drone during an operation against “legitimate military targets in Russia.”
“We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have caused,” he wrote on US social media company X.
Tykhyi said Ukraine was committed to sharing all relevant information with Lithuanian officials to establish the full circumstances of the incident and prevent similar incidents in the future.
“We sincerely thank Lithuania, our ally, for supporting Ukraine in countering Russian aggression, which is the root case of the security threats in our region,” he said.

articles.title: Poland, Bulgaria, now Lithuania: Russia’s suspected arson campaign reaches a third Starlink site serving Ukraine
articles.body:
Someone tried to set fire overnight to a Lithuanian company that stores Starlink communication equipment, but tipped-off guards foiled the attempt, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said. He linked the attack to Russia’s hybrid war against Europe. It is the third suspected sabotage of Starlink infrastructure in Europe in under a month.
Russia keeps attacking Ukraine at the front and from the air while running a sabotage campaign behind the lines in Europe, which ISW has linked into one pattern. Starlink keeps Ukraine’s drone units and front-line troops connected, and Poland pays for much of that service.
Fuel canisters and a control unit
The attack came just after midnight, the prime minister wrote. Security services had warned the company about possible attacks, security was stepped up, and the attempt failed.
The company provides connectivity through nine Starlink satellite antennas used by Ukraine, Sinkevičius told Lithuanian public radio LRT. At almost 2 a.m., intruders tried to burn the antennas and their control unit, leaving behind incendiary liquid in canisters of 3 to 10 liters.
“It is obvious that this is part of Russia’s hybrid war with elements of sabotage,” he said, adding that the client was likely “the Russian side.”
He said he believes the people involved, and how many there were, are known, but gave no details, citing the investigation.
Police Commissioner General Arūnas Paulauskas said no suspects had been detained, any damage was minimal, and the company kept working. A pretrial investigation is under way.
New Starlink restrictions disrupt Ukrainian drone missions. Kyiv adviser says move is tied to “political situation”
A drone the same morning
Hours later, an object that apparently entered from Poland crossed northern Lithuania, and NATO jets failed to identify it, Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said. Possible fragments were found in the Pasvalys district near the Latvian border. Latvia’s military said the object may have blown itself up on a course toward Latvia.
Sinkevičius said the sabotage version had to be checked for the drone too. He called the National Security Commission for Monday, 19 October, to examine both incidents and consider giving services more powers to neutralize drones.
The third Starlink site
In September, a fire destroyed the distribution panel at a Starlink ground station in Wola Krobowska, Poland. Germany detained two Turkish nationals on 12 October, and Warsaw blamed Russian intelligence. In Bulgaria, masked intruders burned 11 of 17 Starlink antennas near Sofia.
