articles.title: Exclusive: Documents Show How Israel Steered Qatari Payments to Gaza
articles.body:
As Israeli voters prepare for elections on Oct. 27, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has tried to defend and distance himself from one of his government’s most controversial policies: allowing Qatar to funnel nearly $2 billion into the Hamas-controlled Gaza Strip for more than a decade. Previously undisclosed documents obtained by TIME, including letters from senior Israeli security officials to Qatari leaders, reveal that Israel encouraged and played a direct role in a payment program that was more extensive than Netanyahu has publicly acknowledged.
Beginning in 2012, Netanyahu’s government helped to facilitate Qatari payments to Gaza that had begun after Hamas seized control in 2007. By 2018, Qatar had sent roughly $1.1 billion into the Strip, according to an analysis provided to Israeli ministers, the Israeli daily Haaretz reported, with the funding designated for humanitarian assistance, fuel, and government salaries. That year, after Israeli officials castigated Qatar for allegedly financing Hamas, the Qataris began demanding formal documentation of an arrangement the two governments had agreed was meant to provide relief to citizens of the beleaguered enclave.
The extent of Israel’s cooperation with the payments was reflected in a 2020 letter from Yossi Cohen, then director of the Mossad, Israel’s intelligence agency, to Qatar’s Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani. “It is indeed a great opportunity to express our gratitude and appreciation for the humanitarian aid efforts that the State of Qatar has provided the last few years to the Gaza Strip,” Cohen wrote. “Undoubtedly, these humanitarian efforts have played a crucial role in improving the humanitarian situation within the Gaza Strip, and ensuring stability and safety in the region.”
The payment arrangement had the support of successive Israeli governments, the Palestinians, the Trump and Biden Administrations, the United Nations, and European powers, according to officials who served in both the Trump and Biden Administrations. The flow of money from Qatar into Gaza has taken on new significance since October 7, 2023, when Hamas terrorists stormed southern Israel, murdered some 1,200 people, and took 251 more hostage. The worst security failure in the country’s history raised troubling questions about whether the financial lifeline helped to sustain Hamas’s grip on power and, in turn, enabled it to carry out the assault.
Since then, Qatar has been frustrated by allegations leveled by Israeli political leaders that its payments to Gaza had helped finance the deadliest massacre of Jews since the Holocaust. “All of Qatar’s financial assistance in Gaza has been directed to Palestinian citizens through mechanisms coordinated with the Israeli authorities and international partners. Under previous aid mechanisms, all financial assistance, as well as goods such as food, medicine and fuel, passed through Israel before entering Gaza,” a spokesperson for Qatar’s International Media Office tells TIME. “Nothing was delivered directly by Qatar; we provided the aid, while delivery was carried out by the United Nations’ organizations in coordination with the Israeli authorities. If any funding reached Hamas, as alleged by individuals and groups with political agendas against Qatar, the responsibility lies with Israel, which oversaw the delivery and created the mechanism.”
Critics have long argued that Netanyahu sought to sustain Hamas rule in Gaza to keep the Palestinians divided between the Islamist terror group and the Fatah-led Palestinian Authority in the West Bank, foreclosing the prospect of a unified Palestinian leadership capable of negotiating a two-state solution. Netanyahu’s wager, according to these critics, was that the aid would give Hamas something to lose and would therefore help contain the group while Israel pursued normalization with the Arab world without resolving the Palestinian question. Instead, as Israel moved closer to a historic agreement with Saudi Arabia, Hamas launched an assault that upended the region, plunging it into war.
The Prime Minister’s office declined to comment for this story.
The documents now give Israelis a fuller accounting of a policy that preceded the catastrophe, as they prepare to render a verdict on the man who presided over both. “It was a policy failure on our part born of good intentions that multiple prime ministers kept going,” says one former Israeli defense official. “But Netanyahu was unquestionably at the center of it. He was the one who championed and accelerated the program, his government was in charge of the way it was run, and now we know as a society that we can never afford to make a mistake like that again.”
Ehud Olmert was still prime minister when Qatar began sending money to Gaza in 2007, after Hamas won control of the coastal enclave. At the outset, the Israeli government was not directly involved in the transfers. That changed under Netanyahu. By 2012, his government had approved a system that gave Israel a direct role in facilitating Qatari assistance: delivering food and medical supplies, determining which Palestinian families qualified for financial aid and disbursing the funds, and enabling Qatari financing to expand Gaza’s electricity supply, according to Israeli and Arab officials, as well as official documents obtained by TIME.
At first, the arrangement was informal. Qatar supplied the money with Israel’s approval, even as Israeli officials publicly criticized Doha for financing Hamas, according to sources familiar with the negotiations. The contradiction aggravated the Qataris, a senior official in the first Trump Administration tells TIME: Israeli officials would denounce the payments in public, then privately ask Doha to renew them.
Qatar, a gas-rich monarchy in the Persian Gulf, is accustomed to walking a fine line. It plays host to both the U.S. Central Command and to senior Hamas officials. The country set up a Hamas political office in Doha at the request of the U.S. in 2011. In contrast to other Gulf monarchies, especially Saudi Arabia, Qatar sees no threat in the Muslim Brotherhood, the political movement that spawned Hamas. After Oct. 7, Qatar's government emerged as the go-between in negotiations among Israel, Hamas and Washington, where Biden Administration officials privately praised the Qataris as honest brokers.
By 2018, Qatar sought written documentation of the Israeli government’s role in the aid agreement. It was subsequently formalized through a trilateral mechanism involving Qatar, Israel, and the United Nations, designed to administer the aid with international and Israeli oversight. On October 2, 2018, Israel and Qatar, together with the United Nations, signed an agreement to finance fuel deliveries into Gaza.
A spokesperson for the United Nations declined to comment for this story but referred TIME to statements the body’s special coordinator for Middle East peace, Tor Wennesland, made in 2021 acknowledging the arrangement. “These efforts are vital to improving the dire socioeconomic and humanitarian situation in Gaza,” he said at a UN Security Council briefing.
In August 2021, Qatar signed another agreement committing $40 million to a cash assistance program that would give nearly 100,000 Palestinian households $100 per month for four months. The arrangements were subsequently extended. American officials were brought into the discussions as well. According to a diplomat briefed on the process, who asked for anonymity to divulge details because they were not authorized to comment publicly, Qatar wanted Washington to understand precisely how the system worked, fearing that Israeli officials might later accuse Doha of financing Hamas without acknowledging Israel’s own role. “The Israelis kept insisting on doing it this way, so that they can control what goes in and out,” the official told TIME, rather than establish “something more regular and something which goes directly to the people.”
Under the system, according to U.S. and Israeli officials, Qatar paid for fuel and electricity purchased from Israel to increase the number of hours Gaza received power, a structure coordinated with Israeli security services. It transferred money through the United Nations for projects in the Strip. And it provided monthly $100 payments to some of Gaza’s poorest families. According to diplomats familiar with the system, Israel vetted the recipients and oversaw the distribution mechanism, with funds transferred through the World Food Programme and eligible families notified by text message before collecting their assistance at designated locations. “If the money ever got in the wrong hands, it was because of the Israelis,” the diplomat said, “because they were the ones overseeing the whole thing.”
Netanyahu’s government was so committed to the policy that when Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas cut payments to government workers in Gaza in 2018, Israeli security officials shuttled Qatari cash into the Strip in suitcases, U.S. and Israeli media reported at the time. Naftali Bennett, then Netanyahu’s education minister, publicly opposed the transfers, denouncing them as “protection money.” Netanyahu briefly suspended the payments in January 2019 amid renewed violence along the Gaza border, using the prospect of their resumption as leverage to pressure Hamas to stop firing rockets.
But while critics on the Israeli right railed against the deal, Netanyahu’s deputies worked behind the scenes to preserve it, according to correspondence obtained by TIME. In July 2019, according to one letter, Qatar notified the Netanyahu government that it was transferring $6 million to 20,000 beneficiaries in Gaza, with each receiving $300. It is unknown how many of those beneficiaries, chosen by Israel, were connected to Hamas or had family members who belonged to the group. Over the last two decades, Hamas has been deeply embedded in Gaza, operating not only as an armed militant organization but also as a political movement and governing authority, employing civil servants responsible for the territory’s public services and infrastructure.
In 2020, as the coronavirus pandemic swept through Gaza, R. L. Maoz, a member of Netanyahu’s National Security Council, urged Qatari officials to maintain the payments despite the Israeli government’s public criticism. “We reiterate the importance of continuing to transfer the Qatari humanitarian financial assistance through the existing mechanism,” Maoz wrote. “We ask that Qatar’s financial assistance not be transferred through mediators or countries other than the ambassador, Mohammed Al-Emadi,” he added, referring to the chairman of the Qatari Committee for the Reconstruction of Gaza. “We greatly appreciate your cooperation and open discourse to safeguard stability and security in the region and to bring our countries and peoples closer together.”
The program survived Netanyahu’s departure from power. His successor, Bennett, had been among its fiercest critics, raising the prospect that the arrangement might finally end. At that point, Qatar prepared to halt the program, a former Biden official tells TIME. Instead, after taking office in 2021, Bennett ended only the delivery of cash-filled suitcases, not the broader flow of Qatari assistance to Gaza, the Associated Press reported. According to people familiar with discussions about the policy, Bennett’s prior objections were a message intended for his domestic political constituency. “There’s no issue,” an Israeli representative told a Biden envoy, according to an official present. “We want to continue with it as is.”
To some of the officials involved, the compact contained a fundamental flaw: both the Israeli government and Hamas retained control over aid intended for ordinary Gazans. “Bibi and Hamas hold the tap, essentially,” one of the officials told me. Hamas could restrict the system to exert pressure internally, the official said, while Netanyahu could restrict it to pressure Hamas. “We knew this was not something that was beneficial for the long term. We need to have something that’s sustainable, that empowers the civilians.”
By 2023, with tensions mounting between Israel and Hamas, Qatari officials pressed for a different model, one that would deliver assistance to Gazans without making civilians dependent on either Hamas or the Israeli government. But Netanyahu’s government wanted the existing framework kept intact, according to multiple sources who spoke to TIME, including an Israeli official and an international diplomat.
Two weeks before October 7, Mossad director David Barnea traveled to Doha and asked Qatar to renew the funding, the New York Times reported in 2023. The Qatari officials agreed but warned Barnea that it would be the last renewal. With tensions rising between Israel’s far-right ministers and Hamas, the arrangement had run its course, Qatar believed. Barnea asked for two more months. The rationale, according to the officials familiar with the conversation, was that continuing assistance to Gaza’s civilians gave Hamas something to lose and therefore gave Israel a measure of leverage over the group. After two months, the parties could reassess Hamas’s behavior and devise a more durable mechanism for delivering aid.
They never got the chance. With the brutal Oct. 7 attack on southern Israel, the Qatari aid arrangement that successive Israeli governments had spent years helping to build, modify, and preserve was over.
Ever since, Netanyahu has faced accusations that he deliberately strengthened Hamas to keep the Palestinians divided—between Hamas in Gaza, and the secular Fatah party that under Abbas governs the West Bank—and forestall a peace agreement. Critics point to remarks Netanyahu allegedly made at a 2019 Likud Party meeting. “Anyone who wants to thwart the establishment of a Palestinian state has to support bolstering Hamas and transferring money to Hamas,” he said, according to a report in the Jerusalem Post. “This is part of our strategy—to isolate the Palestinians in Gaza.”
In a 2024 interview with TIME, Netanyahu denied making the statement, insisting that the payments were meant to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe. “The reason that successive governments agreed to that is that we wanted to make sure that Gaza has a functioning civilian administration to avoid humanitarian collapse,” he said. Without the money to maintain sewage systems, water supplies, and schools, he argued, the territory could have descended into chaos and disease. Netanyahu claims that Iran supplied Hamas with weapons through separate channels, including suspected smuggling routes across Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula.
Netanyahu’s dealings with Qatar have also become a source of controversy in Israel. Netanyahu has been under intense scrutiny in recent weeks over the so-called Qatargate scandal, in which former and current aides to the Israeli premier allegedly received payments to conduct a public relations campaign to cast Qatar in a favorable light for more than a year after the Oct. 7 onslaught.
Now, as international diplomats contemplate Gaza’s reconstruction, they face a version of the same dilemma: how to provide essential assistance without strengthening Hamas or another militant organization. Trump Administration officials, led by envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, are working with Qatar and other Arab governments on a framework that would restore basic services while eliminating Gaza’s dependence on Islamist armed factions. “We want to ensure that the civilians are reliant on themselves and not on anyone else,” an international diplomat tells TIME. “So it’s providing actual opportunities for civilians to make money and be sustainable.”
The question confronting Israel and its international partners is not simply whether money should flow into Gaza, but also who controls it—and whether the next arrangement will avoid the failures of the last.

articles.title: Russian Military Satellite Steers Toward NATO Orbiter Supporting Ukraine
articles.body:
US news and media website Axios reported on Saturday that LeoLabs, a company that monitors potential threats in space, had identified a highly unusual and somewhat concerning maneuver carried out by Russia’s Cosmos 2612 satellite on Friday. The company’s analysis points to a possible deliberate attempt to interfere with US space-based assets, specifically the Finnish ICEYE X36 satellite which supplies imagery to Ukraine and Western governments and is registered at ICEYE’s US branch.
The maneuver saw the Russian satellite reduce the separation to the NATO nation’s orbiter from about 320 kilometers (200 miles) to around five kilometers (three miles) in less than 24 hours. This rapid change in a satellite’s orbit is particularly noteworthy as it uses much of its limited volume of onboard propellant.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Even more worrying, according to unnamed US officials cited by Axios, is that bringing the Russian satellite so close is unacceptable, threatening, and especially alarming given that the objects are moving at around 17,000 mph (27,000 kph) so any error could result in a disastrous collision.
While the move could have an “innocent” explanation, Western analysts consider it more likely that it could involve surveillance or interference of the ICEYE’s output or even in preparation of some form of attack. A direct collision or simple release of an object could severely damage or destroy it. Whilst there is no evidence yet that Russia has malicious intent, the incident highlights the potential vulnerability of commercial space infrastructure whether or not it directly supports military operations.
Russia’s Rassvet Network Threatens Ukraine With Real-Time Strike Control
The US admits to deploying space weapons
According to a BBC report, US Secretary of the Air Force, Troy Meink, announced at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Monday, Sept. 14 that the US had deployed an unidentified space weapon in order to protect it from “evolving threats,” without giving details on the type or capability of the weapon or when it was placed in orbit.
The report cites Dr Bleddyn Bowen, from the UK’s Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), suggesting the US weapon was most likely to have been “some kind of electronic warfare or radio jamming platform” or, less likely, “a kinetic kill vehicle” that would fire a projectile into a satellite to destroy it.”
The US justified its actions by suggesting that Russia and China were already developing programs that would allow it to attack and disrupt Washington’s satellites in a future war.
Russia accuses NATO of using satellites to support Ukraine
On Feb. 1, 2023, the Russian government claimed that NATO’s entire network of satellites was working to support Ukraine’s war effort. In July 2025 the Kremlin complained to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) Radio Regulations Board (RRB) that European nations were using navigation and broadcast satellites for both civil and military purposes to support Ukraine, warning that as a result these were considered to be legitimate targets for Russian countermeasures.
Axios said experts had identified in May this year several instances of Russian satellites “executing a series of concerning maneuvers” around the Finnish craft, which the US military repeatedly warned that Russia was developing anti-satellite weapons.
They suggested that Moscow would seek to disrupt the satellite’s ability to provide high-quality imagery of Russian sites during the war in Ukraine – which could include aggressive space-based actions.

articles.title: Trump defends Russia sanctions relief, accuses Zelensky of rejecting peace
articles.body:
Trump defends Russia sanctions relief, blasts Zelensky on peace
US President Donald Trump on Sunday accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of prolonging the war with Russia, claiming Kyiv had little interest in peace. Trump said negotiations to end the four-year conflict were making “great progress” but alleged Zelensky was reluctant to reach a deal because of European financial support.
US President Donald Trump on Sunday defended his decision to waive some sanctions on Russia, while once again accusing Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky of not wanting to end the war.
"My decision on Russia is a very simple one. I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
The remarks come after Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving broad new sanctions mandated by legislation named for the late US senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Ukraine's defense.
Read moreWho capped Starlink in Ukraine? Musk, Trump and Rubio give three different answers
Trump has also temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel, allowing large quantities to flow into global markets in a bid to lower fuel prices ahead of US elections early next month.
The diesel deal was met with shock by Kyiv and its allies and sparked a feud between Trump and Zelensky that has seen their roller-coaster relationship plummet again.
"Great progress is being made" in talks on the war, "and that includes current hostage negotiations!" Trump said.
"Signing that document at this time will do that, and I can sign it later, or any time that I want!" he said, though it was unclear to what document he was referring.
Asked for more clarity on the statement, the White House did not immediately respond to AFP.
"Perhaps more importantly, Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way," Trump added.
Read moreRubio says Trump to 'analyze' global impact of Russia sanctions during pause
He then reiterated his accusation that Ukraine was purposefully targeting Russian refineries to attempt to hurt the Republican Party in the November 3 election.
Polling shows Trump's party heading for a likely drubbing in the election, with many voters deeply upset by fuel costs, which have soared since the Iran war began in late February.
"Zelensky is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States," Trump said.
"Zelensky doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past, he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," he added.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: US-Russia deal, Trump-Zelensky clash could leave Ukraine out in the cold
articles.body:
US-Russia deal, Trump-Zelensky clash could leave Ukraine out in the cold
Analysts say Trump’s action, including lifting sanctions and tariffs on Moscow, would prompt Putin to continue the war
From US threats to cut off intelligence support for Ukraine to a waiver of tariffs on Russian exports and a diesel deal that could help Russia fund its war, it has been a damaging week for ties between Kyiv and its most important ally, Washington.
US President Donald Trump, frustrated by high energy costs he blames partly on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, has repeatedly criticised Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. A disruption of US-provided satellite internet services raised fears that Ukraine could be vulnerable as it prepares for another winter of Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.
Zelensky responded to Trump’s barbs with an unusually sharp series of public criticisms of Trump, suggesting the US was now favouring Russia. He said Ukraine would defy Trump’s demand to stop striking Russian energy targets, citing Russia’s continued attacks.
Intensifying the discord, Trump waived key US Russia-related sanctions and tariffs on Friday, shortly before they were scheduled to take effect. That prompted Zelensky to say in social media posts that Trump’s action would encourage Russia to continue attacks on Ukraine.

articles.title: Occupied Oleshky Turned Into ‘Death Trap’, Sybiha Says
articles.body:
Russian forces have turned the occupied city of Oleshky in the southern Kherson region into a “death trap,” leaving approximately 1,700 remaining residents trapped under acute starvation, pervasive mining, and relentless drone surveillance, Ukrainia Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned.
In an official public appeal, Sybiha disclosed that the sole overland exit route from the ruined municipality has been heavily mined and placed under continuous Russian drone targeting, rendering escape attempts potentially lethal for trapped non-combatants.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Those who try to flee risk their lives. The adjacent river is also mined. Residents doubt they will survive this winter. The hospital has run out of medicine. Dozens of bodies lie in the streets or in houses, as the Russians forbid residents from burying them,” Sybiha stated.
The foreign minister described extreme shortages of basic sustenance, noting that isolated civilians are struggling to endure on minimal rations while confronting harassment from occupation troops.
“Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, canned goods, and even snails. Residents say that Russian soldiers have threatened them at gunpoint to seize their food,” Sybiha added.
Reiterating that Kyiv has repeatedly pressed for safe civilian evacuations and unhindered humanitarian access, Sybiha issued an urgent appeal to the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and international partners to mobilize every diplomatic and operational conduit to deliver emergency supplies and evacuate those seeking to depart.
Mushrooms and the Autumn Moon
“People cannot survive on statements of concern. They need action. They need a way out. And they need it now,” Sybiha emphasized.
Encirclement and isolation on the Dnipro left bank
Oleshky, situated on the east (left) bank of the Dnipro River approximately five kilometers southeast of the regional capital of Kherson, has been under Russian military occupation since the initial weeks of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The city has been completely cut off from authorized commercial freight convoys and organized institutional aid since late May.
While earlier demographic assessments by Ukrainian authorities indicated several thousand residents remained scattered across the wider river basin, civilian numbers within the municipal core have contracted to roughly 1,700 as conditions have deteriorated ahead of sub-zero winter temperatures.
Local municipal officials have confirmed that central utility grids – including drinking water supply, electrical networks, and municipal gas heating – have suffered significant damage.
With ground logistics paralyzed by dense minefields, destroyed bridge spans, and persistent Russian first-person view (FPV) drone patrols along the riverfront, Ukrainian defense units have intermittently deployed heavy multi-rotor transport drones to air-drop food and medical packages directly into residential yards.
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets previously reported that his office had documented hundreds of verified appeals from civilians trapped in the enclave, noting that residents desperate to flee have attempted to navigate active minefields on foot due to the absence of negotiated humanitarian corridors.
Vatican diplomatic outreach
The escalating emergency in Oleshky has attracted top-level international diplomatic intervention.
On Friday, Oct. 16, Pope Leo XIV held a telephone consultation with Russian President Vladimir Putin to urge an immediate localized ceasefire in Oleshky, calling for verified arrangements to permit emergency food and medical deliveries alongside the safe, voluntary evacuation of non-combatants.
The Vatican confirmed that the pope expressed deep concern over the grave humanitarian collapse in the municipality and pressed Moscow to facilitate unhindered relief operations.
In its official readout of the discussion, the Kremlin claimed that Putin offered what it described as a “detailed explanation” attributing responsibility for the municipal situation to Ukrainian authorities, while expressing general willingness to coordinate with Vatican initiatives.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk has similarly characterized the humanitarian situation in Oleshky as desperate, appealing directly to the Russian Federation to fulfill its legal obligations under international humanitarian law as an occupying power by permitting the immediate evacuation of civilians and allowing international aid agencies unfettered access.

articles.title: Russian drones hit western Ukraine as nationwide attacks kill 10, injure 73
articles.body:
Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least 10 civilians and injured 73 others over the past day, regional authorities reported on Oct. 18.
Russia launched an Iskander-M ballistic missile, 180 Shahed drones, including 26 jet-powered Shaheds, as well as S-8000 and Banderol loitering munitions, also known as Dan-T, and Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, Ukraine's Air Force reported.
Ukrainian forces intercepted 152 drones, including 16 jet-powered drones. Russian strikes hit 20 locations, while falling debris was reported at four other sites.
Three western Ukrainian oblasts came under Russian attack on the morning of Oct. 18, continuing Moscow's recent pattern of targeting critical infrastructure across multiple regions.
In Volyn Oblast, in northwestern Ukraine, Russian drones attacked an industrial facility in the town of Manevychi, sparking a large fire, acting regional Governor Roman Romaniuk said.
Warehouses and production facilities caught fire, with the blaze covering a large area and generating heavy smoke. No casualties or injuries had been reported as of the latest update.
The attack marked the second strike on an industrial facility in Manevychi in three days. An earlier Russian attack on the Agrofrukt LTD facility on Oct. 16 killed one person and injured eight others, Manevychi Mayor Oleksandr Havryliuk said.
In western Ternopil Oblast, Russian drones attacked an energy infrastructure facility near the settlement of Staryi Vyshnivets, Governor Taras Pastukh said. The strike left some consumers without electricity. No casualties had been reported at the time of his statement.
Russian forces also launched a large-scale drone attack on Rivne, in northwestern Ukraine, targeting civilian infrastructure, regional Governor Oleksandr Koval said. The strikes sparked fires at the impact sites. No casualties had been reported as of the latest update.
In Odesa, Russian forces struck the roof of a multistory residential building on the morning of Oct. 18, injuring two people, including a 14-year-old girl, regional Governor Oleh Kiper said.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed seven people and injured 14 others, Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Most of the casualties were reported in Sloviansk, where multiple houses were damaged.
Russian attacks in Kherson Oblast injured 32 people, including one child, regional Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. Russian forces targeted critical infrastructure, social infrastructure, and residential areas across the region.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured four others, regional Governor Ivan Fedorov said. Russian forces launched 10 missiles at the city of Zaporizhzhia. Over the past 24 hours, they carried out 808 strikes on 53 settlements across the region.
In Sumy Oblast, Russian attacks killed two people and injured five over the past 24 hours, according to the regional military administration. Russian forces carried out nearly 50 attacks across the region, damaging or destroying civilian infrastructure.
In Kharkiv Oblast, 12 people were injured in Russian attacks, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Russian forces struck Kharkiv and nine other settlements using ballistic missiles, drones, glide bombs, known as KABs, and a multiple-launch rocket system.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, three people were injured in Russian attacks, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. Russian forces attacked three districts more than 10 times using drones and artillery.
Russian forces again targeted critical infrastructure in the city of Dnipro on the morning of Oct. 18. Information about possible casualties was still being clarified, Hanzha said.
In Chernihiv Oblast, one person was injured when a Russian Geran drone struck a residential yard, regional Governor Viacheslav Chaus said.

articles.title: Iran approves Mehrdad Akhlaqi as minister of defence
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran's new defence minister threatens 'enormous damage' if US attacks
Newly appointed Iranian defence minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi threatened on Sunday to inflict "enormous damage" on the United States and its allies in the Middle East if Washington resumes its military campaign against the country.
"People can rest assured that they will most likely not dare to attack us," Akhlaghi told reporters shortly after securing parliament's vote of confidence. "If they (the US) do, they themselves and the region will suffer enormous damage."
Iran's parliament approved Ketabchi as defence minister on Sunday, ending months of interim leadership and placing a former defence-sector veteran in charge of the country's defence production and procurement apparatus.
Akhlaqi replaces Majid Ebn al-Reza, who took over in an interim capacity after then Defence Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed by US-Israeli strikes in February.
Akhlaqi has spent decades in Iran's defence industry and has held senior roles in its aerospace and missile sectors. The US and EU have imposed sanctions on him over his work in Iran's defence sector.
In a programme presented to lawmakers, Akhlaqi pledged to rebuild the country's military-industrial infrastructure, accelerate defence technology development, and expand cooperation with private-sector companies.
"If the American enemy makes another miscalculation, the response of the valiant Iranian people and the fighters of Islam will be surprising and extensive," he said, adding that Tehran had taken necessary measures to counter the potential use by the US of its "mother of all bombs" against Iran.
CNN reported this week that the US has developed strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known as the "mother of all bombs", against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders renewed combat operations.
The weapon is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal.
"The US President should focus on ensuring his forces are withdrawn safely from our region. If he drops a single bomb, he will have to see how many of his troops end up being carried out of the region in a horizontal position," Akhlaqi said.

articles.title: Zelensky never wanted to end war with Russia – Trump
articles.body:
Zelensky never wanted to end war with Russia – Trump
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky does not want to end the conflict with Russia and probably never did, despite receiving billions in Western aid, US President Donald Trump has claimed while defending his decision to ease sanctions on Moscow.
In a post on Truth Social on Sunday, Trump reiterated his claim that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries had contributed to rising energy prices, hurting American consumers and businesses.
“Zelenskyy doesn’t care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past, he doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did. He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now,” Trump wrote.
He added that Ukraine was “in shambles,” describing its male population as “low, wounded, and/or dead.”
Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports earlier this month in a bid to curb rising energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections. On Friday, he suspended sweeping tariffs targeting major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he was focused on brokering peace between Russia and Ukraine and did not want to “do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.”
Ukraine defied Trump’s demand to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities, launching a drone attack on an oil terminal in St. Petersburg overnight on Sunday and setting it ablaze.
Zelensky said he felt betrayed by Trump, while US media reported that Ukrainian officials had been blindsided by his diesel deal with Moscow.
“I hope that he will change his decisions, because I think that it’s all mistakes, and it will not help us, and it will not help [the] United States,” he told NBC News’ Meet the Press on Sunday.
On Sunday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov suggested that Zelensky had “no desire” to reach a settlement because his government would collapse if Ukraine signed a deal acceptable to both the US and Russia. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Ukraine “cannot alter the course of history” by intensifying strikes deep inside Russian territory.
Russia has long accused Ukraine’s Western backers, including former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson, of sabotaging the 2022 peace talks in Istanbul. Johnson has denied the allegations.
Zelensky, whose five-year presidential term expired in 2024, has refused to call a new election, citing martial law imposed shortly after the conflict with Russia escalated in February 2022. He has since argued that a vote could only be held after a months-long ceasefire. Russia has warned that Ukraine could use a prolonged truce to replenish its military and has offered to suspend attacks only on election day.
Ukraine has been rocked by a series of high-profile corruption scandals since 2025, including an alleged $100 million kickback scheme in its embattled energy sector that implicated Zelensky’s former close business partner Timur Mindich. His government has also faced political controversies, including attempts to curb the powers of Western-backed anti-corruption agencies and the abrupt dismissal of popular Defense Minister Mikhail Fyodorov in July, which sparked protests in Kiev.

articles.title: Putin suggests meeting with Trump, Xi, to discuss Ukraine war resolution - report
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin proposed a meeting with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping next month to discuss ending the Russia-Ukraine war, the Wall Street Journal reported Sunday night, citing people familiar with the discussions.
The talks would not involve Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, an unprecedented move which would be expected to alarm many European countries, WSJ wrote.
According to the report, the Kremlin suggested the three leaders meet on the sidelines of the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which takes place Nov. 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, southern China.
Putin first suggested the meeting while speaking to Trump on October 9, in the same conversation in which the two leaders agreed that the US would buy Russian diesel fuel and facilitate its sale, a former Russian intelligence officer told WSJ.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions over a potential meeting were ongoing.
“There is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place,” he told WSJ.
A senior US official told WSJ that Trump hadn't agreed to the meeting but may be receptive to the idea due to his desire to end the war.
Trump, Zelensky clash over Ukrainian attacks, US sanctions
This comes as Trump and Zelensky publicly criticize the other's decisions, with Zelensky saying on Saturday that Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on its goods days before they were to take effect will embolden Moscow to keep attacking Ukraine, and Trump suggesting that Ukraine needs a new president.
Trump claimed that Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did," in a post on Truth Social earlier on Sunday, calling on the Ukrainian leader to stop attacking Russian diesel refineries.
Neither the White House nor the Chinese Embassy in Washington has commented on the report, but analysts told WSJ that a meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin could advance Xi's ambitions for China's place in global diplomacy.
“China wants to be seen as the pivot of the great powers, and potentially as a mediator between the US and Russia,” Yun Sun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center, a Washington think tank, told WSJ.
However, Chinese officials have expressed concern that the meeting could overshadow China's role in the region at APEC, according to the report.
People familiar with the discussions told WSJ that Xi is also trying to balance support for Putin and economic ties with Europe. A meeting with Putin and Trump to discuss Ukraine could raise the risk of European backlash.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump Envoys Push Russian Gas Transit in Ukraine Peace Talks
articles.body:
US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have urged Ukraine and European allies to consider resuming Russian natural gas transit through Ukrainian pipeline infrastructure as a key economic element of a prospective peace settlement, The New York Times reported.
According to officials familiar with the discussions, the proposal was presented by the Trump administration during high-level consultations with President Volodymyr Zelensky and senior European policymakers.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The initiative has encountered firm opposition across European capitals, particularly in Germany, where officials warn that reviving reliance on Russian hydrocarbons undermines continental energy security.
American negotiators argue that restoring Russian pipeline flows to Europe would provide the Kremlin with a commercial incentive to halt military operations, while generating valuable transit revenues for Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction. Washington also anticipates that sustained inflation and elevated energy costs will eventually prompt European consumers to demand cheaper supplies.
The proposal forms part of a broader, long-term settlement architecture being explored by the White House, encompassing future NATO-Russia relations, post-war security guarantees for Kyiv, and territorial arrangements.
Some Ukrainian and European officials briefed on the discussions suggested that Washington could seek a share of the commercial proceeds generated from the restarted gas trade.
US Tech Curbs on Kyiv Expose Allied Dependency
A White House spokesperson confirmed that the administration’s peace proposals incorporate economic incentives for both Moscow and Kyiv to encourage a durable armistice.
Backchannel references to Nord Stream 2
According to sources cited by The New York Times, discussions between American and Russian representatives have also touched upon the sabotaged Nord Stream 2 undersea pipeline across the Baltic Sea.
One source familiar with the backchannel contacts described restarting intact segments of Nord Stream 2 following a peace accord as the “simplest step” to stabilize regional gas balances.
However, White House officials formally denied that reviving the Baltic pipeline project had been actively discussed in recent engagements.
The gas transit proposal follows earlier economic inducements presented by Witkoff and Kushner during multilateral talks in Miami, which included unfreezing up to $100 billion in immobilized Russian state assets, authorizing a Middle Eastern buyout of Lukoil’s foreign operations, and easing sanctions on Belarusian potash.
German pushback and Berlin security warnings
The prospect of restoring Russian pipeline supplies has provoked decisive resistance in Berlin, formerly the largest purchaser of Russian natural gas in Europe prior to the February 2022 full-scale invasion.
During diplomatic consultations held in Florida, Günter Sautter, foreign and security policy adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, pushed back forcefully against the initiative. German officials emphasized that Russian gas remains Russian regardless of whether transactions are structured through intermediary traders or third-party brokers.
Former German Economy Minister Robert Habeck warned against repeating past strategic mistakes, emphasizing that Germany has fundamentally adapted its energy architecture away from Moscow.
“Europe, and especially Germany, must never again become dependent on Russian gas. We saw how unreliable Russia was,” Habeck stated.
The diplomatic friction unfolds against intense domestic political debate within Germany. The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which has polled near 30 percent in recent nationwide surveys, has campaigned heavily on restoring direct imports of cheap Russian gas to curb consumer inflation and lower industrial electricity tariffs.
German and European officials maintain that restoring energy flows to the Kremlin would undermine European sanctions packages and generate billions of dollars in hard currency that underwrite Moscow’s defense industry, complicating ongoing transatlantic negotiations over post-war security frameworks.

Zelenskyy Says Starlink Restrictions Apply Only in Ukraine While SpaceX Ignores Kyiv’s Inquiries
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused SpaceX of deliberately restricting Starlink satellite communications in Ukraine, saying tests conducted in European Union countries showed that the same limitations did not apply outside Ukrainian territory. He also said the company had stopped responding to inquiries from Ukraine’s Defense Ministry.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking to journalists in a group chat on October 17, Zelenskyy described the restrictions as a planned operation after Ukrainian officials tested Starlink terminals in moving vehicles across EU countries.
The President said Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine remain subject to a speed limit of approximately 161 kilometers per hour (100 mph). The restriction prevents Ukrainian forces from using certain drone interceptors against Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones, forcing them to rely on other air defense systems.
To determine whether the disruption resulted from technical problems or restrictions specifically targeting Ukraine, Ukrainian officials sent several vehicles equipped with Starlink terminals into EU territory.
During the tests, the vehicles traveled at speeds exceeding 180 kilometers per hour (112 mph) where permitted, while their Starlink connections continued operating normally.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine had documented the tests and collected evidence demonstrating that the restrictions applied inside Ukraine but not in EU countries.
He characterized the findings as evidence of a planned operation, although he did not publicly identify who had ordered the restrictions. The President also said Ukrainian military officials and diplomats were continuing efforts to contact SpaceX but had received no response through Defense Ministry channels.
According to Zelenskyy, explanations provided through other channels attributed the disruptions to technical problems. However, he questioned why those problems appeared to affect Ukraine specifically.
The accusations follow reports that SpaceX introduced new restrictions on Starshield, the military version of Starlink, on October 14, without prior notification to Ukraine. The changes reportedly disrupted Ukrainian drone interception, strike operations, and frontline logistics.
SpaceX owner Elon Musk subsequently stated that Starshield was controlled by the US government, while the White House denied involvement and attributed the disruption to technical problems.
On October 15, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported that Starshield connectivity during movement had resumed but said it was still investigating the restrictions.

articles.title: Two officers dead in Saudi recon chopper crash

Two officers dead in Saudi recon chopper crash
Two Saudi Air Force officers died when an AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter crashed in southwestern Najran province, Saudi-led coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki has said. Yemen’s Houthi militants claim they shot it down.
According to the Saudi authorities, the helicopter crashed because of a technical malfunction. Riyadh did not comment on the militant group’s claims.
Separately, the Saudi General Directorate of Civil Defense reported on Sunday that six civilians were injured in a Houthi missile strike on the city of Najran in the same area. Three homes and three vehicles were damaged in the attack, it added.
The militant group, known officially as the Ansar Allah movement, published a video on social media purporting to show the moment of the strike against the helicopter. The black-and-white video shows a glowing object being hit with a projectile, resulting in a major explosion. It is unclear whether the object was a helicopter or whether the video is related to Sunday’s incident.
On Saturday, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree also claimed in a statement on X that the militants shot down a Saudi Apache helicopter near Najran. The post was ridiculed by al-Maliki, who published a photo of several Apaches lined up at an airfield and promised that they “will enter the battlefield soon.”
Najran province borders Yemen and has been targeted in Houthi attacks over recent weeks as violence between the militants and the Saudi-led coalition escalates. A Houthi offensive last month triggered the latest flare up in the civil war, which began in 2014. In a rapid advance, the militants captured the strategic port of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital shipping route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.
The development prompted the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government to launch a counteroffensive to retake the lost territory. The Houthis, an Iranian-backed Shiite group, accused Riyadh of targeting civilians. According to the militants, Saudi forces launched nearly 120 airstrikes in just one day earlier this week. At least 385 people have been killed or wounded by Saudi strikes since September 3, including many women and children, the Houthi health authorities stated.
The group responded by targeting Saudi infrastructure, including civilian airports, using missiles. Last weekend, a strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh left 12 people dead, including four Saudi nationals, and more than 300 injured. Another attack the following day killed a Pakistani national and injured 11 others.

articles.title: Hungary breaks ranks with EU over US-Russia diesel deal
articles.body:
Hungary breaks ranks with EU over US-Russia diesel deal
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar has said that he expects US President Donald Trump to prolong Budapest’s exemption from Washington’s sanctions targeting Russian energy after Trump announced a diesel deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin.
Trump eased restrictions on Russia’s diesel exports following a phone call with Putin last week in an attempt to reduce rising fuel prices ahead of the midterm election in the US on November 3.
The deal faced harsh criticism in the EU, with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni labeling it a “very risky” gamble that could undermine the whole Western sanctions policy towards Russia. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys argued that it “doesn’t help neither the price of oil products nor the unity of the transatlantic community.”
When asked to comment on Trump’s decision during his interview with the outlet 444 on Saturday, Magyar replied by saying that “the US president will make the deals that he wants. On the other hand, this agreement is significant for Hungary.”
Moscow has said that it would immediately release 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 metric tons next month. According to Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak, the fuel will arrive on the US market within 15 to 20 days after the signing of the relevant contracts between the Russian and American companies, which are currently being discussed.
“Hungary has an exemption from sanctions on Russian oil until November. This is extended annually by the Americans. If the US president has concluded an agreement on diesel exports, it would be illogical not to grant Hungary this exemption for at least another year,” Magyar said.
The exemption was agreed between Trump and Magyar’s predecessor, Viktor Orban, who was a harsh critic of Western economic restrictions on Moscow over the Ukraine conflict.
Due to being a landlocked country, Hungary remains heavily dependent on deliveries of Russian pipeline oil and gas. Some 90% of its crude oil in 2025 had been provided by Moscow, according to S&P Global data.
The Hungarian prime minister stressed that he understood that the Russia-US diesel deal was “not welcome from Ukraine’s point of view.”
After it was announced, Vladimir Zelensky lashed out at Trump, calling the agreement “weak” and insisting that the actual reason for the global energy shortage was not Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries as the US president claimed, but the American war on Iran.
Following his address at the EU summit in Brussels on Friday, Zelensky told journalists that “we cannot accept these agreements [between Washington and Moscow]. Because gas deals will follow. And I am absolutely certain of this. After gas, they will lift sanctions on other things as well.”
On Saturday, Trump also signed an executive order to waive “the bone-crushing” sanctions, championed by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham, which proposed 500% tariffs on imports from Russia and 100% tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
White House Deputy Press Secretary Taylor Rogers defended the move, saying that it “provides the president with additional authorities to pursue a peaceful resolution” of the Ukraine conflict. “Enforcing the sanctions provisions now would impede ongoing US efforts to negotiate a durable and comprehensive peace agreement,” she explained.

articles.title: Rubio rebukes Zelensky over Starlink claims

Rubio rebukes Zelensky over Starlink claims
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has rejected Vladimir Zelensky’s claim that Washington ordered restrictions on satellite services used by Ukraine to carry out drone strikes deep inside Russia. The dispute comes amid a public spat between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump over sanctions and strikes on Russian energy facilities.
Earlier this week, Ukrainian officials said SpaceX’s Starlink terminals had suddenly stopped working on drones traveling faster than 160 km/h (100 mph). Zelensky told journalists on Saturday that tests on Starlink equipment in EU countries indicated that the restrictions imposed in Ukraine were “a planned operation.”
When asked to comment on Zelensky’s remarks later that day, Rubio offered a different account.
“I don’t know what Zelensky said. I’m not sure Zelensky knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate,” he told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
“We had nothing to do with it. Nobody in the United States ordered that Starlink speed be slowed down. It sort of happened, but my understanding is it’s been restored. It’s back to where it was before,” the US diplomat said.
Rubio confirmed that Ukraine currently had no access to Starshield, Starlink’s military-grade sister service, but had requested it.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk similarly denied restricting Starlink in Ukraine but clarified that the service must be used for civilian and defensive purposes only, not offensive operations.
The Telegraph, however, reported on Friday that Musk had personally asked Trump to cap Starlink speeds for Ukraine, while Reuters reported that the White House had instructed the Pentagon to slow down Starshield. Trump has denied any involvement and said he did not believe Musk was responsible either.
Zelensky said on Saturday that the Starlink restrictions remained in place. A Ukrainian official told Axios that SpaceX had blamed the cap on “a technical problem.”
Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports earlier this month in an effort to curb rising energy prices ahead of the US midterm elections. On Friday, he went further, suspending new sanctions on Russian oil and gas trade on national security grounds. Trump also sought to pressure Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries, which he blamed for contributing to high energy prices.
Zelensky said he felt betrayed by Trump, who, in turn, argued that the Ukrainian leader was “not a good guy for us to deal with” and should be replaced.

Lithuania drone crash: Ukraine apologizes after air alert
October 18, 2026
Ukraine apologized Sunday after a suspected drone crashed in northern Lithuania, prompting shelter warnings and the deployment of NATO fighter jets.
The incident raised fresh concerns about the spillover of Russia's war against Ukraine into NATO territory, although the drone's origin and whether it carried explosives remained under investigation.
What happened in Lithuania?
Lithuanian authorities told residents in central and northern regions to seek shelter Sunday morning after detecting an unidentified flying object.
Debris damaged a moving civilian vehicle, but no one was injured, national crisis management centre chief Vilmantas Vitkauskas told Lithuanian radio.
Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said the drone probably entered from neighboring Poland. He proposed a joint investigation with Warsaw.
Two Italian Eurofighter jets operating under NATO command were deployed, a NATO spokesperson said. Kaunas said weather conditions prevented visual identification.
Have similar incidents happened before?
Lithuania and its Baltic neighbors have experienced several drone incursions during the war.
Ukrainian drones intended to strike targets in northwestern Russia have previously strayed into Baltic airspace and crashed. Russian-made drones have also entered Lithuania from Belarus.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda described Sunday's incident as another example of the war spilling onto NATO's eastern flank.
Meanwhile, Lithuania said it was treating an attempted arson attack on a Starlink base station near Vilnius as Russia-linked sabotage aimed at undermining Ukraine's military capacity.
National crisis management chief Vilmantas Vitkauskas said Sunday that authorities were searching for suspects who tried to set fire to the facility at about 2 a.m. (2300 GMT Saturday).

articles.title: Romanian F-16 fighter jets shoot down two drones over Romanian territorial waters
articles.body:
Romanian F-16 fighter jets shoot down two drones over Romanian territorial waters
BUCHAREST, Oct 17 - Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the country's territorial waters on Saturday, the defence ministry said.
Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Sunday the drones were likely latest generation Russian drones, flying at speeds similar to fighter jets.
"The ones from last night were flying at 450 km/h, which leads us to think they were Russian-made Geran-4 drones with a turboprop engine," Miruta said. "This is the first time we've shot down drones like these."
The drones were brought down days after two chemical tankers were hit by drones near Romania's Black Sea coast, the latest in a series of attacks highlighting risks to commercial shipping on NATO's eastern flank.
Both vessels were anchored near the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is an export route for Ukraine.
NATO member Romania shares a 614-km (381-mile) border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, and has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Romania started shooting down drones that enter its space earlier this year.
The defence ministry said the two drones entered Romanian waters in the Black Sea on Saturday at 1459 GMT and 1501 GMT, respectively.
"NATO is ready and able to react to any potential threat, 24/7, to safeguard our territory and protect our people," a NATO official told Reuters.
Romania's Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said the North Atlantic Council will have a meeting on Tuesday to discuss Black Sea defence and deterrence.
The two tankers struck earlier this week were hit by Russian drones, a NATO military source told Reuters. Romanian officials are still searching for seven missing crew members.
At least five other cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring Bulgaria in the past two weeks, with 23 sailors reported dead or missing. Most of those incidents occurred outside NATO territorial waters.
In Moldova, on Romania's northeast border, officials said a new drone had crashed in a northern district, near the border with Ukraine. Officials said there were no casualties or damage and specialists were trying to determine the drone's origin.
Five drones identified as Russian fell on Moldovan territory in a little more than 17 hours on Thursday and Friday, prompting the foreign ministry to issue a statement denouncing Russian actions. REUTERS

articles.title: Russia: Huge flames and smoke rise over St Petersburg after drone strikes

Other images showed thick smoke rising from the area of the St Petersburg Oil Terminal, while an oil refinery and depot were also reportedly hit.
