The latest exchange underlines the continuing struggle over energy infrastructure, with both sides treating refineries, terminals and power grids as central targets in a war that shows no sign of abating.

articles.title: Why Ukraine’s freedom-loving Cossacks chose the Russian tsar
articles.body:
Why Ukraine’s freedom-loving Cossacks chose the Russian tsar
On January 8, 1654, drums resounded in the town square of Pereiaslav. Cossacks, townsfolk, and commanders formed a large circle and Hetman Bogdan Khmelnitsky stepped into the center. This was a man who had seen it all: six years of war, stunning victories and crushing defeats, burned cities and villages, and the betrayal of allies. On that day, he offered the people a choice that would shape their future.
He told the people that four figures could potentially rule over them. The first option was the Turkish Sultan – a Muslim who was known to oppress Orthodox Christians in Greece. Then, there was the Crimean Khan – also a Muslim who couldn’t really be trusted since he often betrayed allies. The Polish king was not a viable option, since everyone remembered how the Polish lords had oppressed the population. And finally, there was a fourth option: the Tsar of the East, a fellow Orthodox Christian.
The people responded with a cry, “We want to serve the Eastern Orthodox Tsar!”
The choice between the West and Russia is often considered a recent phenomenon. Yet for the inhabitants of Ukraine, this choice first presented itself 400 years ago – and it was made not by politicians behind closed doors, but by the public in the middle of a town square. Why did these free Cossacks, accustomed to electing their own hetmans and exercising self-governance, choose to serve the Russian tsars? And why did many Cossacks remain loyal to Russia time and again, even when their hetmans betrayed their oath to the tsar?
This week, the Day of the Ukrainian Cossacks was observed, and RT remembers how they first made the choice to join Russia.
17th-century-style Eurointegration
By the mid-17th century, much of present-day Ukraine was under the control of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. And this was far from an appealing image.
The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was governed by the Polish Catholic nobility, many of whom viewed the local Orthodox population as second-class citizens. They referred to Orthodox Ukrainians as ‘bydlo’ (cattle), stripping them of all rights.
The Orthodox population was barred from professional guilds and faced restrictions in holding municipal offices. Peasants were effectively enslaved, while many Orthodox churches and monasteries were seized and shut down. Priests and monks suffered persecution, humiliation, and violence.
The common people lost many of their defenders. Many noble Orthodox families converted to Catholicism en masse – not out of conviction, but to ‘become Polish’. For example, Ieremiah Vishnevetsky, a man from an Orthodox family whose ‘conversion’ was driven by a desire for status and career advancement, became one of the primary oppressors and tormentors of the Orthodox people.
At the same time, the southern territories of what is now Ukraine faced regular raids by the Crimean Tatars, who pillaged border settlements, capturing people and enslaving them. Fleeing from the oppressive rule of the Polish on one side and seeking protection from the constant invasions of the Tatars on the other, Ukraine’s Orthodox population retreated into the so-called Wild Field. In the expansive, fertile steppes stretching from the Dniester to the Don rivers, there was no authority to govern them. These people established their own communities and formed self-defense groups; they became known as Cossacks. Living on the frontier, in conditions far harsher than those of America’s Wild West, they always had their weapons at hand.
The Cossacks launched campaigns against the Crimean Khanate and the Ottoman Empire, but their primary focus was on preserving their Orthodox faith and resisting Polish oppression. Throughout the first half of the 17th century, uprisings frequently erupted across Ukraine, but due to the Cossacks’ poor organization and the superior military training of the Poles, these rebellions were consistently crushed with brutal force.
By 1648, it seemed that the Poles had eradicated all the rebellious Cossacks and subjugated the populace. For the Polish, it seemed like there was nothing more to worry about. However, this was a grave mistake.
Unity of faith
Against the background of the horrifying national and religious oppression raging in Ukraine, the neighboring Orthodox Russian Tsardom presented a stark contrast. At the beginning of the 17th century, Russia had endured a brutal civil war and foreign intervention known as the Time of Troubles. Nevertheless, it had managed to repel external foes and was steadily regaining its strength. This powerful, centralized Orthodox state naturally drew the attention of the Cossacks.
During this period, identity was largely defined by faith, and the terms ‘Orthodox’ and ‘Russian’ were nearly interchangeable. At that time, there was no clear distinction between Russians and Ukrainians; both identified as Russian, viewing themselves as heirs to the medieval state of Kievan Rus’.
While people in the Russian Tsardom and modern-day Ukraine had their linguistic and regional differences, they had a lot more in common with each other than with the Poles. National and religious identities were intertwined, which is why Cossack leader Bogdan Khmelnitsky, in his speech at the Pereiaslav Council emphasized this unity by saying, “We share the same faith.”
However, a shared faith and identity didn’t automatically translate into political decisions. Whenever uprisings happened, Cossack delegations went to Moscow seeking assistance. In 1620, Cossack Hetman Pyotr Sagaidachny wrote to Tsar Mikhail Fyodorovich, expressing the Cossacks’ readiness to serve him. In 1624, Metropolitan Iov Boretsky of Kiev directly appealed to the Russian tsar, asking him to protect the “brotherly people” and to incorporate Malorossiya (literally, Little Russia – one of Ukraine’s historical names) into Russia. But at the beginning of the 17th century, Russia was just recovering from the turmoil of the Time of Troubles and was not prepared for a new war with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, so it responded to these appeals with caution.
Nonetheless, this did not deter the people of modern-day Ukraine. In the 1630s, thousands of Cossacks migrated to the Russian Tsardom, settling along its southern borders. After the defeat of the 1638 uprising, Hetman Yakov Ostrianin led 1,000 Cossacks and their families into Russia. He settled in Chuguev (present-day Kharkov region), where the tsarist government was constructing a new fortress, and helped repel Tatar raids on the southern frontiers alongside Russian troops. Thus, the historical region known as Slobozhanshchina emerged, which encompassed the modern-day Ukrainian cities of Sumy, Kharkov, Izium, and others. Cossacks who served the Tsar settled there, living next to the Russian forces that were stationed in the area.
Ultimately, the unity between the Russian Tsardom and Orthodox Ukrainians was sealed by Bogdan Khmelnitsky.
Free choice
Bogdan Khmelnitsky knew from personal experience the futility of seeking peaceful and respectful relations with the Poles. By age 50, he had a successful military career, numerous campaigns, and years of loyal service to the Polish king behind his back. In 1648, he held the rank of Cossack hundredman (similar to a company commander) in Chigirin. However, taking advantage of Khmelnitsky’s absence, the nobleman Chaplinsky seized his family estate, kidnapped his wife, and assaulted (or, according to some reports, killed) his son. When Khmelnitsky sought justice in the Polish court, he was laughed at. From then on, Khmelnitsky sought both personal and national revenge.
Khmelnitsky sparked a Cossack uprising that quickly gained popular support. As a gifted military leader, he won several battles, decimating the Polish army in Ukraine and capturing its commanders. Following initial victories in the summer of 1648, Khmelnitsky reached out to Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich of Russia, requesting that the Cossacks and their lands be placed “under the tsar’s high hand.” However, accepting the Cossacks as subjects meant Russia would have to engage in war with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, something Moscow wasn’t prepared for at that time.
The next five years of war were incredibly tough for the Cossacks: victories were interspersed with defeats, and their allies – the Crimean Tatars – often betrayed them. The conflict devastated fertile lands and claimed an increasing number of lives. The Cossacks realized that alone, they wouldn’t be able to stand up to the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, then the strongest player in the region. If they were defeated, the Polish nobles would return to Ukraine and exact revenge. Therefore, Khmelnitsky continued his diplomatic outreach to Moscow.
Eventually, the Russian Tsardom recognized that it was ready for a big war. In late 1653, the Zemsky Sobor, a representative assembly, decided to accept the Zaporozhian Host under the “high hand” of the tsar. A large embassy headed by Boyar Vasily Buturlin was dispatched to Ukraine.
In January 1654, a Cossack council convened in Pereiaslav. It was attended by Ukraine’s leaders of the time: Khmelnitsky himself, renowned commanders, colonels, judges, and representatives from 14 of the 17 Cossack regiments.
According to Cossack tradition, however, such a pivotal decision could not rest solely with the elites. So, Khmelnitsky and his comrades went to the town square and addressed the people, who eagerly embraced the news, shouting their desire to be ruled by the “Eastern Orthodox tsar.” The Cossack commanders unanimously agreed to ally with Russia and accepted the Russian tsar as their sovereign.
Following this, Cossack and Russian diplomats traveled throughout Ukraine, and in just the first two months of 1654, over 120,000 people pledged allegiance to the Russian tsar in 183 towns and settlements – a staggering figure considering the logistical challenges of the era. Accounts of those who witnessed these events, both on the Russian and Ukrainian side, reveal that in most cases, Cossacks, townsfolk, and peasants enthusiastically swore loyalty to the Russian tsar, with refusals being exceedingly rare.
The formal incorporation of the Cossack Hetmanate into the Russian Tsardom was sealed by the March Articles of 1654. The Zaporozhian Host found itself under a kind of protectorate of the Russian Tsardom, while enjoying extensive internal freedom. The agreement, ratified by Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich, affirmed the election of the Hetman and Cossack elders, protected the rights and liberties of the Cossacks, townspeople, and Orthodox clergy, ensured the autonomy of local courts and the freedom of tax collection, and allowed the Hetman to establish diplomatic relations with other peoples, except for Poland and the Ottoman Empire. In return, the Russian Tsardom guaranteed military protection for the Cossacks and committed to fighting against the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
At that time, Ukraine enjoyed a remarkably privileged position. Just a short while before, Polish nobles had treated the Cossacks as “cattle,” humiliating and oppressing them. Now, however, the Cossacks had freedom and were backed by the tsar’s mighty army.
But comfort can breed complacency, and some Cossack leaders came to believe that their oaths to the Russian tsar didn’t amount to much.
The Ruin
Three years after the Pereiaslav Council, Khmelnitsky died, and Ivan Vygovsky took over. A man of incredibly flexible views, he initially built his career in the service of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth but later switched sides to become the personal secretary of Bogdan Khmelnitsky.
Vygovsky was a key advocate for joining Russia, yet upon becoming hetman, he reversed his stance and forgot his oath of loyalty to Moscow. Just a year after taking power in 1658, he signed the Treaty of Hadiach with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, which aimed to reincorporate Ukrainian lands into Poland.
However, it soon became apparent that the decision of 1654 wasn’t made solely by the Cossack leadership. Early on, at the stage of negotiations with Poland, figures like Colonel Martyn Pushkar and Zaporozhian Otaman Yakov Barabash opposed the decision to defect to the Polish side and betray their Orthodox brethren. Many Cossacks and townsfolk rallied behind them. For these individuals, returning to Polish rule meant a return to oppression and humiliation. Vygovsky managed to suppress this particular uprising, and commanders loyal to Russia were killed.
After Vygovsky’s open betrayal, however, many prominent Cossack leaders – including those now celebrated as Ukrainian national heroes, such as Ivan Bogun and Ivan Sirko – rose against him. For them, as for the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians at the time, treason against the Russian tsar and submission to the Polish were intolerable.
Consequently, the Cossacks united with Russian forces against the traitors. Notably, in 1658, Kiev was defended from Vygovsky’s troops by the combined forces of Tsarist voivode Vasily Sheremetev and Kiev colonel Vasily Dvoretsky. As the conflict escalated, not only Cossacks but even townspeople and ordinary peasants turned against Vygovsky’s allies. Those who had betrayed their oath to the tsar were often punished or killed by the people.
Pro-Russian Cossacks and Tsarist troops united to inflict a series of defeats upon Vygovsky; he lost power and fled to Poland, where he was ultimately executed without trial, since he was no longer needed. This stands in stark contrast to Dvoretsky, whose descendants remained influential members of the local Malorossian elite until 1917.
This story illustrated that Russia’s influence in Ukraine rested not on fleeting decisions made by individual commanders but on the overwhelming support of the populace. However, at that point, Ukraine plunged into decades of civil strife.
In 1659, Yuriy Khmelnitsky, the son of Bogdan Khmelnitsky, became hetman and signed new agreements with Russia. By then, Russia had begun to grasp the unique political culture of the Ukrainian elites and started to curb Cossack independence. Under the new terms, electing a hetman or making international decisions required the tsar’s approval, and the presence of Russian garrisons increased in Ukrainian cities.
However, soon after signing the treaty with Moscow, Yuriy Khmelnitsky launched a war against the Poles. Having lost this war, he ended up signing another agreement with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
Yet another Cossack hetman had ‘outplayed’ himself, negotiating worse terms with the Poles than with the Russians. As a result, Cossack autonomy was curbed and they were obligated to fight alongside the Poles against the Russian Tsardom.
The Cossack regiments stationed on the eastern bank of the Dnieper river rejected this betrayal, leading to a de facto split of Ukraine into Left and Right Banks. This marked the beginning of Ukraine’s own ‘game of thrones’. Subsequent hetmans and atamans followed a familiar pattern: from declarations of loyalty to Russia to restrictions on Cossack autonomy; from formal allegiance to betrayal and eventual death or exile.
Russia managed to put an end to this chaotic cycle of conflict only by signing the Truce of Andrusovo with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1667, which divided Ukraine along the Dnieper River.
Mazepa’s betrayal and the people’s loyalty
One of the most dramatic tests of the Cossacks’ loyalty to Russia unfolded during the Great Northern War. Russia was fighting Sweden for access to the Baltic Sea, as Sweden was the dominant power in Northern Europe at the time. In the early years, the war proved challenging for Russia, prompting Hetman Ivan Mazepa, who had been in power for over 20 years, to betray his old ally, Tsar Peter the Great, and ally himself with Swedish King Charles XII (whom he believed would emerge as the victor).
In the summer of 1708, General Judge Vasily Kochubey and Colonel Ivan Iskra reported Mazepa’s secret contacts with the Swedes. However, Peter the Great trusted his old friend so much that he dismissed their warnings. Kochubey and Iskra were executed, but once Mazepa’s treachery came to light, they were posthumously rehabilitated; the Kochubey family later received a noble title and several military and state leaders of the Russian Empire were descended from it.
In late autumn 1708, Mazepa finally defected to Charles XII’s side. Notably, only a few thousand people followed him. When it became clear that this was not merely a campaign but outright betrayal, the ranks of Mazepa’s supporters dwindled even further.
The vast majority of Cossacks remained loyal to Russia. They fought alongside Russian troops against the Swedes. Being Orthodox Christians, they could not fathom the idea of siding with the enemies who were, moreover, Protestants. Similarly, ordinary townspeople and peasants stayed true to Russia.
In his first address to the Cossacks, the new hetman Ivan Skoropadsky asserted that “All of Ukraine must be loyal to Moscow, and must not be seduced by the friendship of the Swedes, who, aside from being entirely foreign to Ukraine, are not even neighbors.”
Modern Ukrainian historians tend to romanticize Mazepa as a champion of freedom and independence, but this portrayal is misleading. Mazepa and his circle were simply looking for a new master, driven by a false sense of Russia’s vulnerability. In reality, the people of Ukraine remained steadfastly loyal to Russia and the Orthodox Tsar, with Cossack regiments fighting side by side with tsarist forces during the legendary Battle of Poltava.
From maces to ministerial positions
Following Mazepa’s betrayal, Russia systematically curtailed Cossack autonomy. Despite the unwavering loyalty of the vast majority of Cossacks, the treachery of their leaders became increasingly audacious. In 1722, Peter the Great established the Collegium of Little Russia, essentially a ministry for Ukrainian affairs.
The position of hetman was alternately abolished and reinstated, but the Cossacks’ autonomy was steadily curbed. Those who failed to grasp that times had changed, like the appointed hetman Pavel Polubotok, found themselves imprisoned in the Peter and Paul Fortress.
Concurrently, another trend emerged. Cossack leaders began integrating into the imperial elite, a shift that, for many of them, proved more beneficial than the semblance of freedom.
Alexei Razumovsky, the son of a humble Cossack, arrived in St. Petersburg as a singer in the court chapel and eventually became the favorite (and according to some accounts, the secret husband) of Empress Elizabeth. His brother, Kirill, headed the Russian Academy of Sciences and served as the last hetman. Alexander Bezborodko, the son of a general scribe, rose to become Chancellor of the Russian Empire. Pyotr Zavadovsky became the first Minister of Public Education in Russia. Victor Kochubey, a descendant of the executed judge, served as Minister of Internal Affairs and Chairman of the State Council of the Russian Empire. The list of the descendants of the Cossacks who achieved high office in the Russian Empire goes on and on.
The era of the Cossacks eventually faded into history.
In 1764, Razumovsky laid down his mace. Cossack regiments were transformed into regular hussar and carabiner regiments. The Charter of 1785 equalized the rights of Cossack leaders with those of the Russian nobility.
A century and a half earlier, in 1648, the Cossacks had launched a rebellion against the Poles, fighting for their own rights, laws, and the Orthodox faith. In 1654, they pledged allegiance to the Russian Tsar in Pereiaslav. Later on, many events unfolded: the Cossacks oscillated between Poland, Turkey, and Sweden, yet the majority remained loyal to Russia.
There were numerous reasons for this loyalty. A shared identity and faith made rapprochement with Moscow natural; fear of foreign lords, khans, and sultans united the Cossacks under Russian banners. Moreover, social interests and career aspirations made serving the empire appealing. Some were driven by sincere motives; others acted out of fear or personal gain.
Ultimately, those who remained loyal to the Orthodox Russian Tsar emerged as the winners, exchanging their former unprivileged status for the right to build the empire alongside the Russians.

articles.title: Rubio explains why Trump waived sanctions against Russia, says administration needs time to assess impact
articles.body:
Rubio explains why Trump waived sanctions against Russia, says administration needs time to assess impact
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that President Donald Trump had signed an executive order waiving the imposition of sanctions against Russia under the Graham Act for 60 days to assess how they might affect the US and global economies.
Source: Marco Rubio speaking to journalists, as reported by European Pravda
Quote: "The problem is these sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries – India, for example, and others. And so I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy.
I think when the bill was passed, one of the reasons the waivers were put in there is understanding that they would need some period of time to study this, given all the different things that are going on in the world right now, including the pressure on global energy supplies."
Details: Rubio said that global energy prices have been affected not only by the situation in Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, but also by Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and, supposedly, the war between Russia and Ukraine, "where energy infrastructure is being hit".
He noted that the administration needs 60 days to "take all of that into account and weigh it against each other".
Rubio cited India as an example, saying that the country has voluntarily diversified its supplies but still obtains a significant share of its energy resources from Russia.
When asked by a journalist whether the decision amounts to a gift to Russian ruler Vladimir Putin, the secretary of state said Russian diesel fuel "was going to be sold one way or the other".
Quote: "The diesel that Putin was going to sell, they will make it available to the global market one way or the other. The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get. But this is not unprecedented. If you recall, a few months ago, we also did a 60-day waiver on Russian oil when Hormuz was being challenged."
Details: Rubio noted that conflicts around the world are now interconnected and could therefore create uncertainty in global energy markets.
"So all of these things have to be managed delicately because they're all coming together now. It's not just the Strait of Hormuz anymore. It's what's happening with Saudi Arabia and the uncertainty that that's creating. It's also what's happening between Russia and Ukraine and the constraints that's putting on global energy supplies," he added.
Background:
- On 16 October, Trump signed an executive order waiving the application of sanctions against Russia under the Graham Act. He said the decision was in the US national interest. The deadline for Trump to impose new sanctions on Russia expires on 18 October.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Graham Act could still put pressure on Russia despite Trump's decision not to introduce new restrictions under it for the time being.
- Senator Richard Blumenthal, who helped draft the Graham Act, sharply criticised Trump for refusing to take further steps to put pressure on Russia under the law.

articles.title: Iran to answer 'mother of all bombs' with 'father of bombs': senior IRGC commander
articles.body:
Iran to answer 'mother of all bombs' with 'father of bombs': senior IRGC commander
TEHRAN – Deputy Coordinator of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps, Brigadier General Mohammad Reza Naqdi, has warned the United States against any military miscalculation against Iran, saying Tehran would respond to Washington's "mother of all bombs" with the "father of bombs."
Speaking on Sunday afternoon at the "Self-Sacrificers for Iran" rally in Sari, Naqdi was referring to recent threats by US President Donald Trump to use the GBU-43/B massive ordnance, widely known as the mother of all bombs, against Iran.
"If you make a wrong move, we will come for you with the father of bombs, and all your assets will be at risk," Naqdi said.
He described Trump's remarks as a sign of fatigue and depleted patience in confronting a nation that resists pressure, arguing that the threats reflect the difficulty of dealing with Iran.
Criticizing the threats to use heavy bombs, Naqdi said the enemy had already used heavy weaponry in the past, but those actions had failed to achieve US objectives. He also claimed that parts of the technology used in some of the weapons deployed against Iran are now in the hands of Iranian forces and are under examination.
Warning of the consequences of any military action, he said any miscalculation and escalation could jeopardize the security of US investments and economic activities in the region, including American technology, artificial intelligence and oil companies operating in the region.
On Iran's deterrent power, Naqdi said the country's defense capability in land and naval domains is not limited to military hardware alone, stressing that the will of a people who stand to defend their land is a key element of that power.
"The enemy may be able to take certain actions, but the fundamental question is whether it can achieve its goals. Our defensive readiness and the will of the Iranian people have complicated the enemy's calculations," he said.
He added that US military movements in the region have been affected by Iran's defense capabilities.
Naqdi said such threats may pursue different objectives, including creating division among the people, weakening the resolve of officials and reducing the readiness of the Armed Forces. He stressed the need to preserve national unity, stay vigilant against psychological warfare, and prevent internal disputes.
Maintaining the country's defense preparedness, solidarity between the people and officials, and cohesion of the Armed Forces play a decisive role in countering foreign threats, he said, adding that threats should not cause any doubt in defending national interests.

articles.title: Zelensky: Ukraine has retaken more territory than Russia captured this fall
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces have recaptured more territory than Russian forces have seized this fall, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an Oct. 18 post on social media.
"We are seeing results on the front," Zelensky said, in his evening video message.
The Ukrainian Armed Forces are destroying Russian attempts to launch assaults in Dobropillia, a city in the Donetsk region, while defending their positions in Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia, he highlighted, adding that the "front is strong."
"The trend this year continues," Zelensky said, "Since the start of fall, our warriors have liberated more territory than the Russians have managed to capture. The same was true at other points this year."
Under ‘Operation Vivaldi’ Ukrainian forces have made advances as they pushed into occupied areas of Donetsk Oblast. Ukraine's Third Army Corps unveiled on Oct. 14, that it had retaken another 101 square kilometers in the Lyman sector in Donetsk Oblast.
In total, Operation Vivaldi saw the liberation and return of 16 settlements and 277 square kilometers (106 square miles) to Ukraine, corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi said in a recent announcement.
At the same time, Russian high-ranking military officials continue to present "greatly exaggerated claims of Russian frontline advances that do not correspond to battlefield realities" according to an Oct. 17 post on social media sharing findings from a report published by the Institute for the Study of War, an independent conflict monitor based in the U.S.
Russian forces have lost on average seven kilometers daily thus far in October 2026, the ISW reports, contrary to Putin’s false claim of continued Russian advances.
According to the ISW, the Russian forces make these false claims to present a narrative of military success, "such that Ukraine and its Western partners should capitulate to Russia’s negotiation demands."

articles.title: U.S. resumes intelligence sharing with Ukraine – Zelensky
articles.body:
U.S. resumes intelligence sharing with Ukraine – Zelensky
As reported by Ukrinform, Zelensky said this during an appearance on Meet the Press on NBC News.
“We are very thankful for this. Now it works,” he said.
Zelensky told moderator Kristen Welker that, in the view of Ukrainian officials, SpaceX’s decision to restrict the operation of Elon Musk’s Starlink system was a response to a “message from American government.”
Commenting on President Donald Trump’s statement earlier this week that the Ukrainian leader was “more difficult to deal with than Putin,” Zelensky said he had been “very hones” in his dealings with Trump.
“Maybe it’s not very polite,” he said, but it is “better to have partners who are very open and clear than to have those who are killers, even with a smile on their face.”
Zelensky warned that President Trump’s agreement with Russia on diesel fuel supplies “will strengthen Putin in his will to occupy us.”
Announcing the agreement, Trump expressed hope that it would help address the sharp rise in fuel prices to some extent.
Zelensky, however, noted that the agreement wouldn’t have “a real influence” on oil prices in the United States, as the increase was caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz rather than the situation in Ukraine.
“I don’t know all the reasons why President Trump makes such deals,” he said.
As reported by Ukrinform, with U.S. approval, Russia will immediately supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel to the global market and significantly increase its exports going forward.

articles.title: Russia’s war in Ukraine puts Europe on edge
articles.body:
Talk to Al Jazeera
Russia’s war in Ukraine puts Europe on edge
Fears are growing that Russia’s war in Ukraine could spill over into neighbouring NATO members – and spread regionally.
Some countries would argue it already has – pointing to drone incursions, cyberattacks and sabotage.
European nations say Moscow is targeting Ukraine’s allies to intimidate them. The Kremlin denies the accusations.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski warns Europe should be ready to respond robustly to Russia’s hybrid attacks.
Poland, which borders Ukraine, is home to a NATO logistics hub used for military and civilian support to its neighbour.
The International Centre for Counterterrorism says the country is the ‘primary focus’ of Russia’s sabotage campaign in Europe.
It’s also the country most targeted by cyberattacks, according to research from Harvard, with about four thousand politically motivated attacks per day.
And Poland is on heightened alert.
It’s reported several airspace violations — and authorities say more drone and missile strikes are likely.
Sikorski says that for the war to end Russian President Vladimir Putin would have to admit his original goals are unachievable and that the full-scale invasion of Ukraine was a mistake.

articles.title: St. Petersburg oil site burns as 1,000 Ukrainian drones bite Russia
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone strikes set an oil export terminal ablaze in St. Petersburg Sunday as Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones across Russia in one of its largest aerial bombardments to date.
The attack comes amid deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington , with U.S. President Donald Trump criticizing Kyiv for its strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
One person was killed and five more were wounded in the attack, which sparked fires at both the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the city’s Ruchi oil depot, said local Gov. Alexander Beglov.
A logistics center belonging to Russian retailer Ozon and a data center for local tech giant VK were also targeted, both companies confirmed.
Russia's Defense Ministry said Sunday that its forces had destroyed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agnecy Tass that Kyiv was "resisting" Moscow's invasion, but that Ukraine could not "change the current course of events."
Meanwhile, a woman died and at least two other people were wounded, including a 6-year-old girl, after Russia launched two attacks on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, local officials said.
Two apartment buildings, 18 cars and an educational institution were damaged as a result of the attack, head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration Mykhailo Semikin said.
U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy cease-fire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.
Ukraine confirmed Thursday it had resumed attacks on Russian oil after a three-day hiatus.
Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of his country's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government initially said that it was heeding the cease-fire.
In a post on X Sunday, Zelenskyy said that in the week since Trump’s announcement of an energy cease-fire, Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times.
He also said that in the past night alone, energy facilities in four Ukrainian regions had been attacked and tens of thousands of families were still without power. He accused Russia of trying to cause a blackout.
"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," he wrote.
Zelenskyy also stressed that the war was continuing due to Russia’s invasion – not because Ukraine was defending itself.
"It is Russia that must face pressure for peace to have a chance. Thank you to everyone who understands this and helps," he said.
Trump told reporters Saturday that they don’t know what his decision is yet regarding further sanctions on Russia, despite the executive order he signed Friday night waiving planned restrictions, citing a U.S. national interest.
"We’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out. But it’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world," Trump said at a fundraising dinner at his Florida estate.

articles.title: Zelenskyy speaks with Trump envoys
articles.body:
Zelenskyy speaks with Trump envoys
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke with US President Donald Trump's special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Sunday 18 October.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Details: Zelenskyy noted that he discussed the results of the meeting between the Ukrainian and US teams in Florida with Trump's envoys.
Quote: "Our teams maintain virtually nonstop communication. We are also preparing the next steps in diplomacy. We constantly inform our partners about the real situation with Russian strikes, which do not cease for a single minute and about air defence issues.
A lot here depends precisely on America's position. Ukraine remains ready to work constructively, honestly and towards a real result. I thank everyone in America who supports Ukraine and this particular approach."
Details: Zelenskyy emphasised that "peace comes only through strength and cooperation built on trust".
Quote: "We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America's position is strong and helps bring peace closer. Peace that everyone, except Russia, has been waiting for over the past four and a half years."
Background:
- It was reported that negotiations in Miami between representatives of the US, Ukraine, European countries and NATO on ways to de-escalate and end the war had ended earlier than planned.
- Reuters reported that Witkoff and Kushner have informed the Ukrainian delegation at negotiations in Miami on 9 October that the agreement permitting the export of Russian diesel fuel is part of an effort to bring Russia back to the negotiating table.
- Earlier, Axios reported that Witkoff and Kushner, at a meeting with Ukrainian representatives on 9 October in Florida, threatened to stop providing Ukraine with intelligence due to its refusal to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries.
- Zelenskyy confirmed that Trump's administration warned it could halt intelligence-sharing if Ukraine did not stop striking Russian oil refineries.
- The FT reported that the US proposed that European countries unfreeze some of Russia's sovereign assets and transfer them to an entity controlled by Washington in an effort to revive peace negotiations with Russia.
- According to The New York Times, the Trump administration has proposed that Europe resume buying Russian gas.

Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Newest TOS-3 Dragon Thermobaric Rocket Launcher for First Time, Video
Ukrainian forces have struck Russia’s newest TOS-3 “Dragon” heavy flamethrower system for the first time, using a drone to target the tracked thermobaric rocket launcher approximately 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) behind the front line.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s Third Army Corps on October 17, the strike was carried out by operators of the Muramasa unit, part of the Kraken Unmanned Systems Regiment, during the ongoing offensive operation known as “Vivaldi.”
The Ukrainian military said the Russian launcher was identified after it had conducted a firing mission. Drone operators subsequently located and struck the system, with footage of the engagement released through the corps’ official channels.
The Third Army Corps described the attack as the first reported successful strike against the TOS-3, a recently developed Russian weapon designed to deliver thermobaric rockets against fortified positions and concentrations of troops.
The TOS-3 “Dragon” is the latest addition to Russia’s family of heavy flamethrower systems, following the TOS-1A “Solntsepyok” and TOS-2 “Tosochka.”
Unlike the wheeled TOS-2, the TOS-3 uses a tracked, tank-type chassis intended to improve mobility across difficult terrain while providing greater protection for its crew.
According to specifications shared by the Third Army Corps, the launcher carries 15 tubes for unguided thermobaric rockets and has an estimated firing range of up to 15 kilometers (9.3 miles).
The system is operated by a three-person crew and incorporates additional protective measures, including slat armor and explosive reactive armor intended to improve its survivability against incoming attacks.
Thermobaric weapons use explosive mixtures that generate intense heat and prolonged blast pressure, making them particularly destructive against enclosed positions, trenches, and fortified structures.
The reported strike took place during Operation Vivaldi, an offensive campaign conducted by Ukraine’s Third Army Corps in the northern part of the Donetsk region.
During the same operation, Ukrainian forces deployed unmanned ground vehicles behind Russian positions, contributing to the liberation of two villages and the clearing of another settlement.
Ukrainian units also adapted ground-based attack drones with grenade launchers to engage Russian positions, demonstrating the expanding use of unmanned systems in offensive operations.

articles.title: Trump calls decision to waive sanctions against Russia "very good" for US and "the world"
articles.body:
Trump calls decision to waive sanctions against Russia "very good" for US and "the world"
US President Donald Trump has said his decision to waive sanctions against Russia is "very good" and will be beneficial for both the United States and "the world".
Source: Trump, as quoted by White House Press Pool Reports on X (Twitter)
Details: Reporters asked Trump about his decision to waive sanctions against Russia.
The president said that "a lot of you don't know what my decision is yet".
However, he added that the decision is "very good".
Quote: "It's a very good decision, and it's going to be a decision that's good for the country, and I think good for the world because we're really at a world stage."
Details: Trump went on to mention the war with Iran, which he said is "going very well".
The US president also claimed that his country used to be "dead" but is now "the hottest country anywhere in the world by far".
Background:
- On 16 October, Trump signed an executive order waiving the application of sanctions against Russia under the Graham Act. He said the decision was in the US national interest.
- Senator Richard Blumenthal, who helped draft the Graham Act, sharply criticised Trump for refusing to take further steps to put pressure on Russia under the law.
- On 15 October, 22 Democrat and Republican members of the US House of Representatives wrote to Trump demanding the full and immediate implementation of the sanctions against Russia provided for under the Graham Act.
- Gregory Meeks, a Democrat and Ranking Member of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee, has introduced a bipartisan bill aimed at blocking the US-Russia deal on diesel fuel.
- Kirill Dmitriev, Russian ruler Vladimir Putin's chief economic envoy, called Trump's decision not to impose restrictions on Russia under the Graham Act a "historic moment", claiming that imposing them would have caused "serious damage, primarily to the US economy and global markets".

Ukraine Hits Russia’s Railway Bridge in Bryansk, Blasts Military Supply Depots Across Donetsk
Ukrainian forces struck a railway bridge in Russia’s Bryansk region and several Russian military logistics facilities in temporarily occupied Donetsk region during operations conducted on October 16 and overnight into October 17.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on October 17, the strikes targeted infrastructure used by Russian forces to transport military supplies, store equipment, and coordinate drone operations.
One of the targets was a railway bridge spanning the Unecha River near Sloboda-Seletskaya in Russia’s Bryansk region. Ukrainian military officials confirmed that the bridge had been hit but did not specify the extent of the damage.
The railway crossing is part of the transport infrastructure that can be used to move military cargo. Disrupting such routes could complicate Russian efforts to deliver ammunition, fuel, and military equipment to its forces operating in Ukraine.
Separately, Ukrainian forces struck Russian military supply depots in three locations across temporarily occupied Donetsk region.
The General Staff identified the areas near Novoandriivka, Nikolske, and Mariupol as the locations of the attacks. The facilities were reportedly used to store logistical supplies supporting Russian military operations.
Another strike targeted a Russian unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) command post near Malynivka in Donetsk region. The Ukrainian military did not disclose the type of weapons used or provide an assessment of Russian equipment losses.
Earlier, on October 16, Ukrainian forces targeted a second Russian Mi-28NM attack helicopter in less than a week using a domestically produced VB140 Flamingo interceptor drone over Russia’s Belgorod region. Footage released by Ukraine’s 115th Separate Mechanized Brigade showed the drone approaching the helicopter, although the extent of any damage remains unconfirmed.
